16|⚪ T3 FDE at Anduril|FDE at Anduril|Op.what_it_is: Lattice's Open API is the published, documented application programming interface that allows third-party systems, sensors, and software to integrate programmatically with Lattice -- both consuming data from Lattice (subscribing to entity updates, querying the operational picture) and contributing data or commands into Lattice (publishing entities via the SDK, covered separately, or issuing tasking commands to autonomous assets) -- explicitly designed to be hardware-agnostic so that the API contract doesn't assume any specific vendor's hardware characteristics, only the standardized data and command structures of the Entity Model and Lattice's command abstractions.
16|⚪ T3 FDE at Anduril|FDE at Anduril|Op.why_it_exists: For Lattice to function as a genuinely open, multi-vendor command-and-control platform (as opposed to a closed system that only works with Anduril's own hardware), there must be a clear, stable, publicly documented contract that any third party can build against with confidence that their integration will continue working as Lattice evolves -- this is the Open API's purpose, serving as the formal interface contract underlying the broader open-architecture philosophy (covered in the Lattice OS note) and making concrete, programmable use of the standardized Entity Model (covered separately).
16|⚪ T3 FDE at Anduril|FDE at Anduril|Op.how_it_works:
```
Lattice Open API capabilities (conceptual):

1. Data consumption endpoints:
   Subscribe to real-time entity updates (the standardized Entity
   Model data, covered separately) for a defined area of interest
   or entity type
   Query historical track data for after-action analysis

2. Data contribution endpoints:
   Publish new entities or update existing entity status (this is
   the programmatic interface that the Lattice SDK, covered
   separately, builds upon for sensor integration specifically)

3. Command/tasking endpoints:
   Issue mission tasking to autonomous assets (within the
   authorization and human-in-the-loop constraints appropriate to
   the specific platform and mission type)
   Query asset status and mission progress

4. Hardware-agnostic design principle:
   API contracts are defined in terms of Lattice's standard
   abstractions (entities, missions, tasks) rather than any
   vendor-specific hardware concept -- a command to 'patrol this
   area' is expressed identically in the API regardless of which
   specific manufacturer's drone will ultimately execute it,
   with the platform-specific translation happening at a lower
   layer (as covered in Mission Autonomy's hardware-agnostic
   supervision)

5. Authentication and access control:
   API access is scoped and permissioned (analogous to the role-
   based access control principles covered in enterprise AI
   security) so that third-party integrations only have the
   specific data visibility and command authority appropriate to
   their role and clearance level
```
16|⚪ T3 FDE at Anduril|FDE at Anduril|Op.use_when: Reference the Open API when discussing the concrete technical mechanism that makes Lattice's open-architecture and hardware-agnostic claims actionable for integrators and customers -- it's the formal contract that the SDK, third-party sensor integrations, and Mission Autonomy's cross-vendor supervision all ultimately depend on.
16|⚪ T3 FDE at Anduril|FDE at Anduril|Op.avoid_when: Don't treat 'open API' as implying unrestricted or public access -- as with Lattice OS's open architecture more broadly, API access remains controlled, authenticated, and scoped appropriately to the sensitivity of defense operational data, available to approved integration partners and customers under appropriate security agreements, not a publicly browsable developer API in the consumer software sense.
16|⚪ T3 FDE at Anduril|FDE at Anduril|Op.what_goes_wrong:
- API versioning breaking third-party integrations: as Lattice's capabilities evolve, changes to the Open API's contract (new required fields, deprecated endpoints) can break existing third-party integrations if not managed with the same discipline as the data contract and breaking-change-notification practices covered in enterprise integration material. Fix: apply formal API versioning and deprecation notice periods, treating the Open API contract with third parties as seriously as any production data contract.
- Authorization scope misconfiguration: an integration partner granted broader API access (e.g. tasking authority) than their actual role requires represents a security and operational risk if that access is misused or compromised. Fix: apply least-privilege principles (as covered in insider threat and access control material) explicitly to Open API access grants, regularly reviewing and right-sizing partner access scopes.
16|⚪ T3 FDE at Anduril|FDE at Anduril|Op.real_example: A coalition partner nation's existing battle management system integrating with Lattice via the Open API would subscribe to relevant entity updates for a shared operational area (gaining visibility into Anduril-sensor-detected activity) while also being able to publish their own sensor-derived entities into the same shared picture, all without that partner nation needing to adopt Anduril hardware directly -- the hardware-agnostic Open API contract being the actual mechanism that makes this kind of genuine multi-national, multi-vendor interoperability achievable in practice, not just a stated aspiration.

16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.what_it_is: AIP Bootcamps are Palantir's signature sales and delivery methodology for their AIP (Artificial Intelligence Platform) -- intensive, time-boxed engagements (typically 3-5 days) where Palantir engineers embed directly with a prospective or existing customer's team and build a working AI prototype using the customer's actual data, live, in the room, rather than presenting slides or a generic demo. The bootcamp format compresses what might otherwise be a months-long sales and discovery cycle into a single week, producing a tangible, customer-data-grounded prototype as the direct output, which then becomes the basis for a go/no-go decision on a larger engagement.
16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.why_it_exists: Enterprise AI sales cycles are often slow and abstract -- months of presentations, pilots scoped on paper, and skepticism born from previous AI vendors' unfulfilled promises. Palantir's bootcamp model exists specifically to short-circuit this: instead of asking a customer to trust a vendor's claims, Palantir engineers build something real with the customer's own data within days, letting the working prototype itself make the case for further investment. This mirrors and scales the 'week-1 demo with customer data' principle (covered in Rapid Prototyping material) into a formalized, repeatable, high-intensity sales and delivery motion.
16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.how_it_works:
```
AIP Bootcamp structure (typical 3-5 day engagement):

Day 1: Rapid discovery and data access
  Palantir team meets key stakeholders, identifies 1-3 concrete
  use cases with available data
  Data access established (even partial/sample data) as fast as
  possible -- the team works with whatever can be obtained
  immediately rather than waiting for a lengthy formal data
  access process

Days 2-3: Build
  Palantir engineers (often several, working in parallel on
  different use cases or pipeline stages) build working AIP
  pipelines and applications directly against the customer's data
  Customer's own technical staff often pair alongside Palantir
  engineers, building familiarity with the platform in real time

Day 4: Refine based on stakeholder feedback
  Early prototype shown to business stakeholders mid-week
  Feedback incorporated immediately -- the bootcamp's compressed
  timeline forces fast iteration cycles

Day 5: Final demonstration and next-steps conversation
  Working prototype demonstrated to the full stakeholder group,
  including executives
  Explicit conversation about scope, cost, and timeline for a
  follow-on engagement if the prototype validates the use case

Key success factors:
  Heavy upfront engineering staffing (multiple senior engineers
  for a single customer, for a short but intense period)
  Willingness to work with imperfect data access and imperfect
  data quality rather than waiting for ideal conditions
  Direct executive visibility into the final demonstration,
  shortening the decision cycle for follow-on investment
```
16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.use_when: This bootcamp model is most effective for: complex enterprise sales situations where the customer is skeptical of AI vendor claims generally, situations where a working prototype would dramatically accelerate an internal buying decision compared to a traditional RFP/evaluation process, and customers with genuinely available (even if imperfect) data that can support a meaningful build within days.
16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.avoid_when: A bootcamp-style intensive sprint is not appropriate when data access genuinely cannot be obtained within the engagement window (e.g. lengthy security/legal review required before any data sharing) -- in that case, the discovery and data-access groundwork must happen before a bootcamp can be productively scheduled, or the bootcamp risks producing a low-value, generic demonstration disconnected from real customer data.
16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.what_goes_wrong:
- Bootcamp builds something impressive but operationally disconnected: a prototype built under intense time pressure with simplified or sample data may not actually reflect the complexity of the customer's real production data and integration challenges, leading to overconfidence about how quickly a production system could follow. Fix: be explicit and honest in the final presentation about what the bootcamp prototype does and does not yet address (data quality at scale, integration with production systems, security/compliance requirements) rather than letting the impressive demo imply production-readiness it hasn't actually achieved.
- Customer technical staff burnout from compressed intensity: pairing customer engineers with Palantir's team for a full week of intense building can be exhausting and disruptive to their normal responsibilities if not carefully scoped and communicated in advance. Fix: set clear expectations with the customer's management about the time commitment required from their staff, and ensure it's an explicitly sanctioned priority for that week rather than an unplanned addition to their existing workload.
16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.real_example: A manufacturing company skeptical of AI vendors after a previous failed engagement with another provider agreed to a 4-day Palantir AIP Bootcamp focused specifically on supply chain visibility. By day 4, the Palantir team had built a working AIP application ingesting the company's actual ERP and logistics data, with an AI-assisted natural language interface for supply chain managers to query disruption risk -- a concrete, working result that directly addressed the earlier vendor's failure to deliver anything functional, and became the basis for the company approving a much larger follow-on implementation engagement within weeks rather than the months a traditional sales cycle would have required.

16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.what_it_is: The Discovery, Design, Implementation, Iteration lifecycle is a structured four-phase methodology commonly used by FDEs and AI delivery teams to organize an engagement from initial problem understanding through to a continuously-improving production system. Discovery (understanding the real problem, as covered in the dedicated Discovery note), Design (architecting the technical solution and defining success criteria), Implementation (building and deploying the solution), and Iteration (the ongoing cycle of monitoring, feedback collection, and improvement once the system is live) form a repeatable lifecycle that, unlike a single linear waterfall process, explicitly loops back -- iteration findings often trigger renewed discovery for an expanded scope or adjacent use case, restarting the cycle.
16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.why_it_exists: Without an explicit lifecycle framework, AI engagements risk either skipping critical steps (jumping straight to implementation without proper discovery, a common and costly mistake covered elsewhere) or treating the engagement as a one-time linear delivery with no structured plan for post-launch improvement (despite AI systems needing the kind of evaluation-driven, feedback-based iteration covered throughout this material). This four-phase lifecycle gives FDEs and customers a shared, explicit mental model and vocabulary for where an engagement currently stands and what comes next, making it easier to scope individual phases, set expectations, and plan staffing and budget for each.
16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.how_it_works:
```
Discovery -> Design -> Implementation -> Iteration lifecycle

Discovery (typically 1-4 weeks):
  Stakeholder interviews/workshops, current-state analysis,
  problem decomposition (as covered in the dedicated Discovery note)
  Output: agreed problem statement, success metrics, constraints

Design (typically 1-3 weeks):
  Technical architecture decisions (model selection, data
  pipeline design, integration points)
  Explicit success criteria and evaluation framework defined
  BEFORE implementation begins (evaluation-driven development
  principle, covered in Rapid Prototyping)
  Output: architecture document, agreed scope/SOW, eval plan

Implementation (timeline varies, often 4-12 weeks for an initial
phase):
  Build, test, and deploy the solution against the design
  Includes the POC-to-production progression covered in Customer
  Engagement material, with appropriate scope management to avoid
  creep (covered in Rapid Prototyping)
  Output: deployed, working system; documentation; trained
  customer team

Iteration (ongoing, indefinite):
  Production monitoring, feedback collection (the data flywheel
  pattern), and continuous improvement cycles
  Periodic re-evaluation against success metrics
  May surface new problems or expansion opportunities, which
  triggers a return to Discovery for the next scope increment
  (the lifecycle is circular, not strictly linear)

Lifecycle in practice across a multi-phase engagement:
  Phase 1 use case completes its Implementation and enters
  Iteration; meanwhile, Iteration findings from Phase 1 (e.g.
  'users keep asking about X, which is out of current scope')
  trigger a fresh Discovery cycle scoped to that adjacent need,
  potentially becoming Phase 2
```
16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.use_when: Apply this lifecycle framework explicitly when planning and communicating the structure of any multi-phase AI engagement -- it gives both the FDE and the customer a shared vocabulary for 'where are we in the process' and helps set appropriate expectations for each phase's deliverables and duration, especially useful for distinguishing the open-ended nature of Iteration from the more bounded Discovery/Design/Implementation phases.
16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.avoid_when: Don't force a rigid sequential application of every phase for very small, well-understood tasks where a lightweight version of each phase (a brief conversation standing in for formal Discovery, a quick architecture sketch standing in for formal Design) is proportionate -- the lifecycle is a useful organizing framework, not a mandate for heavyweight process on every engagement regardless of size.
16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.what_goes_wrong:
- Treating Iteration as optional or an afterthought: a team executes Discovery, Design, and Implementation rigorously but treats the engagement as 'done' at deployment, with no planned Iteration phase -- exactly the failure mode covered in iterating from feedback and technical debt material, where systems degrade or fail to improve without ongoing attention. Fix: explicitly scope and resource the Iteration phase (even if lightweight) as part of the original engagement plan, not as a separate, easily-deprioritized afterthought.
- Design phase skipped under time pressure: facing schedule pressure, a team moves directly from Discovery to Implementation without a distinct Design phase to establish architecture and success criteria, leading to the evaluation-after-the-fact problems covered in evaluation-driven development. Fix: protect the Design phase as a minimum-viable but non-skippable step, even if compressed to days rather than weeks for smaller engagements.
16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.real_example: An FDE engagement for a retail company's inventory forecasting AI explicitly structured its statement of work around this four-phase lifecycle: a 2-week Discovery phase (interviews with supply chain planners, current-state analysis of forecasting accuracy), a 1-week Design phase (architecture decision to use a specific time-series model approach, with explicit accuracy targets agreed with stakeholders), a 6-week Implementation phase (building and deploying the forecasting pipeline), and an ongoing Iteration phase (monthly accuracy review against the agreed targets, with findings from month 2 -- forecasts performing poorly for a newly-launched product category -- triggering a scoped mini-Discovery cycle that became the basis for a Phase 2 engagement specifically addressing new-product forecasting.

16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.what_it_is: Deployment Strategist (DS) is a specific role (notably used at Palantir) distinct from the purely technical Forward Deployed Engineer -- a Deployment Strategist focuses on bridging the gap between the technical capability being built and the customer's actual operational workflows, business processes, and organizational change management needed to make that technical capability actually useful in practice. Where an FDE might focus primarily on building the pipeline, model, or application, a Deployment Strategist focuses on questions like: how does this fit into the user's existing daily workflow? What organizational or process changes are needed for this to be adopted? How do we measure and communicate business value to executive stakeholders?
16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.why_it_exists: A technically excellent AI system that doesn't fit into how people actually work, or that requires organizational changes no one has planned for, will fail to deliver value regardless of its technical quality -- a pattern covered repeatedly in this material (POC-to-production handoff failures, stakeholder misalignment, scope/adoption gaps). The Deployment Strategist role exists because this 'last mile' of organizational and operational integration requires a different skill set and focus than pure technical delivery -- business process understanding, change management, and stakeholder communication -- and dedicating a specific role to it ensures it doesn't get deprioritized relative to the more visible technical build work.
16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.how_it_works:
```
Deployment Strategist responsibilities (distinct from, but
collaborating closely with, the technical FDE role):

1. Operational workflow mapping:
   Deeply understands the customer's current operational process
   (similar to current-state analysis in Discovery) specifically
   from a workflow/process perspective, not just a data perspective

2. Adoption and change management:
   Identifies what organizational changes (new responsibilities,
   changed approval processes, new training needs) are required
   for the technical solution to actually be used effectively
   Plans and often directly leads the rollout/change management
   process, distinct from the technical training covered in
   knowledge transfer material

3. Value measurement and executive communication:
   Defines and tracks the business value metrics (often working
   alongside the value quantification/ROI frameworks covered in
   Customer Engagement material)
   Serves as a primary point of contact for executive
   stakeholders specifically on business value and adoption
   progress, complementing the FDE's technical stakeholder
   relationships

4. Feedback loop to technical team:
   Surfaces operational/adoption friction points back to the
   technical FDE team to inform product/pipeline iteration
   (e.g. 'users aren't adopting this because the workflow
   requires too many clicks' is an operational insight that
   directly informs a technical design change)

Collaboration model:
  FDE owns: technical architecture, build, data pipeline quality
  DS owns: operational fit, change management, executive value
           narrative, adoption tracking
  Both roles typically work closely together throughout an
  engagement, with the DS providing the operational/business
  lens the purely technical FDE role may not have bandwidth or
  expertise to cover as deeply
```
16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.use_when: A dedicated Deployment Strategist role (or an FDE explicitly taking on this dual responsibility for smaller engagements) is most valuable for complex enterprise engagements where organizational change management is a significant part of the challenge -- e.g. introducing AI into a workflow that currently has well-established human processes and roles that will need to adapt.
16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.avoid_when: For small, narrowly-scoped technical engagements with minimal organizational change implications (e.g. an internal developer tool with no workflow disruption for end users), a separate Deployment Strategist role is unnecessary overhead, and a single FDE can reasonably cover both technical and light operational considerations.
16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.what_goes_wrong:
- DS and FDE work in silos rather than collaborating: if the Deployment Strategist's operational insights aren't effectively communicated back to the technical team (or vice versa), the technical solution and the operational rollout plan can drift out of alignment, e.g. a workflow redesign assuming a feature the technical team hasn't actually prioritized building. Fix: establish tight, frequent collaboration cadence between DS and FDE roles throughout the engagement, not just at handoff points.
- Value metrics defined too late: if the Deployment Strategist doesn't establish business value tracking until after deployment, there's no baseline to measure improvement against (the same problem covered in value quantification material more broadly). Fix: the DS should establish baseline operational metrics during Discovery, in parallel with the FDE's technical discovery work.
16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.real_example: On a Palantir engagement deploying an AI-assisted claims processing tool for an insurance company, the Deployment Strategist worked separately from (but in close coordination with) the technical FDE team -- mapping the claims adjusters' actual daily workflow in detail, identifying that the proposed tool's output format didn't match how adjusters needed to document their decisions for compliance purposes, and working with the adjusters' management to plan a phased rollout with clear before/after productivity metrics -- operational and change-management work that ran in parallel with, and directly informed, the FDE team's technical pipeline development.

16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.what_it_is: Pre-sales POC scoping and demo construction is the specific discipline of designing and building a proof-of-concept or demonstration during the sales cycle -- before a contract is signed -- intended to win the business by proving technical feasibility and value, as distinct from a post-sale POC (covered in POC-to-production material) which happens after a customer has already committed to an engagement. Pre-sales POCs require careful scoping precisely because they are built under sales pressure (often with limited time and limited data access) while still needing to be credible and compelling enough to influence a purchasing decision, creating a tension between speed/simplicity and genuine technical credibility that must be deliberately managed.
16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.why_it_exists: In competitive enterprise AI sales situations, a prospective customer often wants to see working capability before committing budget -- but building a genuinely working demonstration before any contract exists means the vendor bears the cost and risk of that work without guaranteed return, creating strong pressure to scope the pre-sales POC narrowly and efficiently. Done well, an effective pre-sales POC (similar in spirit to the AIP Bootcamp model, but possibly lighter-weight and used across many sales situations, not just Palantir's specific intensive format) can decisively differentiate a vendor from competitors who only offer slide decks and generic demos.
16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.how_it_works:
```
Pre-sales POC scoping framework:

1. Identify the single highest-leverage capability to demonstrate:
   What specific capability, if proven, would most directly
   address the prospect's stated top concern or skepticism?
   Resist the temptation to demonstrate breadth -- a narrow,
   deep, genuinely impressive demonstration of one capability
   beats a shallow tour of many

2. Negotiate minimum viable data access:
   Even a small, representative sample of the prospect's actual
   data (rather than generic public data) dramatically increases
   credibility (the same principle as the week-1 demo with
   customer data, covered in Rapid Prototyping)
   Pre-sales data access often requires a specific NDA/limited-
   purpose data sharing agreement -- factor this legal/procurement
   step into the timeline

3. Time-box ruthlessly:
   Pre-sales POCs typically must be built in days, not weeks,
   given sales cycle pressure and the unpaid nature of the work
   Scope explicitly to what's achievable in the available time
   rather than over-promising and under-delivering at the
   critical demo moment

4. Build the demo narrative, not just the technical artifact:
   The demonstration must be structured to walk a non-technical
   buyer through a clear, relatable problem -> solution -> value
   story, not just show raw technical output (mirroring the
   technical-to-non-technical communication principles covered
   elsewhere)

5. Plan for the live-demo failure contingency:
   As covered in Rapid Prototyping's week-1 demo material, always
   have a recorded backup and a tested fallback path -- a pre-
   sales demo failure in front of a key decision-maker can be
   sales-fatal
```
16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.use_when: Invest deliberate scoping discipline in pre-sales POCs for any competitive enterprise sales situation where a prospect explicitly wants to see proof before committing budget, and especially where competitors are also offering pre-sales demonstrations -- a well-scoped, narrow, genuinely working demo is a strong differentiator in this context.
16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.avoid_when: Don't invest heavily in an elaborate pre-sales POC for a deal where the actual blocker is not technical credibility but something else (budget approval timing, a competing internal priority, a relationship/trust issue) -- building an impressive technical demo doesn't solve a non-technical blocker, and the investment should be redirected toward whatever the actual obstacle is.
16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.what_goes_wrong:
- Pre-sales POC sets unrealistic expectations for the funded engagement: an impressive but narrowly-scoped pre-sales demo (built with hand-picked favorable data and unlimited engineer attention for a few days) can create an expectation that the full funded engagement will progress at the same speed and quality, when production-scale data and real organizational constraints make this unrealistic. Fix: explicitly and honestly communicate, as part of the pre-sales conversation, what the demo does and doesn't represent about the timeline and complexity of a full production engagement.
- Sunk cost pressure to win deals with disproportionate pre-sales investment: if pre-sales POC effort isn't tracked and evaluated for ROI (win rate, deal size justifying the investment), a sales organization can over-invest engineering time in unlikely-to-close deals. Fix: apply selection criteria (deal size, genuine technical fit, competitive situation) before committing significant pre-sales engineering resources to a specific opportunity.
16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.real_example: In a competitive sales situation for an enterprise document analysis AI platform, the vendor's sales engineering team negotiated access to a small, representative sample of the prospect's actual contract documents under a limited-purpose NDA, and built a narrowly-scoped 3-day pre-sales POC demonstrating accurate extraction of five specific contract clause types the prospect had identified as their top pain point -- rather than attempting to demonstrate the platform's full breadth of capability, this narrow, deep, real-data demonstration directly addressed the prospect's stated skepticism and became the decisive factor in winning the deal over a competitor who had only presented generic marketing demos.

16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.what_it_is: Working backwards from customer pain, using the Amazon PR/FAQ (Press Release / Frequently Asked Questions) methodology, is a product development and planning technique originating at Amazon where a team writes the press release announcing a not-yet-built product or feature, along with an FAQ addressing likely customer and internal questions, before any significant building begins -- forcing the team to articulate the customer benefit and value proposition in concrete, customer-facing language from the very start, rather than starting from a technical capability and working forward to find a use for it. Applied to FDE and AI engagements, this means starting any scoping or solution design exercise by writing what the customer would say about the finished result, then working backwards to determine what must be built to make that statement true.
16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.why_it_exists: Technical teams (including AI/FDE teams) have a natural tendency to start from 'what can we build with this technology' and work forward to find a use case, which frequently produces technically impressive solutions that don't actually address a real customer need (the wrong-problem failure mode covered extensively in Discovery material). Working backwards from a customer-facing articulation of value forces explicit clarity about the actual benefit before any technical commitment is made, surfacing whether the planned solution genuinely addresses real customer pain or is solving a more comfortable but less valuable technical problem.
16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.how_it_works:
```
PR/FAQ structure applied to an AI engagement:

Press Release (written as if the solution is already live):
  Headline: customer-facing benefit, not technical description
    Good: 'Claims adjusters now resolve routine claims in under
          10 minutes instead of 45'
    Bad: 'We deployed a RAG pipeline with vector search over
         claims documentation'
  Opening paragraph: who benefits and how, in plain language
  Customer quote (hypothetical but grounded in real discovery
  conversations): what would an actual end user genuinely say
  about this if it worked as intended?
  Summary of how the solution achieves this (kept brief and
  non-technical at this stage)

FAQ (anticipating real questions):
  External-facing questions:
    'How does this handle [specific edge case stakeholders raised
    in discovery]?'
    'What happens when the AI is uncertain?'
  Internal-facing questions:
    'What's the biggest technical risk to delivering this?'
    'What data do we need that we don't currently have access to?'
    'How will we know if this actually worked, 3 months in?'

Working backwards from the PR/FAQ:
  Once the customer-facing value statement is agreed (often
  through iteration with stakeholders -- 'does this PR actually
  match what you'd want to be true?'), the team works backwards:
  what technical architecture, what data, what evaluation
  framework would actually be required to make this PR true?
  This becomes the input to the Design phase of the broader
  Discovery-Design-Implementation-Iteration lifecycle

Value of the exercise:
  If the team struggles to write a compelling, honest PR/FAQ for
  a proposed technical approach, that's a strong signal the
  approach may not address genuine customer value -- better to
  discover this on paper in an afternoon than after months of
  building
```
16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.use_when: Use the PR/FAQ exercise at the start of scoping any significant new AI initiative or feature, particularly when there's a risk of the team gravitating toward an interesting technical approach without first confirming it addresses genuine, articulable customer value -- it's a fast, low-cost way to pressure-test a proposed direction before committing engineering time.
16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.avoid_when: Don't apply a full, formal PR/FAQ writing exercise for small, well-understood, incremental work where the customer value is already obvious and uncontested -- reserve this technique for genuinely new initiatives or significant scope decisions where the value proposition needs to be explicitly clarified and tested.
16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.what_goes_wrong:
- PR/FAQ written to justify a predetermined technical solution rather than genuinely explore customer value: if a team has already decided what they want to build and writes the PR/FAQ to retroactively justify it, the exercise loses its value as a genuine check on direction. Fix: write the PR/FAQ before settling on a specific technical approach, ideally informed by real discovery conversations with actual customers/users (as covered in the Discovery and workshop facilitation material) rather than internal assumptions about what customers want.
- FAQ section treated as a formality rather than genuinely interrogated: skipping past hard questions in the FAQ (or not including them at all) defeats the purpose of using this technique to surface risk and uncertainty early. Fix: explicitly include the hardest, most uncomfortable internal questions in the FAQ (biggest risks, biggest unknowns) rather than only the easy, flattering ones.
16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.real_example: An FDE team considering whether to build a complex multi-agent AI system for a logistics customer's exception-handling workflow first wrote a PR/FAQ describing the intended outcome in customer terms: 'Logistics coordinators receive proactive alerts about likely delivery delays 24 hours before they would otherwise notice, with a recommended resolution already drafted.' Working backwards from this, the team realized the actual bottleneck wasn't sophisticated agent reasoning at all, but rather a much simpler proactive alerting and early-warning data pipeline that didn't require complex multi-agent orchestration -- a significant simplification in technical approach that the PR/FAQ exercise surfaced before any unnecessary complexity was built, directly applying the 'choosing the simplest working solution' principle covered in Rapid Prototyping material.

16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.what_it_is: Land-and-expand is an account growth strategy where an FDE engagement deliberately starts with a narrow, well-scoped initial use case (the 'land') -- chosen for high likelihood of clear, demonstrable success -- and then uses that initial success as the foundation and credibility base for expanding into additional use cases, departments, or broader scope within the same customer organization (the 'expand'), rather than attempting to address an organization's full AI ambition in a single large, high-risk initial engagement.
16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.why_it_exists: Large, ambitious initial AI engagements carry significant risk: more can go wrong, stakeholder alignment is harder to achieve across a broad scope, and the time to any demonstrable value is longer (delaying the trust-building that subsequent work depends on). Land-and-expand exists because a narrow, successful initial engagement de-risks the relationship for both the customer (who sees concrete value before committing further budget) and the vendor/FDE team (who builds genuine organizational credibility, internal champions, as covered in the dedicated champion-building note, and deep understanding of the customer's environment before taking on more ambitious scope).

16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.use_when: Apply land-and-expand strategy by default for new customer relationships, especially large enterprise accounts where a big-bang, organization-wide initial engagement would carry excessive risk and where building credibility through demonstrated narrow success is likely to unlock significantly more total scope over time than attempting to win it all upfront.
16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.avoid_when: For situations where a customer has already done extensive internal validation and explicitly wants and is prepared to fund a larger initial scope (with appropriate risk mitigation in place, such as phased milestones within that larger engagement), forcing an artificially narrow land phase may unnecessarily slow down a relationship the customer is ready to move faster on -- match the strategy to the actual customer readiness, not a rigid playbook.
16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.what_goes_wrong:

16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.what_it_is: Customer enablement focused on power users is a specific knowledge-transfer strategy (related to but distinct from the broader training customer teams material) that identifies and deeply trains a small group of especially capable, motivated end users -- 'power users' -- within the customer organization to become self-sufficient at configuring, extending, and troubleshooting an AI tool for their own and their colleagues' needs, without requiring ongoing FDE or vendor involvement for routine extensions and adjustments. This differs from training the broader end-user population (who need to know how to use the tool) by specifically building deeper, semi-technical capability in a smaller group who can then support the wider user base and handle configuration tasks that would otherwise require vendor involvement.
16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.why_it_exists: Many AI tools (Genie Spaces, AIP applications, custom internal assistants) have configuration surfaces -- adding new data sources, tuning prompts or trusted examples, adjusting business rules -- that don't require full software engineering skill but do require more depth than a typical end user needs. Without identifying and training power users specifically for this layer, every such configuration change becomes a vendor/FDE dependency, creating both a bottleneck (the vendor isn't always immediately available) and an unsustainable long-term support burden. Power-user enablement creates a self-sufficient tier between 'casual end user' and 'full technical engineering team' that can handle the bulk of ongoing day-to-day configuration needs independently.
16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.how_it_works:

   Look for end users who already show above-average engagement
   and curiosity with the tool (similar identification criteria
   to internal champions, covered separately, but focused

   organizational influence)
   Often 1-3 power users per department/team using the tool

2. Deeper, configuration-focused training:
   Beyond standard end-user training, power users learn:

   (mirroring the hands-on lab design principles covered in
   Workshop Facilitation material)

3. Train-the-trainer extension:
   Power users are often also explicitly trained to train and
   support other end users in their department, multiplying the
   reach of the initial enablement investment beyond just the
   power users themselves

4. Ongoing support tiering:
   Tier 1 (power users): handle routine configuration, common
   troubleshooting, training new end users in their area
   Tier 2 (customer's technical team or remaining FDE support):
   handle genuine technical issues, new integrations, or
   significant new capability development
   This tiering dramatically reduces how often Tier 2/vendor
   involvement is actually needed for day-to-day operation
```
16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.use_when: Invest in power-user enablement for any AI tool with an ongoing configuration surface (new data sources, business rule adjustments, prompt/example tuning) that end users will realistically need updated over time -- particularly valuable for tools deployed broadly across many departments or teams, where a single central technical team cannot realistically handle every department's configuration needs without becoming a severe bottleneck.
16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.avoid_when: For tools with a genuinely static configuration (set once, rarely if ever needs adjustment) or for very small deployments with only a handful of total users, a dedicated power-user program is unnecessary overhead -- standard end-user training plus access to the core technical team for the rare configuration need is sufficient.
16|🔴 T1 Customer Engagement & Delivery|C.what_goes_wrong:
- Power users given configuration access without adequate guardrails: if power users can make configuration changes that affect other users or introduce quality regressions (e.g. editing a shared prompt template used by the whole organization) without any review process, well-intentioned changes can cause unexpected problems. Fix: implement appropriate guardrails (e.g. a review/approval step for changes affecting shared resources, similar to the CI/CD eval-gating principles covered in CI/CD for AI) proportional to the blast radius of what power users can change.
- Power user turnover creates a knowledge gap: if a program relies on one or two specific individuals without building redundancy or documentation, losing that person (role change, departure) recreates the original dependency problem the program was meant to solve. Fix: train multiple power users per area where feasible, and maintain documentation of configuration patterns (not just tacit knowledge in the power user's head) so the capability survives individual turnover.

16|🔴 T1 Rapid Prototyping|Rapid Prototyp.what_it_is: MVP-first (Minimum Viable Product first) is the discipline of identifying and building the smallest possible version of a solution that genuinely demonstrates value to a customer or stakeholder, within days rather than weeks -- deliberately stripping away every feature, polish element, and edge-case handling that isn't strictly necessary to prove the core concept works. Applied to FDE/AI engagements, this means resisting the urge to build a 'complete' solution before showing anything, and instead asking 'what is the absolute smallest thing I could build that would let a stakeholder say yes, this actually works' and building exactly that first.
16|🔴 T1 Rapid Prototyping|Rapid Prototyp.why_it_exists: Teams (especially capable, ambitious engineering teams) have a strong natural pull toward building more complete, more robust, more feature-rich solutions before showing anything to a customer -- but this delays the moment of real validation (does this actually solve the customer's problem?) and risks investing significant effort in a direction that turns out to be wrong. MVP-first exists to compress the time-to-validation as much as possible, directly applying the broader 'choosing the simplest working solution' and 'week-1 demo with customer data' principles to the very first deliverable of an engagement specifically.
16|🔴 T1 Rapid Prototyping|Rapid Prototyp.how_it_works:
```
MVP-first scoping exercise:

1. Start from the PR/FAQ or discovery output (what does success
   actually look like to the customer?)

2. Strip aggressively:
   What is the ONE thing that, if it worked, would make the
   customer say 'yes, this is real, keep going'?
   Remove: authentication, polished UI, error handling for rare
   edge cases, support for anything beyond the single core
   workflow, configurability/flexibility for hypothetical future
   needs
   Keep: just enough to demonstrate the core value proposition
   end-to-end on real (or realistic) data

3. Time-box to days, not weeks:
   If the scoped MVP can't be built in days, it's not minimal
   enough -- cut further rather than extending the timeline

4. Validate before extending:
   Show the MVP to the relevant stakeholder/user as soon as it
   exists, even in rough form, and use their reaction to decide
   what to build next -- rather than building a second feature
   before validating the first

Example MVP scoping for a document Q&A tool:
  Full vision: multi-document upload, user accounts, conversation
  history, citation highlighting, mobile-responsive UI, admin
  configuration panel
  MVP: a single Python script that takes one hardcoded document
  and answers questions about it via command line -- nothing
  else -- built and validated against real content in an afternoon
  before any UI or infrastructure work begins
```
16|🔴 T1 Rapid Prototyping|Rapid Prototyp.use_when: Apply MVP-first thinking at the very start of any new engagement or new feature within an engagement, especially when stakeholder confidence or buy-in is still being established and the cost of building the wrong thing (in time, and in stakeholder patience) is high.
16|🔴 T1 Rapid Prototyping|Rapid Prototyp.avoid_when: Don't apply MVP-first stripping to safety-critical or compliance-critical aspects of a system even in an early prototype -- if the eventual production use case involves PII or regulated decisions, even the MVP needs basic, appropriate safeguards (this is a different concern from feature completeness, and shouldn't be cut for speed).
16|🔴 T1 Rapid Prototyping|Rapid Prototyp.what_goes_wrong:
- MVP scoped so narrowly it fails to actually demonstrate the real value proposition: cutting too aggressively can produce something so minimal that it doesn't actually let stakeholders evaluate whether the core idea works (e.g. a Q&A demo using a single trivial document that doesn't represent the real complexity of the customer's actual corpus). Fix: the MVP must still be 'real' enough on the dimension that matters most for validation -- if the core risk is 'will this work on our messy real documents', the MVP must use real messy documents, even if it strips everything else.
- Teams treat the MVP as throwaway and rebuild from scratch later, wasting the initial investment: if the MVP's code is built with zero consideration for what comes next, useful learnings (and sometimes usable code) get discarded unnecessarily. Fix: build the MVP fast but not carelessly -- keep it simple enough to discard if wrong, but don't introduce gratuitous technical shortcuts that would need pure rework even if the direction is validated as correct.
16|🔴 T1 Rapid Prototyping|Rapid Prototyp.real_example: An FDE engagement scoping an AI-assisted insurance claims triage tool initially considered a full web application with role-based access, a dashboard, and configurable routing rules. Instead, the team built an MVP in two days: a command-line script that took a claim description as input and printed a triage recommendation, run against 20 real historical claims the team had been given informal access to. Showing this rough but real-data-grounded result to the claims manager in week one validated the core triage logic's accuracy was promising, which justified the subsequent investment in a proper web interface and broader integration -- investment that would have been much riskier to commit to without first validating the core concept this cheaply and quickly.

16|🔴 T1 Rapid Prototyping|Rapid Prototyp.what_it_is: Streamlit, Gradio, and Dash are three popular Python frameworks for rapidly building interactive web-based demo and prototype user interfaces directly from Python code, without requiring separate frontend development skills (HTML/CSS/JavaScript) or a dedicated frontend engineer. Streamlit converts a linear Python script into a reactive web app where widgets (text inputs, sliders, file uploaders) automatically trigger re-execution; Gradio is similarly simple but particularly optimized for ML model demos (especially well-suited to image/audio/video inputs and side-by-side model comparisons, and widely used for HuggingFace Spaces); Dash (from Plotly) offers more granular control over layout and interactivity at the cost of slightly more code, making it popular for more sophisticated internal analytics dashboards built by data teams.
16|🔴 T1 Rapid Prototyping|Rapid Prototyp.why_it_exists: FDEs and data scientists frequently need to demonstrate a working capability to non-technical stakeholders quickly, but don't always have a frontend engineer available, and building a full custom web application takes far longer than the demo's urgency allows. These frameworks exist specifically to close that gap: a data scientist or FDE who can write Python can produce an interactive, shareable web interface in under an hour, dramatically lowering the barrier to the kind of 'real, interactive demo' that builds stakeholder trust far more effectively than a static slide deck or a script run from the command line.
16|🔴 T1 Rapid Prototyping|Rapid Prototyp.how_it_works:
```python
# Streamlit: simplest option, reactive script-to-app model
import streamlit as st

st.title('Claims Triage Demo')
claim_text = st.text_area('Paste claim description')
if st.button('Triage'):
    result = triage_model.predict(claim_text)
    st.write(f'Recommended priority: {result["priority"]}')
    st.write(f'Reasoning: {result["reasoning"]}')
# Run: streamlit run app.py -- opens a local web server instantly

# Gradio: similarly simple, strong for ML model demos with rich
# input/output types (images, audio) and built-in sharing
import gradio as gr

def triage(claim_text):
    result = triage_model.predict(claim_text)
    return result['priority'], result['reasoning']

demo = gr.Interface(
    fn=triage,
    inputs=gr.Textbox(label='Claim description'),
    outputs=[gr.Textbox(label='Priority'), gr.Textbox(label='Reasoning')]
)
demo.launch(share=True)  # share=True generates a temporary public URL

# Dash: more code, but finer layout control -- better for more
# complex internal dashboards combining multiple charts/tables
import dash
from dash import dcc, html

app = dash.Dash(__name__)
app.layout = html.Div([
    dcc.Input(id='claim-input', type='text'),
    html.Button('Triage', id='triage-button'),
    html.Div(id='result-output')
])
# Requires explicit callback wiring (more verbose than Streamlit/
# Gradio, but more control over exactly how components interact)
```
16|🔴 T1 Rapid Prototyping|Rapid Prototyp.use_when: Use Streamlit or Gradio for fast, low-effort demo construction in the first days of an engagement (the week-1 demo and MVP-first principles covered elsewhere) -- Gradio specifically when the demo centers on rich media inputs/outputs or needs simple public sharing; Dash when building a more involved internal analytics-style interface where layout control matters more than build speed.
16|🔴 T1 Rapid Prototyping|Rapid Prototyp.avoid_when: Don't use these frameworks for production, customer-facing applications at scale -- as covered in Databricks Apps and deployment infrastructure material, Streamlit and Gradio in particular are not designed for high-concurrency production traffic and lack the security/customization control a real production frontend requires; they are demo and internal-tool frameworks, not production web application frameworks.
16|🔴 T1 Rapid Prototyping|Rapid Prototyp.what_goes_wrong:
- Demo-quality prototype mistaken for production-ready: because these frameworks make it so easy to produce something that looks polished, stakeholders sometimes assume the demo is much closer to production-ready than it actually is. Fix: be explicit in framing the demo ('this is a prototype interface to validate the underlying capability, not the production UI') to manage expectations about what still needs to be built.
- Gradio's `share=True` public URL exposes sensitive data: the convenient public sharing link in Gradio, useful for quick remote demos, can inadvertently expose a demo running against real (potentially sensitive) customer data to anyone with the link. Fix: never use public sharing links for demos involving real customer or sensitive data -- use authenticated, properly access-controlled hosting even for early-stage demos in these cases.
16|🔴 T1 Rapid Prototyping|Rapid Prototyp.real_example: An FDE building a week-1 credibility demo (covered in the dedicated note) for a legal document analysis use case used Streamlit specifically because it allowed building a functional, interactive interface -- file upload, question input, answer display with source citation -- in under two hours, letting the legal team interact with and stress-test the underlying RAG pipeline themselves during the demo session rather than just watching the FDE run pre-selected examples from a terminal, which produced much richer, more credible stakeholder feedback than a static demonstration would have.

Retool is the more established, commercially mature commercial product with broader integration support; Appsmith is a popular open-source alternative offering similar drag-and-drop capability with the option for self-hosting, appealing to teams with stronger data sovereignty or cost-sensitivity requirements.
16|🔴 T1 Rapid Prototyping|Rapid Prototyp.why_it_exists: Many of the internal tools an FDE or AI team needs to build during an engagement -- an annotation review queue, an admin panel for managing a knowledge base, a dashboard showing eval metrics -- don't require the flexibility of a fully custom application, but building even a 'simple' custom internal tool from scratch (frontend, backend API, auth, deployment) takes meaningfully longer than the urgency of an FDE engagement allows. Retool and Appsmith exist specifically to compress this internal tooling build time from days/weeks down to hours, letting an FDE focus engineering effort on the actual AI/data problem rather than on internal tooling plumbing.

Retool/Appsmith typical workflow:

1. Connect a data source:

16|🔴 T1 Rapid Prototyping|Rapid Prototyp.what_it_is: Synthetic data generation with LLMs is the practice of using large language models themselves to generate realistic-looking but artificial data -- example documents, customer records, conversation transcripts, support tickets -- for use in demos, testing, and prototyping when real customer data is not yet available (due to data access delays, privacy restrictions, or simply not yet having a specific customer to build against), or when additional volume or diversity of test data is needed beyond what a limited real dataset provides. This differs from earlier rule-based synthetic data libraries (covered in the next note) in that LLM-generated synthetic data can be far more realistic, varied, and contextually appropriate, since the LLM can generate plausible domain-specific content based on a description of what's needed rather than following rigid templates.
16|🔴 T1 Rapid Prototyping|Rapid Prototyp.why_it_exists: Real customer data access often lags behind the start of an engagement (legal review, security clearance, simple scheduling delays), but an FDE often needs to start building and demonstrating capability immediately to maintain engagement momentum (the week-1 demo principle). LLM-generated synthetic data exists to bridge this gap -- producing realistic-enough example data to build and show an initial capability before real data access is available, or to supplement real data with additional volume/diversity for testing edge cases that may be underrepresented in a limited real sample.

B2B SaaS company that sells project management software. Include
a mix of: billing questions, feature requests, bug reports, and
integration issues. Vary the tone (frustrated, neutral, confused)
and length. Format as JSON with fields: subject, body, category.'''

    model='claude-sonnet-4-6',
    max_tokens=2000,
    messages=[{'role': 'user', 'content': prompt}]
)
synthetic_tickets = json.loads(response.content[0].text)

# real customer ticket data access is available

  Be specific about the domain and realistic constraints in the
  generation prompt (industry jargon, realistic error patterns,
  plausible edge cases) rather than generic placeholder content
  Generate a diverse mix deliberately (don't let the LLM default
  to only 'easy' or stereotypical examples) -- explicitly request
  edge cases and unusual phrasings

  demo/documentation, and never present synthetic-data results as

Fix: explicitly prompt for realistic imperfection (typos, incomplete information, ambiguous phrasing) when generating synthetic data intended to stress-test a system, not just to produce a clean-looking demo.
- Synthetic data inadvertently mirrors training data patterns the model has memorized, masking real capability gaps: because the synthetic data is itself LLM-generated, a model being evaluated against LLM-generated synthetic test cases may perform suspiciously well in ways that don't reflect genuine task capability. Fix: treat synthetic-data evaluation results as directional and provisional only, always re-validating against real data before drawing confident conclusions.

16|🔴 T1 Rapid Prototyping|Rapid Prototyp.what_it_is: Pareto-prioritization (named after the Pareto principle, or '80/20 rule') is a feature scoping discipline that deliberately identifies and builds only the roughly 20% of possible features or capabilities that deliver approximately 80% of the total value to users -- explicitly accepting that the remaining 80% of conceivable features would only add the remaining 20% of value, and deferring or permanently dropping that long tail unless and until evidence shows it's genuinely needed. Applied to AI/FDE engagements, this means systematically ranking candidate features or capabilities by expected value-to-effort ratio and ruthlessly prioritizing the highest-ratio items first, rather than attempting comprehensive coverage of every conceivable use case from the start.
16|🔴 T1 Rapid Prototyping|Rapid Prototyp.why_it_exists: Teams building AI products and prototypes face an enormous space of possible features, edge cases, and capabilities they could address, but limited time and the strong evidence (covered throughout this material's scope management and MVP-first principles) that most value concentrates in a small subset of that space. Pareto-prioritization gives a concrete, defensible decision framework for what to build first and what to explicitly defer, helping teams resist the natural pull toward comprehensive feature coverage that delays time-to-value and risks building many low-value features instead of polishing the few high-value ones.
16|🔴 T1 Rapid Prototyping|Rapid Prototyp.how_it_works:
```
Pareto-prioritization process:

1. Enumerate candidate features/capabilities comprehensively
   (don't prematurely filter at this stage -- get the full list
   of everything that's been requested or imagined)

2. Estimate value and effort for each item:
   Value: how much does this matter to the core use case/users?
   (informed by discovery conversations, usage data if available,
   or stakeholder priority votes -- as covered in workshop
   facilitation's dot-voting technique)
   Effort: rough relative sizing (small/medium/large, or t-shirt
   sizing) rather than precise estimation at this stage

3. Rank by value-to-effort ratio:
   Sort candidates by (value / effort), identifying the small
   subset of high-value, low-effort items that should clearly be
   built first

4. Draw an explicit line:
   Identify roughly where the cumulative value curve flattens --
   typically a small fraction of the total feature list captures
   the large majority of total value
   Everything above the line: build now
   Everything below the line: explicitly defer (not delete --
   document it as a known, deliberately deprioritized item, as
   covered in the related Architecture Decision Records note)

5. Revisit periodically with real usage data:
   Once the prioritized 20% is built and in use, real usage data
   (which features are actually used, what do users ask for that
   isn't covered) should inform whether the original prioritization
   was correct, and what (if anything) from the deferred list
   should now be promoted
```
16|🔴 T1 Rapid Prototyping|Rapid Prototyp.use_when: Apply Pareto-prioritization at the start of scoping any feature set or capability roadmap, especially when facing a long list of stakeholder requests or conceivable use cases with limited time/budget to address them all -- it provides a disciplined, evidence-informed way to make the inevitable trade-off decisions explicit rather than implicit or arbitrary.
16|🔴 T1 Rapid Prototyping|Rapid Prototyp.avoid_when: Don't apply Pareto-prioritization mechanically without considering that some low-frequency, high-effort items might be disproportionately important for specific reasons (e.g. a compliance requirement that only affects a small fraction of cases but is legally mandatory regardless of its 'value' ranking by usage frequency) -- some items need to be built regardless of where they'd rank on a pure value/effort curve.
16|🔴 T1 Rapid Prototyping|Rapid Prototyp.what_goes_wrong:
- Value estimation based on assumption rather than evidence: ranking features by guessed value rather than actual user research or usage data can produce a confidently-wrong prioritization that builds the wrong 20%. Fix: ground value estimates in real discovery conversations, actual usage data where available, or structured stakeholder prioritization exercises (like dot-voting, covered in workshop facilitation) rather than purely internal assumptions about what matters most.
- Deferred 80% becomes a permanent, unaddressed source of stakeholder frustration: if the deferred long tail of features is never revisited or communicated clearly, stakeholders who specifically wanted one of those deferred items may feel ignored, undermining trust even if the prioritization logic was sound. Fix: explicitly communicate what's been deferred and why (the value/effort trade-off reasoning), and establish a clear process for revisiting the deferred list periodically as the dedicated Architecture Decision Records practice supports.
16|🔴 T1 Rapid Prototyping|Rapid Prototyp.real_example: An FDE engagement scoping a customer support AI assistant's capability roadmap had over 40 distinct feature requests collected from discovery interviews across multiple stakeholders. Ranking by value-to-effort, the team identified that just 6 features (accurate answers to the most common question categories, source citation, escalation detection, and a simple feedback mechanism) addressed an estimated 80%+ of the actual daily support volume and stakeholder-stated priority, while the remaining 34 requested features (covering rare edge cases, nice-to-have UI polish, and several speculative integrations) were explicitly documented as deferred. This focused scope let the team deliver a high-quality version of the core 6 features within the engagement timeline, rather than a mediocre, half-finished version of all 40.

16|🔴 T1 Rapid Prototyping|Rapid Prototyp.what_it_is: An Architecture Decision Record (ADR) is a short, structured document capturing a single significant architectural or design decision made during a project -- what was decided, the context and alternatives considered, and the reasoning behind the choice -- maintained as a living, version-controlled artifact (typically as markdown files alongside the codebase) rather than buried in chat history, meeting notes, or someone's memory. Describing ADRs as 'living artifacts' emphasizes that they aren't write-once historical records to be filed and forgotten, but an actively maintained, referenced resource that the team consults when questioning past decisions, onboarding new members, or considering whether changed circumstances warrant revisiting an earlier choice.
16|🔴 T1 Rapid Prototyping|Rapid Prototyp.why_it_exists: AI engagements involve many significant, sometimes non-obvious technical decisions (why this chunking strategy, why this model over an alternative, why this database over another) made under specific constraints and trade-offs at a point in time -- without a record, this reasoning is lost as soon as the people who made the decision move on, leave the project, or simply forget the details months later, leading to the same decision being re-debated from scratch, or worse, a later team reversing a decision without understanding the original (possibly still-valid) reasoning that led to it. ADRs exist specifically to preserve this decision-making context durably and accessibly.

# ADR-007: Use claude-sonnet-4-6 with prompt caching instead of
# fine-tuning for domain-specific terminology

## Status
Accepted (2025-03-14)

## Context
The customer's support AI needs to use domain-specific
terminology consistently. We considered two approaches:
(1) fine-tune a smaller model on domain examples, or
(2) use a frontier model with a comprehensive system prompt +
    prompt caching to keep cost manageable.

## Decision
We chose option 2: claude-sonnet-4-6 with a cached system prompt
containing domain terminology and example responses.

## Alternatives considered
- Fine-tuning (option 1): would reduce per-query cost further,
  but requires 4-6 weeks to collect sufficient training data and
  the customer's timeline did not allow for this in Phase 1.
- Smaller open-weight model self-hosted: rejected due to lower
  baseline quality observed in our evaluation (72% vs 89% on our
  eval suite) and added infrastructure operational burden.

## Consequences
- Lower upfront engineering time, faster Phase 1 delivery
- Higher per-query cost than fine-tuning would eventually achieve
- Revisit in Phase 2: once we have 3+ months of production
  conversation logs, fine-tuning becomes viable and may reduce
  cost significantly -- this ADR should be revisited at that point

## Status updates
- 2025-09-02: Revisited as planned. Production volume now
  justifies fine-tuning investment. See ADR-019 for the updated
  decision.
```
