16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.what_it_is: Domain-Driven Design (DDD) bounded contexts is a software design concept, applied to ontology scoping, where a large business domain is deliberately divided into smaller, explicitly-bounded sub-domains -- each with its own internal model, vocabulary, and rules that are consistent within that boundary but not necessarily consistent with how a neighboring bounded context models the same real-world concept. Applied to ontology design (covered in Palantir's object/property/link model and similar enterprise data modeling efforts), bounded contexts give a principled way to scope an ontology to a specific business area first (rather than attempting one universal, all-encompassing model of the entire enterprise at once), explicitly acknowledging that the same real-world entity (e.g. 'Customer') may legitimately mean different things with different attributes in different parts of the business (e.g. Sales' view of a Customer vs. Support's view).
16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.why_it_exists: Attempting to build a single, universal ontology that perfectly and consistently represents every business concept across an entire large enterprise from day one is both enormously time-consuming and often conceptually impossible -- different departments genuinely use the same words to mean different things, and forcing premature unification creates a model that satisfies no one well. DDD's bounded context concept exists precisely to manage this reality: it gives teams permission and a structured approach to model a specific business area well and consistently within its own boundary, with explicit, deliberate translation/mapping at the boundaries between contexts where they need to interact, rather than either avoiding the problem (one team's monolithic model imposed everywhere) or ignoring it (inconsistent ad-hoc modeling with no acknowledgment of the inconsistency).
16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.how_it_works:
```
Bounded context scoping for an ontology design effort:

1. Identify candidate bounded contexts:
   Look for natural organizational/business boundaries where
   vocabulary and modeling needs genuinely diverge
   e.g. 'Sales' context (Customer = a sales opportunity target
   with deal stage, assigned rep), 'Support' context (Customer =
   an account with ticket history, SLA tier), 'Billing' context
   (Customer = a billing entity with payment terms, invoices)

2. Model each context independently and consistently within
   its own boundary:
   Sales' Customer object has properties relevant to sales
   (deal_stage, assigned_rep, deal_value)
   Support's Customer object has properties relevant to support
   (sla_tier, open_ticket_count)
   Each is internally consistent and useful for its own context,
   even though they don't share an identical schema

3. Define explicit context mapping at boundaries:
   Where contexts need to interact (e.g. a unified customer view
   needs both Sales and Support data), define an explicit mapping/
   translation layer rather than forcing one context's model onto
   the other
   This is where Master Data Management's golden record concept
   (covered separately) often comes in -- a higher-level
   'Customer' entity that both Sales and Support contexts'
   entities link back to via a shared identifier, without forcing
   either context to abandon its own internally useful model

4. Scope ontology-building work per bounded context:
   An ontology design engagement can deliberately start with one
   bounded context (e.g. Support) fully modeled and delivering
   value, before tackling Sales or Billing as a separate,
   explicitly scoped follow-on effort -- directly applying the
   land-and-expand and Pareto-prioritization principles to
   ontology scope specifically
```
16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.use_when: Apply bounded context thinking explicitly when scoping any enterprise ontology design effort spanning more than one department or business function -- it provides a principled justification for starting narrow (a single bounded context) rather than attempting a universal model, and a clear framework for how to later connect multiple contexts without forcing premature, lossy unification.
16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.avoid_when: Don't over-apply bounded context separation within a genuinely small, single-team domain where there's no real vocabulary or modeling divergence to manage -- introducing the concept and its associated boundary-mapping overhead for a domain simple enough to model uniformly from the start adds unnecessary complexity.
16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.what_goes_wrong:
- Premature unification erases legitimate context-specific nuance: a team eager to build 'one true Customer object' for the whole enterprise forces Sales and Support to compromise on a shared schema that serves neither well, losing context-specific properties that mattered to each team's actual workflow. Fix: respect genuine bounded context differences and use explicit mapping/MDM golden-record patterns at the boundary rather than forcing a single shared schema where the underlying business concepts genuinely diverge.
- Context boundaries drawn along technical rather than genuine business lines: defining bounded contexts based on existing system/database boundaries (because that's convenient for the current architecture) rather than genuine business meaning can produce contexts that don't actually reflect where vocabulary and modeling needs diverge, undermining the technique's value. Fix: derive bounded context boundaries from actual discovery conversations about where business vocabulary and concerns genuinely differ (the same discovery techniques covered in Customer Engagement material), not from incidental existing system architecture.
16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.real_example: An ontology design engagement at a large insurance company initially attempted to build one unified 'Policy' object intended to serve underwriting, claims, and customer service simultaneously, but stalled for weeks as each department's representatives disagreed on required properties and relationships. Reframing the effort using bounded contexts -- a distinct Underwriting Policy context, a distinct Claims Policy context, and a distinct Customer Service Policy context, each modeled to serve its own department well, with an explicit shared policy_id mapping layer connecting them -- unblocked the engagement immediately, letting each department's ontology work proceed independently and in parallel rather than waiting for an impossible full consensus on a single universal model.

16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.what_it_is: Bitemporal modeling, as a specific technique within the broader temporal modeling family (also covered with SCD2 elsewhere in this material), explicitly tracks two distinct time dimensions for every fact stored in a database: valid-time (the period during which a fact was true in the real world, regardless of when the database learned about it) and system-time (also called transaction-time -- the period during which the database recorded/believed that fact, regardless of when it was actually true in the real world). The distinction matters because these two timelines frequently diverge: a fact can become true in the real world on one date but only be entered into the system days, weeks, or even months later (e.g. a delayed insurance claim report, or a backdated correction to historical financial data).
16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.why_it_exists: Many critical business and regulatory questions require distinguishing between 'what was actually true at time T' (valid-time) and 'what did our system believe/know at time T' (system-time) -- these are genuinely different questions with different correct answers. A regulator investigating a financial decision needs to know what the system showed the decision-maker at the time the decision was made (system-time as of the decision date), which may differ from the corrected, more accurate picture available today (the current valid-time view, possibly with corrections applied after the fact). Without explicitly modeling both dimensions, a database can only answer one of these questions, typically losing the ability to reconstruct 'what did we believe back then' once corrections or late-arriving data overwrite earlier system states.
16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.how_it_works:
```sql
-- Bitemporal table structure: tracks valid-time AND system-time
CREATE TABLE policy_premium_bitemporal (
  policy_id        VARCHAR,
  premium_amount   DECIMAL(10,2),
  -- Valid-time: when was this premium amount actually correct
  -- in the real world?
  valid_from       TIMESTAMP,
  valid_to         TIMESTAMP,  -- NULL = still currently valid
  -- System-time: when did our database record/believe this?
  recorded_from    TIMESTAMP,
  recorded_to      TIMESTAMP   -- NULL = still the current system belief
);

-- Example: a premium correction discovered and entered late
-- Original entry (entered Jan 10, believed valid from Jan 1):
--   {premium: 500, valid_from: '2024-01-01', valid_to: NULL,
--    recorded_from: '2024-01-10', recorded_to: '2024-03-15'}
--   (this row's recorded_to is set when a correction supersedes it)
--
-- Correction discovered March 15, retroactively fixing the
-- actual valid premium back to Jan 1 (the real-world fact was
-- always 550, our system just had it wrong until now):
--   {premium: 550, valid_from: '2024-01-01', valid_to: NULL,
--    recorded_from: '2024-03-15', recorded_to: NULL}

-- Query: 'What did our system show on Feb 1?' (system-time query
-- -- reconstructs what a user/auditor would have seen then)
SELECT premium_amount FROM policy_premium_bitemporal
WHERE policy_id = 'P001'
  AND recorded_from <= '2024-02-01'
  AND (recorded_to IS NULL OR recorded_to > '2024-02-01');
-- Returns: 500 (what the system believed on Feb 1, even though
-- we now know this was actually incorrect)

-- Query: 'What is the actual correct premium for Jan 1?'
-- (valid-time query, using current/best-known system-time view)
SELECT premium_amount FROM policy_premium_bitemporal
WHERE policy_id = 'P001'
  AND valid_from <= '2024-01-01' AND (valid_to IS NULL OR valid_to > '2024-01-01')
  AND recorded_to IS NULL;  -- the current, most up-to-date belief
-- Returns: 550 (the corrected, currently-believed-true value)
```
16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.use_when: Use full bitemporal modeling specifically when an application must answer both 'what was actually true' and 'what did the system believe at a point in time' as genuinely distinct, both-important questions -- common in regulated financial, insurance, and audit contexts where reconstructing historical system state for compliance or dispute-resolution purposes is a real, recurring need.
16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.avoid_when: Don't add the full complexity of bitemporal modeling (two independent time dimensions per fact) when only one dimension genuinely matters for the use case -- if late-arriving corrections to historical facts are rare or operationally unimportant for the application, simpler SCD2 (valid-time only) or even basic system-time-only auditing may be sufficient and far less complex to build and query against.
16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.what_goes_wrong:
- Confusing valid-time and system-time queries leads to wrong answers for the wrong question: a developer building a 'what did the system show the auditor at the time' report accidentally queries using valid-time logic instead of system-time logic, producing a corrected, current view rather than the actual historical system state being requested -- a serious error in an audit/compliance context. Fix: be explicit and careful in query design and naming conventions about which time dimension a given query is actually using, and validate against known test cases (a known correction event) to confirm the query behaves as intended for both dimensions.
- Bitemporal table growth and query complexity become unmanageable without disciplined querying patterns: as both dimensions accumulate historical versions, queries that don't correctly bound both valid-time and system-time ranges can return unexpectedly large or incorrect result sets (a fan-out style problem, similar to SCD2 join issues covered elsewhere). Fix: build well-tested, reusable query patterns/views for the common 'as of' query types needed, rather than having every consumer write ad-hoc bitemporal queries themselves.
16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.real_example: An actuarial team at an insurance company needed to respond to a regulatory inquiry asking exactly what reserve estimate the company's system showed on a specific historical date, before a since-corrected data entry error was found and fixed. Because their core reserves database used proper bitemporal modeling, the team could precisely reconstruct the system-time view as of the inquiry's specified date (showing the originally-believed, since-corrected figure) while separately and clearly presenting the current, corrected valid-time figure -- satisfying the regulator's actual question (what did you believe and act on at the time) without conflating it with the unrelated question of what the figure should have been with the benefit of hindsight.

16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.what_it_is: Golden record creation is the specific output process within Master Data Management (MDM, covered more broadly elsewhere in this material) where, after entity resolution identifies that multiple source records across systems refer to the same real-world entity, a single authoritative 'golden record' is constructed by selecting or merging the best available value for each attribute from across the matched source records -- governed by explicit survivorship rules that determine which source wins for each field when sources disagree, producing one trusted, canonical representation of that entity that downstream systems and analytics can rely on as the single source of truth.
16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.why_it_exists: Identifying that records across systems refer to the same entity (entity resolution) is only half the problem -- once matched, the system still needs to decide what the actual correct value is for each attribute when different source systems disagree (e.g. CRM says the customer's address is X, ERP says it's Y -- which is correct, or how should they be reconciled?). Golden record creation exists as the explicit, governed process for making and documenting these reconciliation decisions consistently and auditable, rather than leaving downstream consumers to arbitrarily pick whichever source's value they happen to query, which would reintroduce exactly the inconsistency MDM is meant to solve.
16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.how_it_works:
```
Golden record creation process (building on entity resolution):

1. Input: a cluster of matched source records (already
   identified as referring to the same real-world entity via
   entity resolution, e.g. splink-based matching)
   CRM record: {name: 'Acme Corp', address: '123 Main St',
               revenue: $2.1M, last_updated: '2024-01-15'}
   ERP record: {name: 'ACME CORPORATION', address: '123 Main
               Street', payment_terms: 'Net-30',
               last_updated: '2024-06-20'}

2. Apply survivorship rules per attribute (defined explicitly,
   not ad-hoc):
   name: prefer CRM (governance decision: CRM is the formally
         maintained naming authority)
   address: prefer most-recently-updated source (ERP, since it
            was updated more recently and addresses are
            time-sensitive facts)
   revenue: only available in CRM, so CRM value is used by default
   payment_terms: only available in ERP, used by default

3. Construct the golden record:
   {golden_id: 'MDM-2001', name: 'Acme Corp',
    address: '123 Main Street', revenue: $2.1M,
    payment_terms: 'Net-30',
    source_lineage: {crm: 'CRM-4521', erp: 'VND-8833'}}

4. Maintain lineage and auditability:
   Every golden record attribute should be traceable back to
   which source record and survivorship rule produced it, so a
   data steward or auditor can answer 'why does the golden record
   show this value?' rather than treating it as an opaque
   black-box merge

5. Re-run on source updates:
   When any source record updates, golden record creation should
   re-evaluate survivorship rules for the affected attributes,
   keeping the golden record current rather than stale
```
16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.use_when: Implement explicit, governed golden record creation (not just entity matching alone) whenever multiple source systems hold genuinely conflicting data about the same entity and downstream consumers need one trusted, consistent value per attribute -- the survivorship rule design itself is a key governance decision that should involve business stakeholders who understand which source is actually most authoritative for each specific attribute, not just a default technical choice.
16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.avoid_when: Don't build elaborate golden record survivorship logic for attributes where sources never genuinely conflict in practice (e.g. an immutable government-issued ID number that's identical across all source systems by construction) -- reserve the survivorship rule design effort for attributes where genuine, recurring conflict actually occurs.
16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.what_goes_wrong:
- Survivorship rules defined by technical convenience rather than business authority: defaulting to 'most recently updated wins' for every attribute, without considering which source is actually the authoritative system of record for that specific attribute, can produce a golden record with a less accurate value than a more deliberate, business-informed rule would have selected. Fix: design survivorship rules attribute-by-attribute with input from business stakeholders who know which source system is genuinely most trustworthy for each specific data point, not a single blanket rule applied uniformly.
- Golden record creation lacks lineage, becoming an unauditable black box: if the process doesn't preserve which source and rule produced each golden record value, disputes or data quality investigations become very difficult to resolve, since no one can explain why the golden record shows a particular value. Fix: always preserve source lineage and the specific survivorship rule applied for every golden record attribute, treating this as a non-negotiable requirement of the golden record creation pipeline, not an optional nice-to-have.
16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.real_example: A bank's MDM program defined explicit, business-validated survivorship rules for its Customer golden record: legal name and date of birth survive from the core banking system (the authoritative KYC source), current mailing address survives from whichever channel (online banking, branch update, or mail) was most recently confirmed by the customer directly, and risk rating survives from the dedicated risk management system regardless of recency -- a deliberate, attribute-specific rule set developed jointly with compliance, operations, and risk stakeholders, rather than a single uniform 'most recent wins' default, ensuring the golden record reflected genuine business authority for each specific data point rather than an arbitrary technical convenience.

16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.what_it_is: Splink, dedupe.io, and Zingg are three widely-used open-source software libraries specifically designed for entity resolution (also called record linkage or deduplication) -- the process of probabilistically identifying which records across one or more datasets refer to the same real-world entity, covered conceptually in the dedicated entity resolution note elsewhere in this material. Splink (built by the UK's Ministry of Justice, optimized for large-scale linkage using DuckDB/Spark backends) is particularly strong for very large datasets and offers interpretable probabilistic matching with explicit model training. dedupe.io (and its underlying open-source `dedupe` Python library) is a more general-purpose, widely-adopted library with active learning support (it asks a human to label uncertain pairs to improve matching over time). Zingg is a Spark-native entity resolution library designed specifically for big-data-scale deduplication and matching within existing Spark/Databricks pipelines.
16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.why_it_exists: Building a probabilistic entity matching system entirely from scratch (similarity scoring, blocking/indexing strategies to avoid comparing every record to every other record, statistical model training for match probability) is substantial, specialized engineering work that most data teams shouldn't need to reinvent. These libraries exist to provide production-grade, well-tested implementations of the core entity resolution algorithms, each with different strengths suited to different scale, infrastructure, and interactivity needs -- letting an FDE or data engineering team apply entity resolution without building the underlying matching infrastructure themselves.
16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.how_it_works:
```python
# Splink: probabilistic matching with explicit model training,
# strong for large-scale (millions of records) linkage
import splink.duckdb.comparison_library as cl
from splink import DuckDBAPI, Linker, SettingsCreator

settings = SettingsCreator(
    link_type='dedupe_only',
    comparisons=[
        cl.jaro_winkler_at_thresholds('name', [0.95, 0.8]),
        cl.exact_match('date_of_birth'),
    ]
)
linker = Linker(df, settings, db_api=DuckDBAPI())
linker.training.estimate_u_using_random_sampling(max_pairs=1e6)
results = linker.inference.predict(threshold_match_probability=0.7)

# dedupe.io / dedupe: active-learning workflow, asks a human to
# label uncertain pairs to improve matching iteratively
import dedupe

fields = [{'field': 'name', 'type': 'String'},
          {'field': 'address', 'type': 'String'}]
deduper = dedupe.Dedupe(fields)
deduper.prepare_training(data)
dedupe.console_label(deduper)  # interactive: human labels sample
                                 # pairs as match/not-match to train
deduper.train()
clustered_dupes = deduper.partition(data, threshold=0.5)

# Zingg: Spark-native, designed for big-data pipelines
# (typically configured via a JSON config and run as a Spark job
# within an existing Databricks/Spark pipeline, rather than an
# interactive Python session)
```
16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.use_when: Choose Splink for large-scale (millions+ records), performance-sensitive linkage where explicit, interpretable probabilistic model configuration matters. Choose dedupe/dedupe.io when active learning (iteratively improving matching by labeling uncertain pairs) is valuable and the dataset scale is moderate. Choose Zingg specifically when entity resolution needs to run natively within an existing Spark/Databricks pipeline at big-data scale without leaving that ecosystem.
16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.avoid_when: Don't reach for any of these specialized libraries when a simple, reliable exact-match join on a shared unique identifier (covered in the broader entity resolution note's guidance) is available and sufficient -- probabilistic matching tools add complexity and uncertainty that should only be introduced when no reliable exact key exists.
16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.what_goes_wrong:
- Library choice mismatched to actual scale/infrastructure needs: choosing an interactive, Python-session-oriented tool like dedupe for a dataset that's actually too large to process efficiently outside a distributed Spark environment, or conversely choosing a heavyweight Spark-native tool like Zingg for a small dataset that would be handled faster and more simply with a lighter tool. Fix: match the tool choice to actual data scale and existing infrastructure constraints, not just general popularity or familiarity.
- Treating any of these tools as fully automated, requiring no human validation: all three tools produce probabilistic match scores that still require a validation step (a human review queue for borderline matches, as covered in the entity resolution and MDM material) before being trusted for consequential downstream decisions -- treating their output as automatically authoritative without validation risks the same over-aggressive-merging and under-merging failure modes covered in the entity resolution note.
16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.real_example: A data engineering team running entity resolution on a 50-million-row customer dataset within an existing Databricks/Spark pipeline chose Zingg specifically because it integrated natively into their existing Spark job orchestration without requiring data to be exported to a separate Python environment, while a smaller team at a different company working with a 200,000-row supplier dataset and wanting to iteratively refine match quality through direct human feedback chose dedupe's active-learning workflow instead -- both legitimate entity resolution tool choices, selected based on the specific scale and infrastructure context of each team's situation rather than either tool being universally 'better.'

16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.what_it_is: Data contracts between producers and consumers, as a specific ontology and data-modeling discipline, formalize the agreement on data shape, semantics, and quality guarantees specifically at the interface where one team's pipeline (the producer of a dataset, often feeding into an ontology's object types) hands data off to another team or system that consumes it (analytics, ML pipelines, or other ontology-dependent applications) -- a concept covered in depth in the dedicated Enterprise Integration material on data contracts, but specifically relevant here in the context of ontology design because an enterprise ontology's object types and properties are themselves downstream consumers of multiple upstream data producers, making data contract discipline a foundational prerequisite for ontology reliability.
16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.why_it_exists: An ontology's value depends entirely on the reliability and consistency of the underlying data feeding its object types and properties -- if an upstream producer changes a column name or data format without any contract or notification, the ontology's objects silently break or show incorrect values, undermining trust in the entire ontology-based analytics and AI layer built on top of it (the same silent-failure risk covered in data contracts material generally, here applied specifically to the ontology context where many downstream consumers, possibly including AI agents and natural-language query tools, depend on ontology stability).
16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.how_it_works:
```
Data contracts specifically at the ontology ingestion boundary:

1. Identify all upstream data sources feeding each ontology
   object type (e.g. the Supplier object type's properties are
   sourced from a procurement system table, a risk management
   system feed, and a finance system table)

2. Define an explicit contract per source feeding the ontology:
   Schema (columns, types, nullability) the ontology ingestion
   pipeline expects
   Semantic definitions (does 'risk_score' mean the same thing
   the ontology's Risk property expects, on the same scale?)
   Freshness SLA (the ontology's Supplier object should reflect
   data no more than 24 hours stale, requiring the source feed
   to commit to a matching update frequency)

3. Enforce the contract at the ontology ingestion pipeline:
   Validation checks (as covered in the data contracts and data
   quality monitoring material) run before data is allowed to
   update the ontology's objects, catching producer-side changes
   before they silently corrupt the ontology

4. Notify ontology object owners of any breaking producer-side
   change before it happens (the formal breaking-change
   notification process covered in data contracts material),
   since a change affecting an ontology object type may have a
   wide blast radius across every downstream application,
   dashboard, and AI agent built on that object type

5. Treat the ontology object type's own schema as itself a
   contract to its downstream consumers (applications, AIP
   actions, natural-language query tools) -- changes to an
   ontology object's properties need the same breaking-change
   discipline applied one level further downstream
```
16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.use_when: Apply explicit data contract discipline at every boundary feeding an enterprise ontology, especially as the ontology becomes the foundation for an increasing number of downstream applications and AI agents -- the more consumers depend on ontology stability, the higher the cost of an unmanaged upstream breaking change, making contract discipline increasingly valuable as ontology adoption grows.
16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.avoid_when: Don't apply heavyweight, formal data contract processes to early-stage, exploratory ontology prototyping where the object model itself is still actively being iterated on and finalized -- premature formal contracts on an unstable, still-evolving ontology design add process overhead without corresponding benefit until the design has stabilized enough to be worth protecting.
16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.what_goes_wrong:
- Ontology object type changes treated as internal implementation details rather than contracts: a team modifying an ontology object's properties (renaming a field, changing a type) without considering the many downstream applications, dashboards, and AI agents that depend on that object type's stability can cause widespread, hard-to-diagnose breakage across the enterprise. Fix: treat ontology object type schemas with the same breaking-change governance and notification discipline as any other production data contract, given their typically wide blast radius.
- Contract enforcement scoped too narrowly, missing indirect dependencies: validating only the direct source-to-ontology data contract while ignoring that the ontology's properties feed further downstream into AI agent tools and natural-language interfaces (as covered in UC Functions and AIP Actions material) means a subtle data quality issue can still propagate to AI-generated outputs even if the basic schema contract technically passes. Fix: extend data quality and contract validation thinking to consider the full downstream chain, not just the immediate next hop.
16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.real_example: An ontology engineering team at a manufacturing company implemented formal data contracts for every source feed into their Supplier and Purchase Order object types, including automated schema and freshness validation that would block an ontology refresh and alert the data engineering team if any upstream source violated its contract -- when the procurement system team later renamed a column as part of an unrelated system upgrade, the validation caught the violation immediately before it reached the ontology, preventing what would otherwise have been a silent corruption of supplier risk scores used by several downstream AI-powered procurement risk dashboards and an AIP natural-language query tool relied on by category managers.

16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.what_it_is: Operational data modeling and analytical data modeling are two distinct design approaches optimized for fundamentally different access patterns. Operational (OLTP -- Online Transaction Processing) data models are normalized (following 3NF or similar principles) and optimized for fast, frequent, small read/write transactions on individual records -- the kind of access pattern a live application performs constantly (creating an order, updating a customer's address). Analytical (OLAP -- Online Analytical Processing) data models, in contrast, are typically denormalized into dimensional structures (star schemas, OBTs, covered in the dedicated dimensional modeling note) optimized for large-scale aggregation and scanning across many records at once -- the kind of access pattern a business intelligence dashboard or an AI ontology's analytical queries perform. The same underlying business data often needs both representations, transformed from operational source systems into analytical structures via the ETL/ELT pipelines covered in enterprise integration material.
16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.why_it_exists: A data model optimized for one access pattern performs poorly for the other -- a highly normalized operational schema requires many joins to answer an aggregation question (e.g. 'total revenue by region last quarter'), making analytical queries slow and complex; conversely, a denormalized analytical schema is inefficient and risky for the kind of frequent, small, consistency-critical updates an operational application needs (denormalized data requires updating the same value in many places to maintain consistency). Recognizing these are genuinely different modeling problems, requiring different schemas even for the same underlying business concepts, prevents the common mistake of trying to force one schema to serve both purposes well, which usually serves neither purpose well.
16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.how_it_works:
```sql
-- Operational model: normalized, optimized for transactional
-- consistency and fast single-record operations
CREATE TABLE orders (
  order_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id INT REFERENCES customers(customer_id),
  order_date TIMESTAMP,
  status VARCHAR
);
CREATE TABLE order_items (
  order_item_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  order_id INT REFERENCES orders(order_id),
  product_id INT REFERENCES products(product_id),
  quantity INT, unit_price DECIMAL
);
-- Updating an order status: one fast, atomic update to one row
UPDATE orders SET status = 'SHIPPED' WHERE order_id = 12345;

-- Analytical model: denormalized star schema (as covered in
-- dimensional modeling), optimized for fast aggregation across
-- millions of rows
CREATE TABLE fact_sales (
  sale_id BIGINT, date_key INT, product_key INT,
  customer_key INT, region VARCHAR, revenue DECIMAL
);
-- Aggregation query: scans many rows efficiently, no joins to
-- normalized lookup tables needed for the region dimension since
-- it's denormalized directly into the fact table
SELECT region, SUM(revenue) FROM fact_sales
WHERE date_key BETWEEN 20240101 AND 20240331
GROUP BY region;

Transformation pipeline connecting the two:
  Operational source (orders, order_items, customers, products)
  -> ETL/ELT pipeline (extracting, joining, denormalizing,
     aggregating as needed) ->
  Analytical target (fact_sales star schema, or an ontology's
     analytical object properties)
  The same underlying business fact (a sale) is intentionally
  represented differently in each model, optimized for its
  respective access pattern, with the pipeline as the explicit
  translation layer between them
```
16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.use_when: Recognize early in any data modeling or ontology design effort whether the consuming use case is primarily operational (an application needing fast, consistent single-record reads/writes) or analytical (aggregation, reporting, AI-driven analysis across many records) -- and deliberately design separate, appropriately-optimized models for each, connected by an explicit transformation pipeline, rather than attempting a single compromise schema.
16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.avoid_when: For small-scale systems with low data volume and no meaningful performance pressure from either access pattern, the strict separation between operational and analytical modeling may be unnecessary overhead -- a single, reasonably-normalized schema might serve both purposes adequately when data volumes and query complexity are modest enough that performance differences don't actually matter in practice.
16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.what_goes_wrong:
- Running analytical queries directly against a production operational database: heavy aggregation queries run directly against a normalized operational schema (rather than against a properly-modeled analytical replica) can both perform poorly and risk degrading the operational application's performance for real users by competing for the same database resources. Fix: replicate operational data into a separate, appropriately-modeled analytical store (via the ETL/ELT patterns covered elsewhere) rather than running heavy analytical workloads directly against the live operational database.
- Treating an ontology's object model as if it must simultaneously serve both operational transactional needs and analytical aggregation needs without considering the trade-off: an ontology design that tries to be both a fast, consistent operational record AND an efficient analytical aggregation source for every object type can end up compromising on both fronts. Fix: be explicit about which ontology object types and properties primarily serve operational application needs versus analytical/AI query needs, and consider whether different underlying storage/modeling strategies are warranted for each, even within a single conceptual ontology.
16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.real_example: A retail company's ontology design initially modeled Order objects directly against their normalized operational order-management database, which worked fine for simple single-order lookups but performed very poorly when the company's new AI-powered analytics dashboard tried to run aggregation queries (total revenue by category and region) directly against that same operational model. The fix was a deliberate split: the operational Order object type remained backed by the normalized transactional database for application use, while a separate analytical Sales Summary object type was built from a properly denormalized star-schema pipeline specifically for the dashboard and AI analytics use cases -- two distinct, appropriately-optimized models serving the same underlying business reality through different access patterns.

16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.what_it_is: Object permissioning in an ontology context refers to controlling which users can view, modify, or take actions on specific ontology objects (and their properties), using either RBAC (Role-Based Access Control -- permissions assigned based on a user's role, e.g. 'Sales Rep' can view Customer objects in their assigned territory) or ABAC (Attribute-Based Access Control -- permissions determined dynamically by evaluating attributes of the user, the object, and the context against a policy, e.g. 'a user can view a Patient object if the user's department matches the patient's treating department AND the access occurs during the user's active shift'). RBAC is simpler and more common for straightforward permission structures; ABAC is more flexible and expressive for complex, context-dependent permission rules that RBAC's fixed role categories struggle to capture cleanly.
16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.why_it_exists: As ontologies become the foundation for increasingly broad AI-powered access (natural language query tools, agentic actions, covered in UC Functions and AIP Actions material elsewhere), getting object-level permissioning right becomes critical -- an AI agent or natural-language query interface must respect exactly the same access boundaries a human user querying the underlying data directly would, and the permission model needs to be expressive enough to capture genuinely complex enterprise access rules (territory-based sales access, need-to-know classification levels in defense contexts, patient-provider relationships in healthcare) without becoming an unmanageable explosion of narrowly-defined roles.
16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.how_it_works:
```
RBAC example (role-based):
  Roles: SalesRep, SalesManager, SupportAgent, Admin
  Permission rule: SalesRep role can READ Customer objects WHERE
  territory = user's assigned territory
  Simple to reason about and audit ('what can a SalesRep do?'),
  but can require a large number of finely-distinguished roles if
  access genuinely varies along many independent dimensions
  (territory AND product line AND customer tier, for example)

ABAC example (attribute-based):
  Policy: ALLOW READ on Patient object
    IF user.department == object.treating_department
    AND user.clearance_level >= object.sensitivity_level
    AND current_time WITHIN user.active_shift_hours
  More expressive -- a single policy can capture multi-dimensional,
  context-dependent rules that would otherwise require an
  explosion of narrowly-scoped roles under pure RBAC
  Requires the underlying system to evaluate policies dynamically
  against real-time attributes (user, object, environment) rather
  than a simpler static role lookup

Hybrid approach (common in practice):
  Use RBAC for broad, stable categories of access (Admin vs.
  general user) combined with ABAC-style attribute conditions
  layered on top for finer-grained, context-dependent restrictions
  (territory, sensitivity level, time-of-access) -- avoiding both
  RBAC's role-explosion problem and ABAC's full complexity where
  it isn't needed

AI agent/AIP Action implication:
  Whichever model is used, AI agents and tools (UC Functions,
  AIP Actions) operating on ontology objects must evaluate and
  respect the same permission policies as a human user would --
  the agent runs with the calling user's actual permission context,
  not an elevated service-level permission, as covered in the
  UC Functions and insider threat/access control material
```
16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.use_when: Use RBAC as the default starting point for straightforward, stable organizational permission structures where roles map cleanly to access needs. Move to ABAC (or a hybrid model) when permission rules genuinely depend on multiple, dynamic, context-dependent attributes that would otherwise require an unmanageable explosion of finely-distinguished roles under pure RBAC.
16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.avoid_when: Don't introduce full ABAC complexity for a permission structure that genuinely is simple and role-based -- the added expressiveness of ABAC comes with real cost in policy authoring complexity, auditability, and runtime evaluation overhead, which isn't justified when a simpler RBAC model adequately captures the actual access requirements.
16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.what_goes_wrong:
- RBAC role explosion: as genuinely multi-dimensional access requirements accumulate (territory x product line x customer tier x seniority), pure RBAC can require dozens or hundreds of narrowly-distinguished roles to capture every legitimate combination, becoming unmanageable to administer and audit. Fix: recognize when RBAC role proliferation signals a genuinely multi-dimensional, attribute-dependent access pattern, and migrate to ABAC (or a hybrid model) for that specific permission domain rather than continuing to add ever-more-specific roles.
- ABAC policies become an unauditable black box: highly flexible ABAC policies, if not carefully documented and tested, can become difficult for anyone other than their original author to understand or verify, creating a risk that a policy doesn't actually do what stakeholders believe it does. Fix: maintain clear, tested documentation of ABAC policies (analogous to the ADR practice for architecture decisions) and validate them against explicit test cases representing both should-allow and should-deny scenarios, not just trust the policy author's intent.
16|🟡 T2 Ontology Design & Data Modeling|.real_example: A healthcare system's ontology initially used RBAC with roles like 'Cardiology Nurse' and 'Cardiology Physician,' but found this approach couldn't cleanly express the actual required rule that access to a specific Patient object should depend on whether that particular nurse or physician was genuinely part of that specific patient's current care team -- a context-dependent relationship, not a fixed role. The system migrated to an ABAC policy checking the dynamic care-team relationship attribute alongside the broader role category, correctly restricting access to only the clinicians actually treating a given patient at a given time, rather than granting blanket access to every Cardiology-department clinician regardless of their actual involvement with that specific patient.

16|🟡 T2 Enterprise Integration|Enterpris.what_it_is: SAP S/4HANA is SAP's current-generation ERP suite (running on the in-memory HANA database), and integrating with it for AI/data engineering purposes typically involves one or more of: OData (SAP's standard RESTful API protocol for exposing SAP business objects as queryable, filterable HTTP endpoints, the modern preferred integration method), BAPI (Business Application Programming Interface -- older, RFC-based standardized function modules for specific business operations like creating a sales order, still widely used especially for transactional write operations), RFC (Remote Function Call -- SAP's underlying remote procedure call protocol that BAPIs and custom function modules are built on), and the SAP API Business Hub (a centralized public catalog where SAP publishes and documents its available APIs across OData, BAPI/RFC, and other protocols, serving as the primary discovery resource for what's actually available to integrate with for a given S/4HANA system).
16|🟡 T2 Enterprise Integration|Enterpris.why_it_exists: Enterprises running SAP S/4HANA hold their most critical operational data (financials, supply chain, manufacturing, HR) within it, but SAP's internal data model and protocols are notoriously complex and have evolved across decades of legacy compatibility requirements -- OData, BAPI, RFC, and the API Business Hub exist as SAP's official, supported integration surface specifically so that external systems (including AI/analytics platforms like Databricks or Palantir Foundry) can read and write SAP data without needing to understand or directly access SAP's internal database tables and ABAP code, which SAP does not support external systems touching directly.
16|🟡 T2 Enterprise Integration|Enterpris.how_it_works:
```python
# OData integration with SAP S/4HANA (modern, REST-based approach)
import requests

SAP_BASE = 'https://sap-host.company.com/sap/opu/odata/sap/'

# Query Purchase Orders via OData, with filtering
response = requests.get(
    f'{SAP_BASE}API_PURCHASEORDER_PROCESS_SRV/A_PurchaseOrder',
    auth=('sap_user', 'sap_password'),
    headers={'Accept': 'application/json'},
    params={
        '$filter': "CreationDate ge datetime'2024-01-01T00:00:00'",
        '$select': 'PurchaseOrder,Supplier,NetAmount,Currency',
        '$top': 1000
    }
)
purchase_orders = response.json()['d']['results']

# BAPI/RFC integration (older, but still common for transactional
# writes -- typically called via a library like PyRFC from Python,
# or via a middleware layer)
# Example (conceptual): calling BAPI_SALESORDER_CREATEFROMDAT2 to
# create a sales order requires connecting via RFC, constructing
# the BAPI's expected structured input parameters (header data,
# line items), and handling the BAPI's own internal return-code
# based error handling (distinct from HTTP status codes)

# Discovering available APIs: the SAP API Business Hub
# (api.sap.com) is the reference catalog -- before building any
# custom integration, check whether SAP already publishes a
# standard OData service or BAPI covering the needed business
# object, rather than reverse-engineering table structures

Key integration considerations:
  OData is generally preferred for read-heavy analytical
  integration (the kind Databricks/Foundry pipelines need)
  BAPI/RFC remains important for transactional writes where
  business logic validation must happen within SAP itself
  (e.g. creating a purchase order must trigger SAP's own approval
  workflow and validation rules, not just insert a raw database row)
```
16|🟡 T2 Enterprise Integration|Enterpris.use_when: Use OData for analytical/reporting integration (extracting data for an ontology, a data pipeline, or AI feature engineering) where read access and filtering flexibility matter most. Use BAPI/RFC specifically when writing data back into SAP in a way that must trigger SAP's own business logic and validation (not just inserting raw data), since bypassing this would risk data integrity issues SAP's application layer is designed to prevent. Always check the SAP API Business Hub first before building custom integration code.
16|🟡 T2 Enterprise Integration|Enterpris.avoid_when: Never attempt direct database-level access to SAP's underlying tables, bypassing the OData/BAPI/RFC API layer entirely -- this is both unsupported by SAP (voiding support agreements) and risks bypassing SAP's authorization model and data integrity validation, a risk explicitly called out in the broader ERP/CRM integration material covered elsewhere in this phase.
16|🟡 T2 Enterprise Integration|Enterpris.what_goes_wrong:
- API rate/performance limits underestimated: SAP S/4HANA OData endpoints, especially in production environments shared with live transactional workloads, often have stricter rate limits or performance considerations than a typical modern cloud API, and a naive bulk-extraction pipeline can both hit limits and degrade SAP's own operational performance. Fix: coordinate with the customer's SAP Basis team on appropriate extraction batch sizes and scheduling (often off-peak hours) to avoid contention with SAP's primary transactional workload.
- Field name and business logic complexity underestimated: SAP's data model uses dense, often cryptic field names (with decades of legacy naming conventions) and complex business logic (e.g. how a purchase order's status actually progresses) that aren't self-evident from the API response alone. Fix: engage the customer's SAP functional/technical experts early to validate field mappings and business logic interpretation, rather than assuming raw API responses are self-explanatory.
16|🟡 T2 Enterprise Integration|Enterpris.real_example: A Databricks FDE building a supply chain risk pipeline needed purchase order and supplier data from a manufacturing customer's SAP S/4HANA system. Rather than attempting custom table-level extraction, the FDE worked with the customer's SAP team to identify the relevant standard OData services already published in the customer's SAP API Business Hub catalog (API_PURCHASEORDER_PROCESS_SRV and related supplier master data services), building the extraction pipeline against these documented, supported endpoints -- a far more reliable and maintainable approach than reverse-engineering SAP's internal table structure, and one that survived a subsequent SAP version upgrade without requiring pipeline changes, since the OData service contract remained stable across the upgrade.

16|🟡 T2 Enterprise Integration|Enterpris.what_it_is: Salesforce offers several distinct integration APIs optimized for different data volume and latency needs beyond the standard REST API (covered in the ERP/CRM integration material elsewhere): Bulk API 2.0 (designed specifically for extracting or loading very large volumes of records -- millions of rows -- using asynchronous batch jobs rather than synchronous request/response calls, with a separate, much higher rate limit than the standard REST API), Streaming API (a push-based mechanism using CometD/long-polling that notifies subscribed clients of record changes in near-real-time, rather than requiring clients to poll), and Platform Events (a more structured, custom event-driven mechanism within Salesforce that lets developers define and publish custom business events -- not just generic record-change notifications -- that external systems can subscribe to, fitting into the broader event-driven architecture patterns covered in Phase 16's enterprise integration material).
16|🟡 T2 Enterprise Integration|Enterpris.why_it_exists: Salesforce's standard REST API, while flexible, is not designed for either very-high-volume batch extraction (it would quickly exhaust standard API call limits, as noted in the broader ERP/CRM integration discussion) or real-time change notification (it requires polling, which is both inefficient and introduces latency). Bulk API 2.0, Streaming API, and Platform Events each exist to address one of these specific gaps -- giving integration architects purpose-built tools matched to the actual data volume and latency requirements of a given integration, rather than forcing every integration pattern through the same general-purpose REST interface.
16|🟡 T2 Enterprise Integration|Enterpris.how_it_works:

```python
# Bulk API 2.0: asynchronous batch job for large-volume extraction
from simple_salesforce import Salesforce, bulk

sf = Salesforce(username='...', password='...', security_token='...')

# Bulk query (handles pagination/batching internally for millions
# of rows, far more efficient than paginated REST queries)
results = sf.bulk.Account.query(
    "SELECT Id, Name, AnnualRevenue FROM Account WHERE LastModifiedDate > 2024-01-01T00:00:00Z"
)
# Returns results via an async job that Salesforce processes and
# makes available for download, separate from REST API rate limits

# Bulk load (e.g. writing AI-computed scores back at scale)
job_results = sf.bulk.Account.update([
    {'Id': acc_id, 'AI_Risk_Score__c': score}
    for acc_id, score in ai_predictions
])  # Submitted as a batch job, not individual REST calls per record

# Streaming API: subscribe to real-time record change notifications
# (via CometD client library, conceptual)
# client.subscribe('/data/AccountChangeEvent', callback=handle_change)
# def handle_change(message):
#     account_id = message['data']['payload']['ChangeEventHeader']['recordIds'][0]
#     # Trigger AI processing (e.g. re-score this account) in
#     # near-real-time as soon as Salesforce reports the change

# Platform Events: custom business event publishing
# Define a custom Platform Event in Salesforce (e.g.
# 'High_Value_Opportunity_Created__e'), publish it from Salesforce
# Apex code when a business condition is met, and subscribe from
# an external AI service to trigger immediate processing --
# similar conceptually to the webhook/pub-sub patterns covered in
# event-driven architecture material, but native to Salesforce's
# own event bus
```
16|🟡 T2 Enterprise Integration|Enterpris.use_when: Use Bulk API 2.0 for any extraction or load operation involving more than roughly tens of thousands of records, where the standard REST API's per-call overhead and rate limits would be prohibitive. Use Streaming API or Platform Events when an AI system needs to react to Salesforce data changes in near-real-time (e.g. triggering AI analysis the moment a new high-value opportunity is created) rather than on a batch/polling schedule.
16|🟡 T2 Enterprise Integration|Enterpris.avoid_when: Don't use Bulk API for small, frequent, low-latency operations (a single record update in response to a user action) -- the asynchronous batch job overhead makes it slower and more complex than a simple synchronous REST call for small-scale operations. Don't use Streaming API/Platform Events when a simple scheduled batch sync is sufficient and real-time reaction isn't actually required by the use case.
16|🟡 T2 Enterprise Integration|Enterpris.what_goes_wrong:
- Bulk API job monitoring overlooked: because Bulk API jobs are asynchronous, a pipeline that submits a bulk job but doesn't properly poll for completion status and handle partial failures (some records in a batch may fail while others succeed) can silently miss failed records. Fix: always implement explicit job status polling and per-record failure handling for Bulk API jobs, rather than assuming the job completed successfully just because it was submitted without error.
- Streaming API connection drops without reconnection logic: long-lived streaming connections (via CometD) can drop due to network issues or Salesforce-side session expiration, and without proper reconnection and replay logic (Salesforce supports event replay from a specific point), a consuming application can silently miss events during the disconnected period. Fix: implement robust reconnection logic with Salesforce's replay ID mechanism to resume exactly where the stream left off, rather than assuming a single persistent connection is reliable indefinitely.
16|🟡 T2 Enterprise Integration|Enterpris.real_example: A Salesforce FDE building an AI-powered account scoring system needed to both backfill scores for 3 million existing accounts (using Bulk API 2.0 for the one-time historical load) and then keep scores updated in near-real-time as account data changed going forward (using Platform Events, with a custom 'Account_Updated_For_Scoring__e' event published whenever relevant fields changed, triggering an external AI service to recompute that specific account's score within seconds) -- using each Salesforce integration API for the specific data volume and latency characteristic it was actually designed for, rather than forcing both the bulk backfill and the ongoing real-time updates through the same standard REST API.

16|🟡 T2 Enterprise Integration|Enterpris.what_it_is: ServiceNow Integration Hub is ServiceNow's native integration platform for connecting ServiceNow workflows (incidents, change requests, service catalog items) with external systems, built around 'Spokes' -- pre-built, packaged integration connectors for common third-party systems (e.g. a Slack Spoke, an AWS Spoke, a generic REST Spoke for custom APIs) that provide ready-made actions and triggers without requiring custom integration code for each connection. Workflow Data Fabric is a more recent ServiceNow capability that extends this further, allowing ServiceNow workflows to access and act on external data sources (including data living outside ServiceNow's own database) directly within workflow logic, without first needing to fully replicate that external data into ServiceNow.
16|🟡 T2 Enterprise Integration|Enterpris.why_it_exists: IT service management workflows (incident resolution, change approval, service requests) frequently need to interact with external systems -- looking up data in another system, triggering an action elsewhere, or incorporating external context into a decision -- and building custom point-to-point integration code for every such interaction across ServiceNow's IT Service Management platform doesn't scale. Integration Hub Spokes exist to provide a library of pre-built, reusable connectors maintained centrally (by ServiceNow or third parties) rather than requiring custom code per integration. Workflow Data Fabric extends this further specifically to reduce the need for full data replication into ServiceNow when a workflow just needs to read or act on external data occasionally, addressing data duplication and freshness concerns that a 'copy everything into ServiceNow first' approach would create.

16|🟡 T2 Enterprise Integration|Enterpris.avoid_when: Don't use ServiceNow's no-code Spoke/Flow tooling for complex, performance-sensitive, or highly custom integration logic that would be better served by a dedicated external service with its own proper API and testing infrastructure -- ServiceNow's workflow tooling is well-suited to orchestrating relatively simple integration steps within an ITSM process, not as a general-purpose application development platform.

RaaS exposes Workday's custom and standard reports as callable web service endpoints (typically returning XML or JSON), letting an external system retrieve exactly the data shape that a Workday report was already configured to produce, leveraging Workday's existing reporting layer rather than requiring separate raw data extraction logic. RaaS's report-based approach specifically leverages the fact that Workday's own report-building tools are already familiar to many customers' HR/finance analysts, letting them define the exact data shape needed without requiring a developer to write custom API integration code for every new data need.
