16|🟡 T2 Workshop Facilitation & Training.use_when: Use a dedicated documentation portal tool (rather than a generic wiki or scattered documents) for any AI system handoff deliverable intended to be a long-lived, actively-referenced resource for the customer's team -- particularly valuable for API documentation (ReadMe's interactive features) and for documentation that needs to scale across multiple products, versions, or a large user base over time.
16|🟡 T2 Workshop Facilitation & Training.avoid_when: Don't set up a full documentation portal platform for a small, short-lived engagement where a simpler README file or a few well-organized markdown documents in the project's existing repository would be entirely sufficient -- the additional setup and tool-learning overhead isn't justified for documentation that won't grow significantly or persist long enough to benefit from dedicated portal features.
16|🟡 T2 Workshop Facilitation & Training.what_goes_wrong:
- Documentation portal set up but never actually maintained after initial handoff: a well-built documentation portal at handoff time gradually becomes stale as the system evolves, if there's no clear ownership or process for the customer's team to keep it updated. Fix: as covered in the broader documentation material, establish explicit post-handoff ownership for documentation maintenance, and consider building documentation updates into the same change-management process used for the underlying system (e.g. requiring a documentation update as part of any significant feature change's review process).
- Wrong tool chosen for the customer's actual technical comfort level: selecting Docusaurus's more developer-centric, code-based authoring workflow for a customer team without strong engineering comfort can create friction that discourages them from actually maintaining the documentation themselves post-handoff, when a simpler hosted platform with a more accessible content editor might have been better matched to their actual skill level. Fix: consider the customer team's specific technical comfort level and ongoing maintenance capacity when selecting a documentation platform, not just the tool's feature set in isolation.
16|🟡 T2 Workshop Facilitation & Training.real_example: An FDE delivering a custom AI API service to an enterprise customer built the API documentation using ReadMe specifically because its interactive API explorer let the customer's own application developers test real API calls with their own credentials directly within the documentation, dramatically reducing the back-and-forth questions about exact request/response formats that a static documentation page would have generated -- a deliberate tool choice matched to the specific need (API-centric documentation for a technical developer audience) rather than a default or arbitrary platform selection.

16|🟡 T2 Workshop Facilitation & Training.what_it_is: Diátaxis is a systematic framework for organizing technical documentation into four distinct types, each serving a genuinely different user need and requiring a genuinely different writing style: Tutorials (learning-oriented -- step-by-step lessons that take a beginner through a complete, successful experience, prioritizing the learner's confidence and concrete success over comprehensive coverage), How-to guides (task-oriented -- focused, practical instructions for accomplishing a specific, real-world goal, assuming the reader already has basic competence and just needs the steps for this particular task), Reference (information-oriented -- comprehensive, accurate, structured technical description, e.g. a complete API reference, optimized for being looked up rather than read sequentially), and Explanation (understanding-oriented -- discussion of concepts, background, and the 'why' behind design decisions, helping the reader build a deeper mental model rather than accomplish an immediate task).
16|🟡 T2 Workshop Facilitation & Training.why_it_exists: A huge amount of poor technical documentation results from mixing these four fundamentally different purposes together in a single document -- a tutorial that tries to also be a comprehensive reference becomes overwhelming and undermines the beginner's ability to follow along; a how-to guide that stops to explain deep conceptual background loses the reader who just needs the specific steps; a reference document written in a narrative, explanatory style becomes hard to scan and look things up in quickly. Diátaxis exists to make explicit that these are genuinely different writing tasks with different audiences and different success criteria, and that good documentation deliberately separates them into distinct, appropriately-structured content rather than blending them together.
16|🟡 T2 Workshop Facilitation & Training.how_it_works:
```
Applying Diátaxis to AI/FDE documentation deliverables (directly
extending the broader documentation material's runbook/
architecture-doc/training-material categories with this more
precise four-way structure):

Tutorial example (learning-oriented, for a new team member):
  'Your First Query: Building a Simple RAG Pipeline'
  Walks a complete beginner through setting up a minimal working
  example end-to-end, prioritizing a successful, confidence-
  building experience over comprehensive feature coverage
  Deliberately omits edge cases, advanced configuration options,
  and exhaustive error handling -- those belong elsewhere

How-to guide example (task-oriented, for someone with basic
competence needing to accomplish something specific):
  'How to Add a New Document Source to the Knowledge Base'
  Assumes the reader already understands the basic system and
  just needs the specific steps for this one task
  Direct, numbered steps, minimal conceptual digression

Reference example (information-oriented, for lookup):
  'API Endpoint Reference' or 'Configuration Parameter Reference'
  Comprehensive, systematically structured, optimized for
  scanning and looking up a specific detail (e.g. 'what does the
  chunk_overlap parameter do and what's its valid range?')
  Not meant to be read start-to-finish, but to be searched/jumped
  into at the exact relevant section

Explanation example (understanding-oriented, for deeper context):
  'Why We Chose Semantic Chunking Over Fixed-Size Chunking'
  Discusses the underlying reasoning, trade-offs, and design
  philosophy -- directly connects to the Architecture Decision
  Records practice covered in Rapid Prototyping material, since
  ADRs are essentially a specific form of Explanation-type content

Organizing documentation following this structure:
  Rather than one large, undifferentiated 'documentation' folder,
  explicitly organize content into four sections matching these
  categories, helping both writers (clarifying what kind of
  content they're producing and how to write it) and readers
  (quickly finding the type of content matching their current need
  -- learning, doing a task, looking something up, or
  understanding why)
```
16|🟡 T2 Workshop Facilitation & Training.use_when: Apply the Diátaxis structure when organizing any substantial documentation deliverable for a customer handoff (covered in the broader documentation material) -- explicitly separating tutorial, how-to, reference, and explanation content helps ensure each piece of documentation actually serves its intended reader well, rather than producing a single undifferentiated document that serves all needs poorly.
16|🟡 T2 Workshop Facilitation & Training.avoid_when: Don't force the full four-way Diátaxis structure onto a very small, simple documentation deliverable where the content naturally fits into just one or two of these categories (e.g. a small internal tool that only needs a single how-to guide and doesn't warrant separate tutorial/reference/explanation sections) -- apply the framework's distinguishing principle (don't mix these writing modes) without necessarily building out all four categories when the content genuinely doesn't require it.
16|🟡 T2 Workshop Facilitation & Training.what_goes_wrong:
- Tutorials bloated with comprehensive reference-style detail, undermining the beginner experience: a tutorial that tries to also serve as a complete reference (explaining every possible configuration option along the way) becomes overwhelming for a true beginner, defeating the tutorial's actual purpose of building confidence through a simple, successful first experience. Fix: ruthlessly scope tutorials to the minimum needed for a successful first experience, explicitly linking out to separate reference documentation for readers who want comprehensive detail, rather than including everything inline.
- How-to guides written with tutorial-style hand-holding that frustrates experienced users: a how-to guide that includes extensive beginner-level explanation and context (appropriate for a tutorial) frustrates a competent user who already understands the system and just wants the specific steps for their current task. Fix: write how-to guides assuming genuine baseline competence, getting directly to the actionable steps, and linking to Explanation-type content for readers who want the deeper why rather than including it inline.
16|🟡 T2 Workshop Facilitation & Training.real_example: A Databricks FDE restructuring a customer's existing, sprawling single-document Confluence page covering their AI pipeline into a Diátaxis-organized structure split it into: a 'Getting Started' tutorial (a new data engineer's first successful pipeline run), a set of focused how-to guides ('How to Add a New Data Source,' 'How to Adjust the Reranker Configuration'), a comprehensive parameter reference table, and a set of explanation documents covering the architecture decisions (directly reusing several existing ADRs as the basis for this section) -- feedback from the customer's team after the restructuring specifically noted that new team members could now follow the tutorial without being overwhelmed by configuration details, while experienced team members doing routine tasks could jump directly to the relevant how-to guide without wading through introductory material meant for beginners.

16|🟡 T2 Business Intelligence & Analytic.what_it_is: LookML is Looker's (Google Cloud's BI platform) proprietary modeling language for defining a semantic layer on top of raw database tables -- declaratively specifying dimensions, measures, joins, and business logic once in version-controlled LookML code, which Looker then compiles into SQL automatically whenever a user builds a report or explores data, rather than requiring every analyst to write correct, consistent SQL joins and aggregations themselves for every query. This is a specific, mature implementation of the broader 'semantic layer' concept (covered more generally in the dedicated semantic layers note) that predates and influenced many of the more recent semantic layer tools.
16|🟡 T2 Business Intelligence & Analytic.why_it_exists: Without a semantic layer, every analyst writing their own SQL queries against raw tables risks inconsistent business logic (one analyst's definition of 'active customer' differs subtly from another's, one person's revenue calculation includes refunds and another's doesn't) and requires deep knowledge of the underlying schema and correct join paths. LookML exists to centralize this business logic definition once, in a governed, version-controlled way, so that every report and dashboard built on top of it uses consistent, correct definitions -- and importantly for AI applications, this same governed semantic layer can become the foundation that an AI natural-language query tool (like Looker's own AI features, or an external tool like Genie covered elsewhere) translates user questions against, inheriting the semantic layer's consistency rather than each AI query reinventing business logic from scratch.
16|🟡 T2 Business Intelligence & Analytic.use_when: Leverage an existing LookML semantic model as the foundation for AI-powered natural language analytics whenever a customer already has a mature Looker deployment -- this avoids duplicating business logic definition work and ensures AI-generated queries inherit the same governed, consistent definitions analysts already trust.
16|🟡 T2 Business Intelligence & Analytic.avoid_when: Don't introduce Looker/LookML specifically to support an AI analytics use case if the customer has no existing Looker investment and a different semantic layer tool (covered separately) or a more direct approach (e.g. an ontology-based system like Palantir's) would better fit their existing stack and AI architecture.
16|🟡 T2 Business Intelligence & Analytic.what_goes_wrong:
- LookML model and underlying data drift out of sync without anyone noticing: if the underlying database schema changes without a corresponding LookML update, dimensions/measures can silently break or return incorrect results -- a specific instance of the broader data contract risks covered elsewhere, here at the semantic layer specifically. Fix: apply the same schema validation and breaking-change-notification discipline to LookML model changes as to any other production data contract.
- AI query tool bypasses the semantic layer for performance or flexibility reasons, reintroducing inconsistency: under pressure to support a query pattern the LookML model doesn't cleanly accommodate, a team builds a workaround that queries the raw tables directly, undermining the centralized consistency benefit the semantic layer was meant to provide. Fix: extend the LookML model to properly support new query patterns rather than bypassing it, preserving the single-source-of-truth benefit even when it requires more upfront semantic modeling effort.
16|🟡 T2 Business Intelligence & Analytic.real_example: A retail company with an established Looker deployment wanted to add natural-language AI querying for their business analysts. Rather than building a separate AI data layer from scratch, the FDE configured the AI query tool to generate Looker API calls against the existing, already-validated LookML explores rather than generating raw SQL directly against the warehouse -- meaning the AI-generated answers used exactly the same revenue, customer, and order definitions the company's existing dashboards already used, eliminating the risk of the AI tool quietly using a different (and inconsistent) definition of a core business metric than what analysts saw in their standard Looker dashboards.

16|🟡 T2 Business Intelligence & Analytic.what_it_is: ThoughtSpot is a business intelligence platform built specifically around search-based analytics -- allowing business users to type natural-language-like search queries (e.g. 'revenue by region last quarter') directly into a search bar interface, with the platform translating this into the appropriate query against underlying data and instantly generating an appropriate visualization, rather than requiring users to navigate a traditional BI tool's menu-driven report-building interface. ThoughtSpot was an early and influential mover in bringing this search-driven, more natural-language-adjacent interaction model to enterprise analytics, predating the more recent wave of LLM-powered analytics tools (like Databricks Genie, covered elsewhere) that have since extended this concept further using actual large language models.
16|🟡 T2 Business Intelligence & Analytic.why_it_exists: Traditional BI tools require users to learn a specific tool's report-building paradigm (selecting dimensions and measures from menus, configuring chart types, building filters step by step) -- a meaningful barrier for business users who know what question they want answered but don't want to learn a complex tool's interface. ThoughtSpot exists to lower this barrier by making the interaction feel more like a search engine (a familiar, low-friction interaction pattern most users already understand) than a traditional BI report builder, broadening self-service analytics access to a wider population of business users.
16|🟡 T2 Business Intelligence & Analytic.how_it_works:
```
ThoughtSpot search-based analytics flow:

1. Data is modeled into ThoughtSpot's semantic layer (similar in
   concept to LookML's semantic modeling, defining tables,
   relationships, and business logic once)

2. Business user types a search query into the search bar:
   'revenue by region last quarter'

3. ThoughtSpot's search engine (using its own NLP/search
   technology, with increasing LLM-powered enhancement in more
   recent versions) parses this into:
     Measure: revenue
     Dimension: region
     Filter: last quarter

4. Generates the appropriate underlying query and automatically
   selects and renders an appropriate visualization (e.g. a bar
   chart of revenue by region) without the user needing to
   manually configure chart type or query structure

5. Iterative refinement:
   User can refine the search ('revenue by region last quarter,
   excluding online channel') and the visualization updates
   accordingly, supporting an exploratory, conversational-feeling
   analysis flow

Relationship to more recent LLM-powered analytics (Genie, etc.):
  ThoughtSpot's search-based approach was built primarily on
  structured search/NLP technology rather than large language
  models initially, representing an earlier generation of
  'natural-language-adjacent' analytics interfaces
  More recent LLM-powered tools (covered in the Databricks Genie
  material) extend this concept further with genuine natural
  language understanding and more flexible, conversational
  multi-turn interaction, representing the next evolution of the
  same underlying goal ThoughtSpot pioneered: making analytics
  accessible without requiring traditional BI tool expertise
```
16|🟡 T2 Business Intelligence & Analytic.use_when: Consider ThoughtSpot when a customer wants to broaden self-service analytics access to a less technical business user population and values its mature, established search-based interaction model -- particularly relevant for organizations already invested in ThoughtSpot who want to extend or compare its capability against newer LLM-powered alternatives.
16|🟡 T2 Business Intelligence & Analytic.avoid_when: Don't introduce ThoughtSpot specifically for a greenfield AI analytics initiative when a more modern, genuinely LLM-powered tool (covered in the Genie and broader AI analytics material) would provide more flexible, conversational natural language understanding -- ThoughtSpot's search-based model, while still valuable and actively evolving with LLM enhancements, represents a different generation of the underlying technology than purpose-built LLM analytics tools.
16|🟡 T2 Business Intelligence & Analytic.what_goes_wrong:
- Search query ambiguity produces unexpected or incorrect visualizations: a natural-language-style search query can be genuinely ambiguous (e.g. 'top customers' -- by revenue? by order count? by tenure?), and if the search engine's default interpretation doesn't match the user's actual intent, they may not realize the displayed result answers a different question than they meant to ask. Fix: similar to the RAG hallucination-confidence concerns covered elsewhere, ensure the interface clearly shows exactly how the search query was interpreted (which measure, which definition) so users can verify and correct misinterpretation rather than trusting an ambiguous result at face value.
- Underlying semantic model quality limits search accuracy: as with any semantic-layer-dependent tool, ThoughtSpot's search accuracy depends heavily on the quality and completeness of the underlying data model definitions -- poorly modeled or incompletely annotated data leads to poor search results regardless of the search technology's sophistication. Fix: invest in thorough semantic model definition and metadata quality (column descriptions, synonyms for common business terms) as the foundation for good search-based analytics, the same underlying-data-quality dependency covered for Genie Spaces elsewhere.
16|🟡 T2 Business Intelligence & Analytic.real_example: A consumer goods company using ThoughtSpot for self-service sales analytics found that brand managers (with no SQL or BI tool training) could independently answer their own ad-hoc questions ('sales of product X in the Northeast last month compared to the same period last year') by simply typing the question into ThoughtSpot's search interface, dramatically reducing their dependence on the central analytics team for routine ad-hoc questions -- though the analytics team specifically invested significant effort defining synonyms and business-term mappings in the underlying semantic model (e.g. mapping common informal product nicknames brand managers used to the formal SKU names in the database) to ensure search queries using the team's natural, informal vocabulary actually resolved correctly.

16|🟡 T2 Business Intelligence & Analytic.what_it_is: Cube, AtScale, and dbt Semantic Layer are three modern, more BI-tool-agnostic implementations of the semantic layer concept (introduced via LookML elsewhere) -- centralizing business metric and dimension definitions once, but designed specifically to serve multiple different downstream consumers (various BI tools, AI applications, ad-hoc SQL users) rather than being tied to one specific BI platform's proprietary modeling language. Cube is an open-source (with a commercial cloud offering) semantic layer designed to sit between data warehouses and various consumption layers (BI tools, custom applications, APIs). AtScale is an enterprise-focused semantic layer platform with strong support for high-performance, large-scale OLAP-style query acceleration. dbt Semantic Layer extends dbt (the popular open-source data transformation tool) with metric definitions that live alongside the existing dbt transformation models, letting metric logic be defined in the same place and same version-control workflow as the broader data pipeline transformation code.
16|🟡 T2 Business Intelligence & Analytic.why_it_exists: LookML's semantic modeling is powerful but tightly coupled to Looker specifically -- if an organization wants to serve multiple different BI tools, a custom AI application, and ad-hoc analyst SQL queries all from the same single, consistent set of business metric definitions, a Looker-specific semantic layer doesn't serve consumers outside the Looker ecosystem. These more tool-agnostic semantic layer products exist specifically to decouple the 'define the metric once, correctly' benefit from any single specific BI tool, making the semantic layer a genuinely shared, multi-consumer foundation -- directly relevant to AI applications, since an AI natural-language query tool can be just one more consumer of a shared, already-governed semantic layer rather than requiring its own separate metric definition effort.
16|🟡 T2 Business Intelligence & Analytic.how_it_works:
```yaml
# Cube semantic layer: defining a metric once, accessible to
# multiple downstream consumers via a unified API
cubes:
  - name: orders
    sql_table: analytics.orders

    measures:
      - name: total_revenue
        sql: revenue_usd
        type: sum
        filters:
          - sql: "{CUBE}.status != 'refunded'"

      - name: order_count
        type: count

    dimensions:
      - name: order_date
        sql: order_date
        type: time
      - name: region
        sql: region
        type: string

# This single definition is now queryable via:
# - Cube's own REST/GraphQL/SQL API (for custom AI applications)
# - Connected BI tools (Tableau, Power BI, etc. via Cube's
#   connectors)
# - Direct SQL-like queries from analysts
# All consumers get the exact same 'total_revenue' definition
# (excluding refunds), eliminating the inconsistency risk of each
# consumer tool defining revenue separately

# dbt Semantic Layer: metrics defined alongside existing dbt
# transformation models (in YAML, within the dbt project)
metrics:
  - name: total_revenue
    label: Total Revenue
    model: ref('fct_orders')
    calculation_method: sum
    expression: revenue_usd
    filter: |
      {{ Dimension('order__status') }} != 'refunded'

AI integration relevance:
  An AI agent or natural-language query tool calling into any of
  these semantic layers' APIs (rather than generating raw SQL
  against warehouse tables directly) inherits the centralized,
  validated metric definitions -- directly reducing the SQL
  hallucination and inconsistent-business-logic risks covered in
  the Genie and RAG material elsewhere in this phase
```
16|🟡 T2 Business Intelligence & Analytic.use_when: Adopt a tool-agnostic semantic layer (Cube, AtScale, or dbt Semantic Layer) when an organization needs consistent metric definitions served across multiple different consumers (several BI tools, custom applications, and AI agents simultaneously) rather than being centered around a single BI platform -- particularly valuable when building a new AI analytics capability that should reuse, not duplicate, existing governed metric definitions already used elsewhere in the organization.
16|🟡 T2 Business Intelligence & Analytic.avoid_when: Don't introduce a new, separate semantic layer tool if the organization already has a mature semantic layer (e.g. an established LookML model) that adequately serves the AI use case's needs -- prefer extending and connecting to existing semantic infrastructure over introducing redundant, competing metric definition systems that risk creating exactly the inconsistency these tools are meant to prevent.
16|🟡 T2 Business Intelligence & Analytic.what_goes_wrong:
- Semantic layer adopted but legacy direct-SQL access paths remain, undermining consistency: introducing a new semantic layer for some consumers while other teams/tools continue querying the underlying warehouse tables directly (bypassing the semantic layer entirely) means the consistency benefit is only partially realized, with the legacy direct-access paths still able to drift from the centralized definitions. Fix: actively migrate and deprecate direct warehouse access paths in favor of the semantic layer over time, rather than treating semantic layer adoption as additive without addressing existing inconsistent access patterns.
- Performance overhead of the semantic layer's query translation underestimated for high-volume AI query patterns: an AI application generating many semantic-layer queries (e.g. for batch processing or high-frequency interactive use) can encounter performance characteristics different from what a human analyst's occasional dashboard refresh would experience, and these AI-specific load patterns need to be load-tested explicitly. Fix: benchmark the semantic layer's performance specifically under the AI application's expected query volume and pattern, not just typical human-analyst usage assumptions.

16|🟡 T2 Business Intelligence & Analytic.what_it_is: Embedded analytics refers to integrating BI dashboards, charts, or AI-powered analytics directly within another application's user interface (e.g. a SaaS product showing usage analytics dashboards to its own customers, rather than those customers needing to log into a separate standalone BI tool) -- using one of several common technical integration patterns: iframe embedding (the simplest approach, embedding a BI tool's dashboard URL directly within an iframe element on the host application's page), JWT-based authentication (using signed JSON Web Tokens to securely pass the host application's user identity and permissions into the embedded analytics, ensuring the embedded dashboard respects the same access control the user already has in the host application), and white-label SDKs (more sophisticated embedding libraries provided by BI vendors that allow deeper, more native-feeling integration with custom styling, removing visible branding from the underlying BI tool, going beyond a simple iframe to feel like a genuinely native part of the host application).
16|🟡 T2 Business Intelligence & Analytic.why_it_exists: Many AI/analytics products need to deliver their insights within the context of an existing application a customer already uses daily, rather than requiring customers to navigate to a separate, distinct analytics tool -- a meaningful adoption barrier the broader rapid prototyping and customer enablement material covered elsewhere consistently emphasizes minimizing. Embedded analytics technical patterns exist specifically to make this in-context delivery technically practical and secure, with JWT-based authentication in particular solving the specific challenge of ensuring an embedded dashboard's data access respects the same permission boundaries (covered in the access control material elsewhere) the user already has in the host application, rather than requiring a separate, parallel authentication and authorization system.

# JWT generation for secure, permission-aware embedding
# (server-side code in the host application)
import jwt
import time

def generate_embed_token(user_id: str, customer_account_id: str) -> str:
    payload = {
        'sub': user_id,
        'exp': int(time.time()) + 3600,  # 1-hour token validity
        # Critical: pass the host application's own permission
        # context (e.g. which customer account this user belongs
        # to) so the embedded dashboard applies the SAME row-level
        # filtering the user already has in the host application
        'filters': {'customer_account_id': customer_account_id},
        # Optionally restrict which specific dashboards/data this
        # embedded session can access
        'permissions': ['view_analytics']
    }
    return jwt.encode(payload, EMBED_SIGNING_SECRET, algorithm='HS256')

# The BI tool's embedding infrastructure verifies this JWT's
# signature (using a shared secret with the host application) and
# applies the embedded filters/permissions automatically, ensuring
# the embedded analytics respects the host app's own access control
# rather than requiring a separate parallel permission system

# White-label SDK approach (conceptual, vendor-specific syntax
# varies): a JavaScript SDK provided by the BI/analytics vendor
# that renders components natively within the host application's
# own UI framework, with custom CSS theming to match the host
# app's branding, going beyond an iframe's visual and
# interaction limitations
```

Use a white-label SDK over a simple iframe when a more deeply integrated, native-feeling user experience matters for product quality, and a simple iframe when faster implementation and lower integration complexity outweighs the visual/interaction polish difference.
16|🟡 T2 Business Intelligence & Analytic.avoid_when: Don't build embedded analytics infrastructure for an internal-only tool where users already have direct access to the underlying BI platform and embedding within another application provides no genuine adoption or workflow benefit -- the additional integration complexity (JWT signing infrastructure, permission mapping) is only justified when there's a genuine need to deliver analytics within a different host application's context.
16|🟡 T2 Business Intelligence & Analytic.what_goes_wrong:
- JWT permission mapping incorrectly implemented, leaking data across customer accounts: if the JWT generation logic incorrectly maps or fails to properly restrict the embedded session's data access filters, a multi-tenant SaaS product's embedded analytics could leak one customer's data into another customer's embedded dashboard view -- a serious security and trust failure. Fix: rigorously test the JWT-based permission mapping with explicit test cases for every customer/account boundary, treating this with the same access-control testing rigor covered in the broader security and compliance material, since embedded analytics permission bugs can have severe multi-tenant data leakage consequences.
- Token expiration handling not implemented gracefully: if an embedded session's JWT expires while a user is actively viewing a dashboard (common for longer user sessions), without proper token refresh handling the embedded view can fail or show a confusing error rather than transparently refreshing access. Fix: implement automatic token refresh logic in the host application (generating and supplying a new JWT before the current one expires) for any embedded analytics session expected to remain open for longer than the token's validity window.

16|🟡 T2 Business Intelligence & Analytic.what_it_is: OLAP (Online Analytical Processing) cube design refers to structuring data specifically for fast, multi-dimensional analytical queries (slicing and dicing data across multiple dimensions simultaneously -- e.g. revenue by product, by region, by time period, by customer segment, in any combination), and the Kimball methodology (named after Ralph Kimball, a foundational figure in data warehousing) is the most widely-adopted, established approach for designing this kind of dimensional data model -- directly building on and extending the star schema and dimensional modeling concepts covered in the dedicated Phase 16 note on dimensional modeling, with Kimball's methodology providing the broader, more complete set of design principles (conformed dimensions, slowly changing dimensions, the bus matrix for planning an entire data warehouse's dimensional model) beyond just the basic star schema structure itself.
16|🟡 T2 Business Intelligence & Analytic.why_it_exists: Business intelligence and analytics users need to ask multi-dimensional questions fluidly ('show me revenue by region, but now break that down further by product category, and now filter to just this quarter') without each new dimensional combination requiring a completely new, custom-built query or data structure -- the Kimball methodology's dimensional modeling approach (fact tables surrounded by dimension tables, as covered in the dimensional modeling material) exists specifically to support this kind of flexible, fast, multi-dimensional analytical querying pattern efficiently at scale, and has remained the dominant, proven approach for data warehouse design for decades specifically because it reliably delivers this analytical flexibility.
16|🟡 T2 Business Intelligence & Analytic.how_it_works:
```
Kimball methodology core principles (extending the basic star
schema covered in dimensional modeling material with the broader
methodology's complete design approach):

1. Bus matrix planning (enterprise-wide dimensional model planning):
   Before building individual star schemas, map out the full set
   of business processes (sales, inventory, shipping, returns)
   across rows, and the dimensions relevant to each (date,
   product, customer, store) across columns -- identifying which
   dimensions are shared ('conformed') across multiple business
   processes

2. Conformed dimensions (a key Kimball principle):
   The same dimension table (e.g. dim_date, dim_product) is
   reused consistently across multiple fact tables for different
   business processes, rather than each business process having
   its own separate, potentially inconsistent date or product
   dimension
   This conformance is what allows cross-process analysis (e.g.
   comparing sales fact data and returns fact data using the same
   shared dim_product) to work correctly and consistently

3. Grain definition (critical, often underestimated step):
   Explicitly define the grain (level of detail) of each fact
   table before building it -- 'one row per individual sale line
   item' is a different grain than 'one row per daily product-
   store aggregate,' and mixing grains within a single fact table
   is a classic, serious dimensional modeling error

4. Slowly Changing Dimensions (SCD, covered in more depth in the
   temporal modeling material elsewhere):
   Kimball's methodology formally defines SCD types (Type 1
   overwrite, Type 2 versioned history, and others) as the
   standard approach for handling dimension attributes that
   change over time

5. Application to AI/analytics:
   A well-designed Kimball-style dimensional model is precisely
   the kind of structure that performs well for both traditional
   BI dashboard queries AND as the underlying data source for an
   AI natural-language query tool (Genie, ThoughtSpot, or a
   semantic-layer-backed AI agent) -- the same dimensional
   clarity that helps a human analyst build a correct query also
   helps an AI-generated query be correct, since the conformed,
   well-defined structure reduces ambiguity
```
16|🟡 T2 Business Intelligence & Analytic.use_when: Apply Kimball dimensional modeling methodology (bus matrix planning, conformed dimensions, explicit grain definition) when designing the underlying analytical data warehouse that will support both traditional BI tools and AI-powered analytics querying -- this foundational data modeling discipline benefits AI query accuracy just as much as traditional human-driven BI, since both depend on a clear, consistent, well-defined dimensional structure.
16|🟡 T2 Business Intelligence & Analytic.avoid_when: Don't invest in full enterprise-wide Kimball bus matrix planning for a small, single-purpose analytics project where a simple, narrowly-scoped star schema (covered in the dimensional modeling material) is entirely sufficient -- reserve the full methodology's broader planning rigor for genuine enterprise-scale data warehouse design efforts spanning multiple business processes.
16|🟡 T2 Business Intelligence & Analytic.what_goes_wrong:
- Grain mixing within a single fact table causes silent, hard-to-detect aggregation errors: if a fact table inconsistently mixes different levels of detail (some rows at the line-item grain, others accidentally aggregated to a daily summary grain), aggregation queries can silently double-count or undercount, producing wrong numbers that look plausible and may go unnoticed for a long time. Fix: rigorously define and enforce a single, consistent grain for every fact table, with explicit validation checks (similar to the data quality monitoring practices covered elsewhere) confirming grain consistency as new data loads.
- Conformed dimensions not actually enforced across different business process fact tables: teams building separate fact tables for different business processes (sales, returns) sometimes build separate, slightly inconsistent dimension tables for convenience rather than genuinely sharing conformed dimensions, undermining the cross-process analytical capability the conformed-dimension principle is meant to enable. Fix: establish and enforce a single, centrally-governed set of core dimension tables (the same MDM golden-record discipline covered in the ontology design material) that all relevant fact tables reference, rather than allowing each team to build their own separate dimension tables.
16|🟡 T2 Business Intelligence & Analytic.real_example: A retail company's data warehouse, originally built with inconsistent grain and non-conformed dimensions across different teams' separately-built fact tables, made cross-functional analysis (comparing sales performance against inventory and returns data together) unreliable and error-prone. A redesign following Kimball methodology explicitly defined a conformed dim_product and dim_date used consistently across new sales, inventory, and returns fact tables (each with explicitly documented, enforced grain), and this redesigned, properly conformed dimensional model subsequently became the direct foundation for an AI-powered natural-language analytics tool that could now reliably answer genuinely cross-functional questions ('which products had high return rates relative to their sales volume last quarter') that the previous, inconsistent data model structure had made unreliable to answer correctly even with careful manual SQL, let alone AI-generated queries.

16|🟡 T2 Project Scoping & Feasibility|Pr.what_it_is: Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) analysis for AI projects is a structured framework for estimating the complete, full-lifecycle cost of an AI initiative -- going beyond the obvious upfront costs (initial development, licensing) to systematically capture often-underestimated ongoing costs: infrastructure/compute (the cost management material covered elsewhere), ongoing model API or hosting costs, data pipeline maintenance, monitoring and observability tooling, periodic re-evaluation and retraining, customer support/operations staffing, and the opportunity cost of the engineering time required to maintain the system over its expected lifetime, not just to build it initially.
16|🟡 T2 Project Scoping & Feasibility|Pr.why_it_exists: AI projects are particularly prone to TCO underestimation compared to traditional software projects, because the ongoing operational costs (LLM API spend scaling with usage, the need for continuous evaluation and quality monitoring, model updates, data pipeline maintenance as source systems evolve) are less intuitive and less visible during initial scoping than they are for more traditional software with more predictable, stable ongoing costs. A rigorous TCO framework exists specifically to surface these often-underestimated ongoing costs during project scoping and feasibility assessment, before committing budget based on an initial development cost estimate that dramatically understates the true multi-year cost of operating the system.

16|🟡 T2 Project Scoping & Feasibility|Pr.use_when: Build a multi-year TCO estimate during the Project Scoping & Feasibility phase of any significant AI initiative, explicitly presenting it alongside (not instead of) the value/ROI projection, so decision-makers see the complete financial picture rather than an initial-development-cost-only estimate that would make the project look more favorable than its true total cost actually supports.
16|🟡 T2 Project Scoping & Feasibility|Pr.avoid_when: Don't build an elaborate, highly detailed multi-year TCO model for a small, low-risk pilot or proof-of-concept where the actual financial exposure is modest and a simpler, less rigorous estimate is proportionate to the decision being made -- reserve the full TCO rigor for genuinely significant, multi-year commitment decisions.
16|🟡 T2 Project Scoping & Feasibility|Pr.what_goes_wrong:
- Ongoing LLM API costs projected using pilot-scale usage rather than realistic production-scale growth: a TCO estimate built using the current small pilot's API usage, without modeling how costs will scale as usage grows toward full production adoption, dramatically underestimates the actual ongoing cost once the system reaches its intended scale. Fix: explicitly model usage growth scenarios (conservative, expected, aggressive adoption) and project the corresponding cost scaling, rather than extrapolating linearly from a small pilot's modest usage.
- Maintenance and technical debt costs omitted entirely from the TCO estimate: many TCO estimates focus heavily on infrastructure and API costs while omitting the ongoing engineering time required for evaluation, monitoring, and addressing the technical debt that naturally accumulates over a system's life (the technical debt material covered elsewhere). 16|🟡 T2 Project Scoping & Feasibility|Pr.what_it_is: A Build vs Buy vs Partner decision matrix is a structured framework for evaluating, for any given AI capability need, whether an organization should build a custom solution in-house, buy an existing off-the-shelf product/vendor solution, or partner (engaging an external team -- an FDE consulting engagement, a specialized vendor's professional services -- to build a more customized solution leveraging their platform or expertise) -- systematically weighing factors like cost, time-to-value, required ongoing maintenance capability, strategic differentiation value, and the organization's existing internal capability against each of these three paths, rather than defaulting to whichever option a particular internal champion happens to prefer.
16|🟡 T2 Project Scoping & Feasibility|Pr.why_it_exists: Organizations facing a new AI capability need often gravitate toward one default option based on organizational culture or bias (an engineering-heavy culture defaults to 'build,' a procurement-heavy culture defaults to 'buy') without systematically evaluating whether that default is actually the right choice for the specific situation -- a structured decision matrix exists to force explicit consideration of the genuine trade-offs across all three paths, surfacing situations where the organization's default instinct would actually be the wrong choice for this particular capability need.
16|🟡 T2 Project Scoping & Feasibility|Pr.how_it_works:
```
Build vs Buy vs Partner decision matrix framework:

Evaluation dimensions (scored or assessed for each option):

1. Strategic differentiation:
   Does this capability provide genuine competitive
   differentiation, or is it a commodity capability many
   competitors also need?
   High differentiation value -> leans toward Build (worth the
   investment to own and control a differentiating capability)
   Commodity capability -> leans toward Buy (don't reinvent
   something a mature vendor already solves well)

2. Time-to-value:
   How quickly is this capability needed?
   Urgent need -> leans toward Buy or Partner (faster than
   building from scratch, similar to the rapid prototyping
   principle of using existing tools rather than building
   everything custom)
   Longer runway available -> Build becomes more viable

3. Internal capability and ongoing maintenance capacity:
   Does the organization have (or is willing to build) the
   internal team capable of maintaining a built solution
   long-term? (connecting to the TCO and knowledge transfer
   material covered elsewhere -- a built solution requires
   ongoing internal capability, not just initial development)
   Limited internal AI/ML capability -> leans toward Buy or
   Partner (with explicit knowledge transfer, covered in Customer
   Engagement material, to build capability over time)

4. Total cost of ownership comparison:
   Compare the multi-year TCO (covered in the dedicated TCO note)
   across all three paths -- Buy/Partner often has lower upfront
   cost but ongoing licensing/engagement fees; Build has higher
   upfront cost but potentially lower long-term marginal cost at
   scale, depending on the specific situation

5. Customization/fit requirements:
   How well do existing off-the-shelf solutions actually fit the
   specific need, versus requiring extensive customization that
   might approach the cost/complexity of building custom anyway?

Decision matrix output:
  Score or qualitatively assess each option across these
  dimensions for the specific capability need, making the
  trade-offs explicit and documented (similar to the
  Architecture Decision Record practice covered in Rapid
  Prototyping material) rather than an implicit, undocumented
  default choice

16|🟡 T2 Project Scoping & Feasibility|Pr.use_when: Apply a structured build/buy/partner evaluation explicitly during the Project Scoping & Feasibility phase for any significant new AI capability decision, especially when there's organizational disagreement or bias toward a particular default option that hasn't been rigorously tested against the alternatives.
16|🟡 T2 Project Scoping & Feasibility|Pr.avoid_when: Don't apply the full formal decision matrix process for small, low-stakes capability decisions where the right choice is genuinely obvious and uncontested (e.g. using an established, well-fitting off-the-shelf tool for a clearly commodity need) -- reserve the structured rigor for genuinely significant, non-obvious decisions with real trade-offs worth deliberating.
16|🟡 T2 Project Scoping & Feasibility|Pr.what_goes_wrong:
- Build chosen for strategic-sounding reasons without honest internal capability assessment: an organization decides to build a custom AI capability in-house, citing strategic differentiation value, without honestly assessing whether they actually have (or are realistically willing to invest in building) the internal team capability to build AND maintain it long-term -- leading to a built system that becomes unmaintained technical debt once initial development momentum fades. Fix: weight the internal capability and ongoing maintenance capacity dimension honestly and heavily in the decision, not just the strategic value dimension, since strategic value alone doesn't guarantee successful long-term execution of a build decision.
- Buy decision made without adequately assessing customization gap: an organization selects an off-the-shelf vendor solution based on attractive marketing and pricing, without rigorously testing whether it actually fits their specific, sometimes unusual requirements, discovering significant customization gaps only after committing to the purchase. Fix: conduct a rigorous fit assessment (potentially via a pre-sales POC, covered in Customer Engagement material) against the organization's actual specific requirements before finalizing a Buy decision, not just a feature-checklist comparison against marketing materials.
16|🟡 T2 Project Scoping & Feasibility|Pr.real_example: A mid-sized financial services company evaluating an AI-powered fraud detection capability initially leaned toward Build (their engineering culture defaulted to building most capabilities in-house), but a structured decision matrix evaluation revealed: fraud detection is a relatively commodity capability with several mature vendor solutions already trained on much larger, more diverse fraud datasets than the company could assemble internally (low strategic differentiation, since their competitive advantage lay elsewhere); the company had limited internal ML engineering capacity already stretched across other priorities; and time-to-value was urgent given an active fraud trend the company was experiencing. This honest assessment led the company to choose Buy (a specialized fraud detection vendor) over their initial Build instinct, deploying a working solution within weeks rather than the many months a custom build would have required, while reserving their limited internal ML capacity for capabilities more directly tied to their genuine competitive differentiation.

16|🟡 T2 Project Scoping & Feasibility|Pr.what_it_is: ROI modeling with sensitivity analysis extends the basic ROI/value quantification framework (covered in Customer Engagement material) by explicitly testing how the projected return on investment changes under different assumptions -- rather than presenting a single, fixed ROI estimate, sensitivity analysis systematically varies key uncertain inputs (e.g. AI accuracy improvement percentage, adoption rate, usage volume growth) across a realistic range (conservative, expected, optimistic scenarios) to show decision-makers not just a single projected number but the range of plausible outcomes and which specific assumptions the ROI conclusion is most sensitive to.
16|🟡 T2 Project Scoping & Feasibility|Pr.why_it_exists: A single-point ROI estimate ('this project will deliver $2M in annual savings') creates a false sense of precision and certainty about numbers that are, in reality, built on uncertain assumptions about AI accuracy, user adoption, and usage patterns that haven't actually been observed yet at the time of the estimate -- sensitivity analysis exists specifically to be honest about this uncertainty, showing decision-makers the actual range of plausible outcomes and, critically, which assumptions matter most to the conclusion (so that those specific assumptions can receive extra scrutiny or be validated early through a pilot, rather than the project committing to a single confident number that may not hold up).
16|🟡 T2 Project Scoping & Feasibility|Pr.how_it_works:
```
Sensitivity analysis framework for an AI project's ROI model:

1. Identify key uncertain inputs (the ones the ROI estimate is
   most dependent on):
   AI accuracy/effectiveness (e.g. 'AI correctly handles 75% of
   queries without human escalation' -- how confident is this
   number, really, before the system has been built and tested?)
   User adoption rate (what % of the target user population will
   actually use the new AI capability, versus continuing old
   workflows?)
   Usage volume growth (will usage stay flat, or grow as the
   capability becomes more trusted/known?)

2. Define a realistic range for each uncertain input:
   Conservative: AI handles 60% of queries, 50% adoption rate
   Expected: AI handles 75% of queries, 75% adoption rate
   Optimistic: AI handles 85% of queries, 90% adoption rate

3. Calculate ROI/value under each scenario combination:
   Conservative scenario ROI: e.g. $800K annual savings
   Expected scenario ROI: e.g. $2M annual savings
   Optimistic scenario ROI: e.g. $3.2M annual savings

4. Identify which input the conclusion is most sensitive to:
   A tornado diagram or similar visualization showing which
   single input, when varied across its realistic range while
   holding others at their expected value, causes the largest
   swing in the ROI outcome -- this is the assumption most worth
   validating early (e.g. through a pilot measuring actual
   adoption rate, covered in the POC-to-production material)
   before committing to a larger investment based on it

5. Present the full range, not just a single number, to decision-
   makers:
   'Even in our conservative scenario, this project delivers
   positive ROI with a 4-month payback period -- and our most
   critical assumption to validate early is user adoption rate,
   which we recommend testing explicitly during the pilot phase
   before scaling the full investment'
```
16|🟡 T2 Project Scoping & Feasibility|Pr.use_when: Build sensitivity analysis into any significant AI investment ROI presentation, particularly for projects with genuinely uncertain key assumptions (a novel use case without established benchmarks, or a use case heavily dependent on user adoption behavior that's hard to predict confidently) -- this builds more credible, defensible business cases than a single-point estimate, and helps focus pilot validation efforts on exactly the assumptions that matter most.
16|🟡 T2 Project Scoping & Feasibility|Pr.avoid_when: Don't build elaborate sensitivity analysis for situations with well-established, low-uncertainty inputs (e.g. a well-understood automation use case with extensive prior benchmark data from similar implementations) -- the additional analytical rigor isn't needed when the underlying assumptions are already well-validated and low-risk.
16|🟡 T2 Project Scoping & Feasibility|Pr.what_goes_wrong:
- Sensitivity ranges defined too narrowly, creating false confidence: if the conservative-to-optimistic range for key inputs is defined too narrowly (not genuinely capturing realistic worst-case uncertainty), the resulting sensitivity analysis can create a false sense that even the 'conservative' case is safely positive, when a genuinely wider, more honest uncertainty range might reveal real downside risk. Fix: deliberately stress-test the conservative scenario with genuinely pessimistic (not just slightly-below-expected) assumptions, to honestly surface whether the project remains viable even under real adverse conditions, not just mild ones.
- Sensitivity analysis conducted but not actually used to inform pilot design: identifying that adoption rate is the most sensitive, uncertain assumption is only valuable if this insight actually shapes how the pilot phase is designed (e.g. explicitly measuring and validating adoption rate as a primary pilot success metric) -- if the sensitivity analysis insight is generated but then ignored in subsequent pilot planning, its value is lost. Fix: explicitly connect sensitivity analysis findings to the pilot's success metrics and evaluation plan (the evaluation-driven development principles covered in Rapid Prototyping material), ensuring the most uncertain, most consequential assumptions get prioritized validation during the pilot.
16|🟡 T2 Project Scoping & Feasibility|Pr.real_example: An FDE presenting a business case for an AI-powered inventory forecasting system to a retail company's executive team built a sensitivity analysis showing that while the expected-case ROI was very strong, the project's value was most sensitive to forecast accuracy improvement (rather than to adoption, since the system would automate forecasting rather than depend on end-user behavior change) -- this finding directly informed the pilot phase design, which specifically prioritized rigorous, holdout-validated accuracy measurement against the existing forecasting process before any decision to scale the system company-wide, rather than the team's original plan to roll out to all regions simultaneously based on early, less rigorously validated accuracy numbers from a small initial test.

16|🟡 T2 Project Scoping & Feasibility|Pr.what_it_is: MoSCoW and RICE are two complementary, structured prioritization frameworks used during MVP scoping (extending the MVP-first principle covered in Rapid Prototyping material with more formal prioritization rigor). MoSCoW categorizes candidate features into four buckets -- Must have (the MVP fails without this), Should have (important but not strictly necessary for the MVP), Could have (nice-to-have, included only if time/resources allow), and Won't have (explicitly excluded from this scope, addressing the same explicit out-of-scope documentation principle covered in scope management material). RICE is a quantitative scoring framework that ranks features by calculating Reach (how many users does this affect) x Impact (how much does it matter to each affected user) x Confidence (how confident are we in the reach/impact estimates) / Effort (how much work is required) -- producing a single comparable score for ranking competing feature candidates against each other.
16|🟡 T2 Project Scoping & Feasibility|Pr.why_it_exists: Pareto-prioritization (covered in Rapid Prototyping material) establishes the principle that most value concentrates in a small subset of features, but doesn't by itself provide a structured, repeatable process for actually sorting a long list of candidate features into that prioritized subset -- MoSCoW and RICE exist as concrete, structured methods for doing exactly this sorting, each suited to slightly different scoping situations: MoSCoW's qualitative bucketing is fast and intuitive for stakeholder discussions, while RICE's quantitative scoring provides a more rigorous, defensible ranking when comparing many candidate features with genuinely different effort and impact profiles.

16|🟡 T2 Project Scoping & Feasibility|Pr.use_when: Use MoSCoW for fast, collaborative stakeholder scoping discussions (it's intuitive and easy for non-technical stakeholders to engage with directly, similar to the dot-voting prioritization technique covered in workshop facilitation material) and RICE when comparing a longer list of candidate features with genuinely different effort/impact profiles where a more quantitative, defensible ranking would help resolve disagreement or simply provide more rigor than intuitive bucketing alone.
16|🟡 T2 Project Scoping & Feasibility|Pr.avoid_when: Don't apply RICE's quantitative scoring rigor when the underlying reach/impact/confidence estimates would themselves be essentially guesses with no real basis -- forcing false precision onto genuinely unknown quantities can create misleading confidence in a ranking that's actually just dressed-up intuition. In those cases, MoSCoW's simpler qualitative bucketing is more honest about the actual level of certainty involved.
16|🟡 T2 Project Scoping & Feasibility|Pr.what_goes_wrong:
- MoSCoW bucket inflation, where everything becomes 'Must have': without disciplined facilitation, stakeholders tend to push for as many features as possible into the Must Have category, defeating the framework's purpose of forcing genuine prioritization. Fix: explicitly cap the number of Must Have items (a common practice is limiting Must Haves to a small percentage of total scope, forcing genuine trade-off decisions) and require an explicit justification for why each Must Have item would genuinely cause the MVP to fail without it, not just that it would be nice to have.
- RICE scores calculated once and never revisited as new information emerges: a RICE-based prioritization is locked in at the start of a project and never updated even as the team learns more (e.g. discovering during early development that a particular feature is much easier or harder to build than initially estimated). Fix: treat RICE scores as living estimates to be refreshed as effort and confidence estimates improve with real project learning, similar to the Architecture Decision Record practice of revisiting decisions when underlying conditions change.
16|🟡 T2 Project Scoping & Feasibility|Pr.real_example: An FDE scoping an MVP for an AI-powered contract review tool used MoSCoW in an initial stakeholder workshop to quickly sort 25 candidate features into the four buckets, then applied RICE scoring specifically to the 8 features that landed in the Should Have bucket (too many to all fit within the available MVP timeline, requiring further prioritization within that bucket) -- the RICE scores revealed that a seemingly minor feature (highlighting specific contract clauses matching a configurable risk checklist) had a much higher RICE score than a more visually impressive but narrower-reach feature (a contract comparison view), redirecting the team's limited remaining MVP development time toward the higher-RICE-score feature despite it initially seeming less impressive in stakeholder demos.

16|🟡 T2 Project Scoping & Feasibility|Pr.what_it_is: Constraint mapping is the systematic process of identifying and documenting the full range of hard limits and boundaries that will shape an AI project's feasible solution space -- explicitly categorized across regulatory constraints (the legal/compliance requirements covered extensively in the security and compliance material, like data residency, HIPAA, FedRAMP authorization levels), technical constraints (existing system limitations, available data quality/access, integration complexity covered in the Enterprise Integration material), and organizational constraints (budget, available internal skill/capacity, political/stakeholder dynamics, timeline pressures from business cycles or competitive factors) -- conducted explicitly and early in project scoping rather than discovering these constraints reactively partway through implementation when they're much more costly to address.
16|🟡 T2 Project Scoping & Feasibility|Pr.why_it_exists: AI projects frequently encounter late-discovered constraints that force costly rework or even project failure -- a regulatory requirement discovered after architecture decisions are already made, a technical integration limitation discovered after a timeline has been committed to, or an organizational political dynamic discovered only when a key stakeholder unexpectedly blocks a decision -- and many of these late discoveries could have been surfaced earlier through deliberate, systematic constraint mapping during Discovery and Feasibility assessment, rather than assuming the solution space is unconstrained and only encountering the actual limits reactively as the project proceeds.

16|🟡 T2 Project Scoping & Feasibility|Pr.use_when: Conduct explicit constraint mapping as a core activity within the Project Scoping & Feasibility phase, ideally before committing to specific architecture decisions or detailed scope -- treat this with the same discovery rigor covered in the broader Discovery material, since constraints discovered late are far more costly to address than constraints surfaced early.
16|🟡 T2 Project Scoping & Feasibility|Pr.avoid_when: Don't conduct exhaustive constraint mapping for very small, simple, low-risk engagements where the relevant constraints are already obviously well-understood and minimal -- match the rigor of the constraint mapping exercise to the actual complexity and risk of the project.
16|🟡 T2 Project Scoping & Feasibility|Pr.what_goes_wrong:
- Constraints assumed rather than verified with the actual responsible stakeholders: a team assumes a particular regulatory or technical constraint based on general industry knowledge or a quick assumption, rather than verifying the specific constraint with the customer's actual compliance, legal, or technical stakeholders who have authoritative knowledge of the specific situation. - Constraints mapped once at project start but never revisited as the project evolves: organizational, regulatory, or technical constraints can change during a project's lifetime (a new regulation, a budget change, a reorganization affecting stakeholder dynamics), and a constraint map built once at the very start and never revisited can become stale and misleading. Fix: periodically revisit and update the constraint map at key project milestones, similar to the living-document treatment recommended for Architecture Decision Records.
16|🟡 T2 Project Scoping & Feasibility|Pr.real_example: An FDE scoping an AI-assisted clinical documentation project conducted explicit constraint mapping during Discovery, directly engaging the hospital's compliance officer (regulatory: HIPAA BAA requirements, covered elsewhere), the IT security team (technical: network architecture and air-gapped/VPN connectivity requirements), and the CFO's office (organizational: a specific budget ceiling and a hard go-live deadline tied to a board presentation) -- this explicit, multi-stakeholder constraint mapping surfaced early that the hospital's existing EHR integration (a technical constraint) would take longer than the CFO's desired timeline (an organizational constraint) allowed, leading to an explicit, informed conversation about scope reduction (deferring full EHR integration to a later phase) rather than the team discovering this timeline conflict only weeks before the committed deadline.

16|🟡 T2 Project Scoping & Feasibility|Pr.what_it_is: A RACI matrix is a structured tool for clarifying roles and responsibilities across a project by categorizing every key stakeholder's involvement in each significant decision or task into one of four categories: Responsible (the person who actually does the work), Accountable (the person ultimately answerable for the outcome, typically the single decision-maker with final sign-off authority), Consulted (people whose input should be sought before a decision, but who don't have decision authority), and Informed (people who need to be kept aware of decisions/progress but have no input role). Applied to AI/FDE engagement stakeholder mapping (extending the broader stakeholder management material covered in Customer Engagement), a RACI matrix makes explicit, for every significant project decision, exactly who has what role -- preventing the common failure modes of decisions made without appropriate consultation, or decisions stalling because no one is clearly Accountable for actually making the call.
16|🟡 T2 Project Scoping & Feasibility|Pr.why_it_exists: Without explicit role clarity, AI projects frequently suffer from either decision paralysis (no one feels empowered to make a call, so decisions stall waiting for unclear consensus) or the opposite problem (a decision is made without consulting someone whose input was actually essential, leading to rework or stakeholder frustration when they discover a decision was made without their input). A RACI matrix exists to make these roles explicit and agreed upon in advance, for every category of significant decision an engagement will need to make, removing ambiguity about who needs to be involved and at what level for any given type of decision.

16|🟡 T2 Project Scoping & Feasibility|Pr.use_when: Build an explicit RACI matrix for any AI engagement with multiple stakeholders across different organizational functions (technical, business, legal/compliance, end users) where decision-making roles aren't already obviously clear -- particularly valuable for larger, more complex engagements where the cross-functional collaboration material's coordination challenges are more pronounced and benefit from this explicit role clarity.
16|🟡 T2 Project Scoping & Feasibility|Pr.avoid_when: Don't build a formal RACI matrix for very small engagements with only one or two stakeholders where roles are already obviously clear without needing a formal tool to clarify them -- the structured overhead isn't justified when there's no genuine ambiguity to resolve.
16|🟡 T2 Project Scoping & Feasibility|Pr.what_goes_wrong:
- Accountable role assigned to someone who doesn't actually have or accept that authority in practice: a RACI matrix marks a specific business sponsor as Accountable for go-live decisions, but in practice, that person defers every decision to someone else (perhaps an executive who wasn't included in the matrix), meaning the documented RACI doesn't reflect actual decision-making reality. Fix: validate the Accountable assignments directly with the named individuals, confirming they genuinely hold and are willing to exercise that decision authority, rather than assuming a title or role implies actual decision-making power in this specific organization's real dynamics.
- RACI matrix built once and then ignored in practice: a carefully constructed RACI matrix is documented at project start but never actually referenced during real decision points, with the team falling back into ad-hoc, unclear decision-making despite having a documented framework available. Fix: actively reference and use the RACI matrix at actual decision points ('per our RACI, this is a decision where you have Accountability -- here's the recommendation, what's your call?'), making it a living working tool rather than a one-time documentation exercise filed away and forgotten.
16|🟡 T2 Project Scoping & Feasibility|Pr.real_example: An FDE engagement at a large insurance company built an explicit RACI matrix during Discovery specifically because the initial stakeholder landscape was confusing -- multiple business unit leaders seemed to have overlapping interest in the AI claims triage project, with no one clearly empowered to make final decisions. The RACI exercise, conducted directly with the relevant executives, surfaced that one specific VP of Claims Operations was willing to and should hold Accountability for the project's key decisions, while the other interested business unit leaders were appropriately positioned as Consulted -- this explicit clarification, confirmed directly with all parties, prevented several potential mid-project decision conflicts where multiple leaders might otherwise have each assumed they held final decision authority over the same choices.

16|🟡 T2 Domain Expertise Tracks|Domain E.what_it_is: ICD-10, SNOMED CT, LOINC, and RxNorm are the four major standardized medical coding/terminology systems that healthcare AI applications must understand and correctly handle: ICD-10 (International Classification of Diseases, 10th revision -- primarily used for diagnosis coding and billing/administrative purposes), SNOMED CT (Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine Clinical Terms -- a much more comprehensive, granular clinical terminology covering diseases, findings, procedures, and more, used primarily for clinical documentation rather than billing), LOINC (Logical Observation Identifiers Names and Codes -- the standard for identifying laboratory tests and clinical observations/measurements, e.g. a specific LOINC code for 'blood glucose level'), and RxNorm (the standard for identifying medications/drugs, normalizing the many different brand names, generic names, and formulations of the same underlying drug into a consistent set of codes).
16|🟡 T2 Domain Expertise Tracks|Domain E.why_it_exists: Clinical data arrives from many different source systems using inconsistent terminology -- the same diagnosis might be described in slightly different free-text language by different physicians, the same lab test might have different local codes in different hospital systems, and the same medication might be referenced by brand name in one system and generic name in another -- these four coding systems exist specifically to provide standardized, unambiguous reference vocabularies for each of these distinct clinical domains (diagnoses/billing, comprehensive clinical concepts, lab/observations, medications respectively), and any healthcare AI system processing or generating clinical information needs to correctly map to and interpret these specific coding systems rather than relying on potentially ambiguous free text alone.

16|🟡 T2 Domain Expertise Tracks|Domain E.use_when: Develop fluency with the specific coding system(s) relevant to a given healthcare AI use case -- ICD-10 for billing/administrative AI applications, SNOMED CT for clinical documentation AI, LOINC for lab/diagnostic AI applications, and RxNorm for medication-related AI applications -- recognizing that a single healthcare AI system may need to correctly handle multiple of these systems simultaneously and navigate the non-trivial mappings between them.
16|🟡 T2 Domain Expertise Tracks|Domain E.avoid_when: Don't assume a clean, simple one-to-one mapping always exists between these different coding systems (e.g. between SNOMED CT clinical concepts and ICD-10 billing codes) -- the actual mappings are often many-to-many and context-dependent, and an AI system naively assuming simple translation can produce incorrect administrative or clinical conclusions.
16|🟡 T2 Domain Expertise Tracks|Domain E.what_goes_wrong:
- Incorrect ICD-10 to SNOMED CT (or vice versa) translation causing billing or clinical accuracy issues: an AI system that naively assumes a simple lookup table can translate between these coding systems, without accounting for the genuine many-to-many complexity and context-dependence of real mappings, can produce incorrect translations that affect billing accuracy or clinical decision support reliability. Fix: use established, maintained mapping resources (e.g. the official ICD-10/SNOMED CT mapping tables maintained by relevant standards bodies) rather than building ad-hoc translation logic, and validate translation accuracy with clinical coding experts before relying on AI-generated code assignments in production.
- RxNorm normalization gaps causing missed drug interaction detection: an AI medication safety system fails to correctly normalize a less common brand name or an unusual dosage formulation to its correct RxNorm code, causing it to miss a genuine interaction with another medication that would have been correctly identified if both drugs had been properly normalized to their RxNorm codes first. Fix: use a comprehensive, regularly-updated RxNorm normalization service/database (such as the National Library of Medicine's own RxNorm API) rather than a partial or self-maintained drug name mapping table, and explicitly test normalization coverage against the actual range of medication names/formulations likely to appear in the specific patient population.
16|🟡 T2 Domain Expertise Tracks|Domain E.real_example: A healthcare AI company building an AI-assisted clinical documentation improvement tool (helping ensure physician notes support accurate billing codes) needed to map free-text clinical documentation (often using SNOMED CT-aligned clinical language, as that's how the underlying EHR's problem list was structured) to the correct, specific ICD-10 codes required for billing -- a genuinely difficult mapping problem given that SNOMED CT's granularity often doesn't have a clean 1-to-1 ICD-10 equivalent. The team worked with certified medical coding professionals to validate the AI's proposed ICD-10 code suggestions against a representative sample of real clinical documentation, discovering and correcting several systematic mapping errors (cases where the AI consistently chose a less specific ICD-10 code than the clinical documentation actually supported) before the tool was trusted for production use in supporting (not replacing) the hospital's professional medical coders.

16|🟡 T2 Domain Expertise Tracks|Domain E.what_it_is: This domain expertise area covers the core messaging and connectivity standards underlying global financial transactions: SWIFT (the Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication -- both the secure messaging network itself and its traditional MT message format standards used for interbank communication, including international wire transfers, now migrating toward ISO 20022-based MX messages as covered in the dedicated ISO 20022 note), FIX (Financial Information eXchange protocol -- the dominant standard specifically for electronic trading, used for communicating buy/sell orders, executions, and market data between trading firms, exchanges, and brokers in real time), and real-time payment systems (modern payment rails like the US's FedNow and RTP -- Real-Time Payments network, the UK's Faster Payments, and similar systems globally, which settle payments within seconds rather than the days traditional ACH/wire transfers can take, typically built on ISO 20022 messaging).
16|🟡 T2 Domain Expertise Tracks|Domain E.why_it_exists: Financial services AI applications -- fraud detection, payment processing automation, trading-related analytics -- must operate within and correctly interpret the specific messaging standards and network infrastructure that the global financial system actually runs on, each serving a genuinely distinct purpose: SWIFT for interbank wire transfers and correspondent banking communication, FIX specifically for trading/securities transactions (a different domain with different latency and message-type requirements than payment transfers), and real-time payment rails representing the modern evolution toward instant settlement that traditional batch-oriented payment systems couldn't achieve, each requiring genuine domain-specific understanding to build AI applications that correctly process and act on these distinct message types.
