16|🟡 T2 Domain Expertise Tracks|Domain E.what_goes_wrong:
- Real-time payment fraud model latency requirements underestimated: a fraud detection model designed and validated against traditional batch payment processing timelines (where there's time for more thorough, multi-second analysis) fails to meet the dramatically tighter latency requirements of real-time payment rails, where a decision must be made within the payment's near-instant processing window. Fix: explicitly design and benchmark fraud detection models against the specific latency budget of the target payment rail (often well under a second for real-time payment systems), potentially requiring model tiering (covered in cost management material) or simpler, faster models for the real-time decision point with more thorough analysis happening asynchronously for pattern detection across transactions.
- FIX message parsing logic incorrectly applied to a different message version or exchange-specific variant: FIX protocol implementations vary somewhat across different exchanges and trading venues (different supported tag sets, different version adoption), and an AI system built and tested against one exchange's specific FIX implementation may not correctly handle messages from a different venue without explicit validation. Fix: explicitly validate FIX message parsing logic against each specific exchange/venue's actual implementation and version, rather than assuming uniform FIX protocol behavior across all trading venues.
16|🟡 T2 Domain Expertise Tracks|Domain E.real_example: A bank's FDE engagement building a real-time payment fraud detection system for their FedNow integration had to fundamentally redesign their existing batch-payment fraud model's architecture: the existing model took several seconds to run a comprehensive risk analysis, acceptable for traditional ACH payments with overnight batch processing, but completely incompatible with FedNow's sub-second settlement requirement. The redesigned system used a fast, lightweight initial risk score (sub-100ms) to make the real-time go/no-go decision, with the more comprehensive, slower analysis running asynchronously afterward to flag patterns for investigation and to continuously improve the fast model's training data -- a direct architectural consequence of real-time payment rails' fundamentally different latency constraints compared to the traditional batch payment processing the team's existing fraud model had been built for.

16|🟡 T2 Domain Expertise Tracks|Domain E.what_it_is: AML (Anti-Money Laundering) and KYC (Know Your Customer) are the regulatory framework and associated compliance processes financial institutions must implement to detect, prevent, and report potential money laundering and terrorist financing activity -- KYC specifically covers customer identity verification and risk profiling at account opening and ongoing monitoring, while AML more broadly covers transaction monitoring, suspicious activity reporting, and the overall compliance program structure. OFAC (Office of Foreign Assets Control) sanctions screening is the specific, related compliance requirement to screen customers and transactions against government-maintained sanctions lists (e.g. the OFAC Specially Designated Nationals list), ensuring a financial institution doesn't knowingly or unknowingly conduct business with sanctioned individuals, entities, or countries -- both AML/KYC and sanctions screening are increasingly AI-assisted domains, since the underlying detection task (finding suspicious patterns or matching identities against lists, often with name variations and transliteration challenges) is well-suited to AI/ML techniques.
16|🟡 T2 Domain Expertise Tracks|Domain E.why_it_exists: Financial institutions are legally required (under the Bank Secrecy Act and related regulations in the US, and similar frameworks internationally) to actively prevent their systems from being used for money laundering, terrorist financing, or transactions with sanctioned parties -- failure to do so carries severe regulatory penalties (well-documented cases of multi-billion-dollar fines for AML/sanctions compliance failures at major banks) and represents genuine real-world harm (enabling illicit finance, sanctions evasion). AI is increasingly central to meeting these obligations at scale, since the volume of transactions and customer relationships modern financial institutions handle far exceeds what manual review alone could adequately screen, but this also means AI errors in this domain carry serious legal and reputational consequences, making rigor in this specific application area especially critical.

16|🟡 T2 Domain Expertise Tracks|Domain E.what_it_is: DoDAF (Department of Defense Architecture Framework) is the DoD's standardized methodology and set of viewpoints for describing and documenting complex military systems and enterprise architectures, used to ensure different stakeholders (operational planners, systems engineers, acquisition officials) can communicate about a system's architecture using a consistent, structured set of views (operational views describing what needs to happen, systems views describing how systems implement it, and others). TOGAF (The Open Group Architecture Framework) is a more general, commercial/civilian enterprise architecture framework that's also referenced and sometimes adapted within defense and government contexts, particularly for IT/business architecture rather than DoDAF's more operational/warfighting focus. JADC2 (Joint All-Domain Command and Control, introduced at a higher level alongside the Anduril Lattice/interoperability material) is the overarching DoD strategic concept and initiative for connecting all sensors, shooters, and decision-makers across every military domain (air, land, sea, space, cyber) into a unified, AI-enabled command and control network -- the broader strategic vision that systems like Lattice and various service-specific C2 modernization efforts are each contributing implementations toward.
16|🟡 T2 Domain Expertise Tracks|Domain E.why_it_exists: Large, complex defense programs involving many different stakeholders, systems, and decades-long lifecycles need a standardized way to document and communicate architecture decisions that remains consistent across different program phases, different contractors, and different government oversight reviews -- DoDAF exists specifically to provide this standardized documentation framework for defense systems. JADC2 exists as the unifying strategic concept addressing a specific, recognized operational gap: historically, different military services and domains (Army, Navy, Air Force, Space Force) developed largely separate C2 systems that couldn't easily share data or coordinate across domains, and as warfare increasingly requires rapid, cross-domain coordination (a target detected by a space-based sensor needing to rapidly inform a ground-based response, for example), JADC2 represents the DoD's strategic push to break down these traditionally siloed, domain-specific C2 architectures.

16|🟡 T2 Domain Expertise Tracks|Domain E.what_it_is: Tactical Data Links are the actual radio communication protocols and infrastructure that implement real-time tactical information sharing between military platforms -- Link 16 (introduced at a higher level in the Anduril interoperability material) is the dominant NATO/US tactical data link for air, sea, and ground forces, using a jam-resistant TDMA (Time Division Multiple Access) radio protocol to share track data, status information, and some command information in near-real-time. Link 22 is a newer tactical data link, developed jointly by NATO nations, designed specifically to extend Link 16's capabilities to longer ranges and address some of Link 16's bandwidth and capacity limitations, particularly relevant for naval and longer-range coordination scenarios where Link 16's range constraints become limiting.
16|🟡 T2 Domain Expertise Tracks|Domain E.why_it_exists: Coalition military operations require platforms from different services and different nations to share tactical situational awareness (where are friendly forces, where are detected threats) in near-real-time, in often electronically contested environments where adversaries may attempt to jam or intercept communications -- tactical data links exist specifically as the actual radio-layer infrastructure making this real-time, secure, jam-resistant information sharing technically possible, distinct from (though connected to) the higher-level data standards and entity models (covered in the Lattice Entity Model material) that define what information is being shared over these links.

```
Link 16 technical characteristics (the dominant standard):
  TDMA radio protocol: time-divided access slots allow multiple
  platforms to share the same radio frequency without collision,
  with each platform transmitting only in its assigned time slots
  Frequency hopping and other anti-jam techniques: designed
  specifically for survivability in contested electronic warfare
  environments
  Message standard: J-series messages (e.g. J2.0/J2.2 for air/
  surface track reports, J3.5 for threat warning) -- the actual
  content structure transmitted over the Link 16 radio layer
  Range limitation: line-of-sight or near-line-of-sight,
  effectively limiting range for surface/ground platforms
  (though airborne relay platforms can extend effective range)

Link 22 as an extension addressing Link 16 limitations:
  Greater range: designed to support longer-range communication,
  particularly valuable for naval forces operating beyond Link
  16's effective range without relay
  Higher capacity: addresses some of Link 16's bandwidth
  constraints as the volume of tactical data needing to be shared
  has grown over time
  Interoperability consideration: Link 22 doesn't simply replace
  Link 16 -- many environments need to support both, with
  appropriate gateway/relay systems translating between them
  where forces using different links need to share information

AI system integration relevance (connecting to the broader
interoperability material):
  An AI-enabled C2 system (like Lattice, covered elsewhere) that
  needs genuine coalition interoperability must correctly
  implement Link 16 (and increasingly Link 22 for relevant
  scenarios) message parsing and generation, requiring actual
  hardware terminals (e.g. MIDS-JTRS for Link 16) and validated,
  tested integration -- not just a conceptual data model
  compatibility, but genuine radio-layer protocol implementation
  and testing with real or simulated tactical data link traffic
```
16|🟡 T2 Domain Expertise Tracks|Domain E.use_when: Develop genuine technical fluency with Link 16 (and increasingly Link 22) specifically when an AI/FDE engagement involves real interoperability requirements with existing coalition tactical systems -- this requires understanding not just the conceptual data sharing goal but the actual radio-layer protocol characteristics (TDMA timing, message types, range limitations) that shape what's technically achievable.
16|🟡 T2 Domain Expertise Tracks|Domain E.avoid_when: Don't assume conceptual familiarity with 'tactical data links' as a category substitutes for the specific, detailed technical knowledge required for an actual Link 16 or Link 22 integration project -- these are complex, decades-refined military communication standards requiring genuine specialist expertise (often involving the specific hardware terminal vendor and the customer's communications engineering team) for real integration work, not something a general AI/software engineer can implement correctly from general principles alone.
16|🟡 T2 Domain Expertise Tracks|Domain E.what_goes_wrong:
- Underestimating Link 16's bandwidth/capacity constraints for AI-generated data volume: an AI system designed to share rich, detailed sensor fusion output assumes it can transmit this over Link 16 without considering Link 16's genuine bandwidth limitations, discovering that the actual message volume needed exceeds what the tactical data link can practically support, especially when sharing the network with many other platforms' traffic. Fix: design AI-generated tactical data sharing with explicit awareness of the target tactical data link's actual bandwidth constraints, potentially requiring data prioritization or summarization logic to fit within the available capacity, rather than assuming unlimited bandwidth as might be reasonable for a typical enterprise network integration.
- Link 16/Link 22 interoperability assumed without actual hardware-level testing: a system's data model is theoretically compatible with Link 16/22 message structures, but without actual testing using real or accurately simulated tactical data link hardware and traffic conditions, subtle implementation issues (timing, message prioritization under congestion, actual radio propagation characteristics) can remain undiscovered until a real operational test reveals them. Fix: conduct genuine hardware-level interoperability testing (the same JITC-style joint interoperability testing covered in the broader interoperability material) rather than relying solely on data model compatibility analysis.
16|🟡 T2 Domain Expertise Tracks|Domain E.real_example: An Anduril-context FDE engagement integrating Lattice with a NATO ally's existing Link 16 infrastructure had to work closely with the ally's communications engineering team and the specific Link 16 terminal hardware vendor to validate that Lattice's generated track data correctly conformed to Link 16's J2.2 surface track message format and fit within the available bandwidth allocation on the shared tactical network, discovering during initial testing that the default update rate Lattice was configured to transmit at would have consumed an excessive share of the available Link 16 capacity if deployed at scale across many sensor platforms simultaneously -- requiring an explicit message prioritization and rate-limiting configuration to ensure the AI-generated tactical data shared the available Link 16 bandwidth appropriately alongside other platforms' traffic.

16|🟡 T2 Domain Expertise Tracks|Domain E.what_it_is: GS1 standards are the globally-adopted system of standardized identifiers and data structures for supply chain and retail products -- including the familiar barcode/GTIN (Global Trade Item Number) system, but extending to standardized location identifiers (GLN), and structured product data exchange formats. EDI X12 (covered at a higher level in the dedicated Enterprise Integration note) remains a core supply chain transaction format. EPCIS (Electronic Product Code Information Services) is a specific GS1 standard for capturing and sharing supply chain event data -- recording when, where, and what happened to a specific tracked item or batch (e.g. 'this pallet was shipped from this location at this time,' 'this case was received at this warehouse') -- providing a standardized way to build detailed, traceable supply chain visibility and track-and-trace capability across multiple trading partners.
16|🟡 T2 Domain Expertise Tracks|Domain E.why_it_exists: Global supply chains involve products moving through many different organizations (manufacturers, distributors, retailers, logistics providers) that each need a shared, unambiguous way to identify the same physical products and locations (GS1's GTIN/GLN system solving exactly this identification problem globally) and to communicate detailed event-level visibility about where products actually are and what's happened to them as they move through the supply chain (EPCIS solving this event-tracking problem) -- without these standards, every pair of trading partners would need bespoke, incompatible product identification and event-tracking schemes, making any kind of cross-organization supply chain visibility (exactly the kind of capability an AI-powered supply chain risk or visibility system needs) far more difficult to achieve.

16|🟡 T2 Domain Expertise Tracks|Domain E.what_goes_wrong:
- Incomplete EPCIS adoption across the supply chain creates visibility gaps: an AI supply chain visibility tool built assuming comprehensive EPCIS event coverage discovers significant gaps where smaller or less digitally mature trading partners don't publish EPCIS events at all, creating blind spots in the AI's visibility and risk analysis precisely at the points (often smaller, less sophisticated suppliers) where supply chain risk is frequently concentrated. Fix: explicitly map and account for EPCIS/digital tracking coverage gaps across the actual supply chain, potentially supplementing AI analysis with alternative data sources (the kind of EDI-based or even manual tracking data covered in the broader enterprise integration material) for trading partners without EPCIS capability, rather than assuming uniform digital visibility.
- GTIN/GLN identifier inconsistency due to incorrect or inconsistent assignment practices: despite GS1's standardization intent, real-world implementation errors (a supplier reusing a GTIN for a genuinely different product variant, or inconsistent GLN assignment for a location that's been reorganized) can undermine the clean entity identification the standard is meant to provide. Fix: apply the same entity resolution validation discipline covered elsewhere even to nominally standardized GS1 identifiers, since real-world implementation inconsistencies mean GTIN/GLN-based matching, while generally more reliable than ad-hoc identifiers, still benefits from validation rather than blind trust.
16|🟡 T2 Domain Expertise Tracks|Domain E.real_example: A retail company's AI-powered supply chain risk system initially assumed comprehensive EPCIS event coverage across their full supplier network, but discovered during implementation that only their largest, most sophisticated suppliers (representing perhaps 60% of total volume) actually published EPCIS events, while smaller suppliers tracked shipments through far less structured means (basic EDI 856 Advance Ship Notices, or in some cases just email and phone communication). The FDE team redesigned the AI system to use EPCIS events as the primary, richest data source where available, falling back to the less granular EDI-based shipment data for the remaining suppliers, and explicitly flagging in the visibility dashboard which specific shipments had EPCIS-level detailed tracking versus only coarser EDI-level visibility -- an honest representation of the actual, inconsistent data coverage rather than presenting uniform confidence across genuinely non-uniform underlying data quality.

16|🟡 T2 Domain Expertise Tracks|Domain E.what_it_is: MES (Manufacturing Execution System) is the software layer managing and tracking real-time production operations on a factory floor -- work order execution, quality tracking, equipment status, production scheduling at the shop-floor level. SCADA (Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition) is the lower-level system directly monitoring and controlling physical industrial equipment and processes (sensors, PLCs -- Programmable Logic Controllers, actuators) in real time. ISA-95 is the international standard defining the structured hierarchy and information exchange model connecting these operational technology (OT) layers (SCADA, MES) with the business/IT layers above them (ERP systems like SAP, covered elsewhere) -- defining a standard reference model (often depicted as a pyramid: Level 0 physical process, Level 1 sensing/control, Level 2 supervisory/SCADA, Level 3 MES, Level 4 ERP/business planning) for how information should flow between these traditionally separate layers. OT/IT convergence refers to the ongoing industry trend of breaking down the traditional separation between operational technology (the physical, real-time control systems) and information technology (business systems, data analytics, and increasingly AI), driven by the recognition that AI-powered analytics and optimization require data flowing from the OT layer up into AI/analytics systems, and sometimes AI-driven decisions flowing back down into operational control.
16|🟡 T2 Domain Expertise Tracks|Domain E.why_it_exists: Manufacturing environments historically built OT systems (SCADA, industrial control systems) with a strong emphasis on real-time reliability, safety, and isolation from broader IT networks (precisely because a compromised or malfunctioning control system on a physical industrial process can cause real physical harm, unlike a typical IT system failure) -- this created a deliberate, historically well-justified separation from the more connected, internet-facing IT world. ISA-95 exists to provide a structured, standardized way to bridge this separation when business value (production visibility, AI-powered optimization, predictive maintenance) genuinely requires data flow across these layers, while OT/IT convergence as a broader trend reflects the ongoing, sometimes tense balancing act between unlocking this AI/analytics value and preserving the safety/reliability/security properties that justified the original OT/IT separation in the first place.

```
  controlling Level 1 equipment across a production area)
  Level 3: manufacturing operations management (MES -- tracking

  pipeline that can safely read (ideally without writing back
  into, given OT safety/security concerns) data from these
  traditionally isolated OT layers

  (Level 3) layer, optimizing scheduling and resource allocation
  using both shop-floor data (from below) and business priority
  data (from ERP, above)
  Quality prediction AI: may need both Level 1/2 sensor data
  (process parameters during production) and Level 3 MES quality
  tracking data (actual measured quality outcomes) to build
  predictive quality models

OT/IT convergence architecture pattern (addressing the safety/
security tension):
  Unidirectional data flow (often via a DMZ-style network
  architecture, similar in spirit to the network architecture
  and egress control principles covered in security material,
  here specifically protecting OT systems from IT-side
  compromise): OT sensor data flows up to IT/AI systems for
  analysis, but direct write-back control from AI systems into
  OT control systems is typically much more restricted, reviewed,

  safety stakes of OT control
```
16|🟡 T2 Domain Expertise Tracks|Domain E.use_when: Apply ISA-95's structured layer model when scoping any manufacturing AI integration, explicitly identifying which specific layer(s) the AI application needs to read data from (and, much more cautiously, whether it needs to write any decisions back into operational control) -- this framework helps clarify integration complexity and the appropriate level of safety/security rigor required, since Level 1/2 OT integration carries fundamentally different risk than Level 3/4 IT integration.
16|🟡 T2 Domain Expertise Tracks|Domain E.avoid_when: Don't treat OT/IT convergence as a simple, purely technical integration challenge without genuinely engaging the customer's OT safety and security teams (a specific instance of the cross-functional collaboration principle covered elsewhere) -- OT systems often have safety certification and regulatory requirements (and a justified cultural caution given the real physical safety stakes) that a purely IT/AI-focused team can easily underestimate or overlook.
16|🟡 T2 Domain Expertise Tracks|Domain E.what_goes_wrong:
- AI system granted write access to OT control systems without adequate safety review: an AI optimization system is given the ability to directly adjust production parameters or equipment settings without the rigorous safety review and fail-safe design that any OT control change normally requires, creating genuine physical safety risk if the AI's recommendation is wrong or the integration has a bug. Fix: default to read-only AI integration with OT systems (AI recommends, human operators with appropriate OT safety training execute any actual control changes) unless a full, rigorous safety case has been built and reviewed for any AI system with direct write access to physical control systems -- mirroring the human-in-the-loop principles covered extensively elsewhere, here with the added gravity of genuine physical safety consequences.
- OT network security boundary compromised by an AI integration pathway: connecting an AI/analytics system to traditionally isolated OT networks, even for read-only data access, can inadvertently create a new attack surface or pathway that could be exploited to compromise the OT environment, a serious industrial security concern (and the subject of significant real-world industrial cybersecurity incidents). Fix: apply the same rigorous network architecture, egress control, and security review principles covered in the broader security material specifically and carefully to any OT/IT integration pathway, given the elevated real-world consequences of an OT security compromise compared to a typical IT system breach.
16|🟡 T2 Domain Expertise Tracks|Domain E.real_example: A manufacturing company's FDE engagement building a predictive maintenance AI system needed sensor data (vibration, temperature) from SCADA systems monitoring critical production equipment. Rather than connecting the AI pipeline directly and bidirectionally to the live SCADA network (which the customer's OT security team correctly identified as an unacceptable risk to their carefully isolated, safety-certified control environment), the team implemented a strictly unidirectional data flow architecture: a dedicated, one-way data diode-style connection exported sensor readings from the SCADA network into a separate IT-side data lake for AI analysis, with absolutely no pathway for any signal or command to flow back from the IT/AI side into the OT network -- the predictive maintenance AI's output (maintenance recommendations) was delivered to human maintenance planners through a completely separate IT-side application, never directly interfacing with or controlling the actual production equipment, satisfying the OT security team's safety and security requirements while still delivering the AI-powered predictive maintenance capability's business value.

16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.what_it_is: An AI inventory is a comprehensive, centrally-maintained catalog of every AI/ML model and system deployed or in development across an entire enterprise -- capturing for each one: its purpose, owner, risk tier (connecting to the model risk management material covered elsewhere), data sources, deployment status, and key technical characteristics. A model registry is the more technical implementation supporting this inventory -- a system (e.g. MLflow's Model Registry, covered in the Databricks material, or a similar tool) that tracks model versions, lineage, and deployment status programmatically, serving as the authoritative technical source the broader enterprise AI inventory draws from.
16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.why_it_exists: As AI adoption spreads across a large enterprise, with different teams independently building and deploying models for different purposes, organizations frequently lose track of exactly how many AI systems they actually have running, what each one does, who's responsible for it, and whether it's actually covered by appropriate risk management and compliance processes -- this 'shadow AI' or untracked-AI-sprawl problem creates genuine governance risk (an unmonitored, undocumented model making consequential decisions, with no clear path to audit or remediate it if something goes wrong). An enterprise AI inventory and model registry exist specifically to give the organization (and its risk/compliance functions) genuine visibility into its actual AI footprint, which is the foundational prerequisite for any of the broader governance activities (risk tiering, bias audits, EU AI Act compliance classification) covered elsewhere in this material -- you cannot govern what you don't even know exists.
16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.how_it_works:
```
Enterprise AI inventory structure and process:

1. Inventory data captured per AI system/model:
   Name, description, business purpose
   Owner (the accountable individual/team, connecting to the
   RACI matrix material covered elsewhere)
   Risk tier classification (per the model risk management/
   SR 11-7 and EU AI Act frameworks covered elsewhere)
   Data sources and sensitivity (connecting to data governance
   material)
   Deployment status (development, pilot, production, retired)
   Model registry reference (linking to the technical artifact
   in MLflow or equivalent)

2. Discovery process (finding existing, possibly undocumented
   AI systems):
   Survey of teams/departments to self-report AI systems in use
   Technical discovery (scanning cloud infrastructure and API
   usage logs for LLM API calls or ML model serving endpoints
   that may not have been formally registered)
   This discovery process itself often surfaces significant
   'shadow AI' that wasn't previously tracked centrally

3. Ongoing maintenance process:
   New AI systems must be registered before/as part of moving to
   production (a governance gate similar in spirit to the CI/CD
   evaluation gates covered elsewhere, but at the organizational
   governance level rather than the individual deployment pipeline)
   Periodic review and re-validation of inventory entries (is
   this model still in production? has its risk tier changed?)

4. Use of the inventory by governance/compliance functions:
   Risk committees use the inventory to prioritize review and
   monitoring resources toward the highest-risk-tier systems
   Compliance teams use it to identify which systems require

   Security teams use it to ensure appropriate security review
```

16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.use_when: Establish or contribute to an enterprise AI inventory and model registry as a foundational governance capability for any organization with multiple AI systems across different teams -- this should generally be one of the first AI governance capabilities built, since it's the prerequisite visibility layer that all other governance activities (risk tiering, bias audits, compliance classification) depend on.
16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.avoid_when: Don't build an elaborate, heavyweight enterprise AI inventory system for a very small organization with only one or two AI systems total, where informal tracking is genuinely sufficient given the small scale -- match the formality of the inventory/registry infrastructure to the actual scale and complexity of the organization's AI footprint.
16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.what_goes_wrong:
- Inventory built once but never maintained, becoming stale and incomplete: an initial inventory-building effort captures the AI systems known at that point in time, but without an ongoing registration process for new systems, the inventory rapidly becomes incomplete and unreliable as new AI initiatives launch without being added. Fix: establish inventory registration as a mandatory gate in the path to production deployment (similar to other governance gates covered elsewhere), not a one-time historical documentation exercise.
- Shadow AI persists because the discovery process wasn't thorough enough: relying solely on self-reported survey data for the initial inventory misses AI systems that teams either forgot to report or didn't think to include (e.g. an analyst's personal use of an LLM API for a recurring business process that was never formally recognized as 'an AI system'). Fix: supplement self-reported inventory data with technical discovery methods (scanning for LLM API usage in cloud billing data, network egress logs) to catch AI usage that wouldn't surface through self-reporting alone.
16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.real_example: A large insurance company's risk management function, prompted by emerging EU AI Act compliance requirements, conducted an enterprise-wide AI inventory effort and discovered the existence of approximately 40 distinct AI/ML systems across the organization, more than double the roughly 18 systems previously known to the central risk team through informal awareness -- the discovery process specifically combined a department self-reporting survey with a technical scan of cloud billing records for LLM API usage, which caught several teams' AI-powered tools that had never been formally registered with any central governance function, directly enabling the risk team to subsequently prioritize EU AI Act risk-tier classification work across this now-complete inventory rather than the previously incomplete picture.

16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.what_it_is: An Algorithmic Impact Assessment (AIA) is a structured, documented process for evaluating the potential effects -- both intended and unintended, particularly on individuals and groups -- of deploying an algorithmic/AI system before (and sometimes periodically after) deployment, conceptually similar to a privacy impact assessment but focused specifically on algorithmic decision-making's broader societal and individual effects (fairness, due process, transparency, accountability), not just data privacy narrowly. AIAs are increasingly required by specific government regulations (some US state and local government AI procurement requirements, Canada's federal AI directive, and elements of the EU AI Act's broader risk management requirements covered elsewhere) and are also adopted voluntarily by organizations as part of responsible AI governance practice even where not strictly mandated.
16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.why_it_exists: AI systems, particularly those making or influencing consequential decisions about people, can have significant impacts that aren't captured by traditional technical testing alone (does the model achieve target accuracy?) -- impacts on fairness across different groups, on individuals' ability to understand and contest decisions, on broader societal trust, and on unintended consequences that only become visible when considering the system's effects holistically rather than just its narrow technical performance. AIAs exist to force this broader, structured consideration explicitly and proactively, before deployment, rather than discovering significant negative impacts only after a system is already affecting real people in production.
16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.how_it_works:
```
Algorithmic Impact Assessment structure (typical framework,
adaptable to specific regulatory requirements where applicable):

1. System description:
   What does the AI system do, what decisions does it make or
   influence, who is affected?

2. Necessity and proportionality assessment:
   Is using an algorithmic/AI approach actually necessary and
   proportionate for this decision, or would a simpler, more
   transparent approach serve the purpose adequately? (connecting
   to the choosing-the-simplest-solution principle covered
   elsewhere, here applied specifically to the question of
   whether AI/algorithmic decision-making itself is warranted)

3. Risk and impact identification:
   Fairness/bias risk: could this system have disparate impact
   across different groups? (connecting directly to the bias and
   fairness testing material covered elsewhere)
   Due process/contestability: can affected individuals
   understand and meaningfully contest decisions? (connecting to
   the GDPR Article 22 and explainability material covered
   elsewhere)
   Unintended consequence risk: what could go wrong beyond the
   system's intended purpose? (e.g. could the system create
   perverse incentives, or be gamed/manipulated by affected
   individuals or adversaries?)

4. Mitigation measures:
   For each identified risk, what specific mitigation is in
   place? (human review checkpoints, bias testing and remediation,
   explicit appeals processes, ongoing monitoring)

5. Stakeholder consultation:
   Many AIA frameworks specifically require consulting with
   representatives of affected groups (not just internal
   technical and business stakeholders) as part of the assessment
   process, surfacing impact considerations that an purely
   internal review might miss

6. Ongoing monitoring and re-assessment:
   AIAs are often not a one-time pre-deployment exercise but
   require periodic re-assessment as the system or its usage
   context evolves, similar to the model risk management
   ongoing-monitoring principle covered elsewhere
```
16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.use_when: Conduct an Algorithmic Impact Assessment for any AI system making or significantly influencing consequential decisions about individuals, particularly in government/public-sector contexts where AIAs are increasingly explicitly mandated, and as a voluntary best practice for any organization deploying consequential AI systems even absent a specific legal mandate, as a genuine risk-reduction and responsible AI practice.
16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.avoid_when: Don't require a full, formal AIA process for low-stakes, low-consequence AI applications (an internal productivity tool with no individual-level consequential decisions) -- match the rigor of the impact assessment to the actual potential consequence and affected population, similar to the broader risk-tiering principle covered throughout the governance material in this phase.
16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.what_goes_wrong:
- AIA conducted as a paperwork exercise disconnected from actual deployment decisions: an AIA is completed and filed, but its findings (identified risks and required mitigations) don't actually influence the system's final design or deployment approval, making the assessment a compliance formality rather than a genuine risk-reduction practice. Fix: ensure the AIA's findings are genuinely incorporated into deployment go/no-go decisions and design requirements, with a clear accountability structure (connecting to the RACI matrix material) for ensuring identified mitigations are actually implemented, not just documented.
- Stakeholder consultation requirement satisfied superficially: a required stakeholder consultation step is conducted as a token gesture (a brief, poorly-attended public comment period) rather than genuine engagement that could actually surface meaningful concerns from affected communities. Fix: design genuine, accessible consultation processes (potentially using the discovery workshop and user journey mapping techniques covered elsewhere, adapted for engaging affected community representatives) rather than minimal-compliance consultation theater.
16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.real_example: A city government deploying an AI-assisted tool for prioritizing building code violation inspections (a system that could disproportionately affect certain neighborhoods if not carefully designed) conducted a formal Algorithmic Impact Assessment as required by the city's AI procurement policy, which included a public comment period and direct consultation with community organizations from neighborhoods likely to be most affected by the prioritization algorithm's decisions. This consultation surfaced a specific concern -- that prioritizing inspections based partly on historical violation density could perpetuate a feedback loop disproportionately targeting lower-income neighborhoods that had historically received more inspections for reasons unrelated to actual current violation risk -- leading the city to redesign the prioritization algorithm's feature set to remove this specific historical-density input before deployment, a substantive design change directly traceable to the AIA's stakeholder consultation requirement, not something the city's internal technical team had identified on their own.

16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.what_it_is: A bias audit is the formal, systematic process of measuring an AI system's outputs across different demographic groups using specific, well-defined fairness metrics -- extending the bias and fairness testing material covered earlier in this phase (which introduced disparate impact ratio and calibration) with two additional, commonly-used and sometimes competing fairness definitions: Demographic Parity (also called statistical parity -- requiring that the rate of positive outcomes, e.g. loan approval rate, be equal across different demographic groups, regardless of whether the groups have genuinely different underlying qualification rates) and Equalized Odds (requiring that the model's true positive rate and false positive rate be equal across different demographic groups -- a different, sometimes incompatible standard than demographic parity, focused on equal error rates rather than equal outcome rates).
16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.why_it_exists: Different fairness definitions capture genuinely different ethical and legal concerns, and -- a mathematically proven and practically important fact -- it is generally impossible for a model to simultaneously satisfy demographic parity, equalized odds, AND calibration (covered in the earlier bias and fairness testing material) when the underlying base rates genuinely differ across groups, meaning any bias audit must make an explicit, justified choice about which fairness definition(s) matter most for the specific use case and legal context, rather than assuming a single universal definition of 'fair' that a model could simply be optimized to satisfy across all definitions simultaneously.
16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.how_it_works:
```python
# Bias audit measuring multiple fairness definitions
from fairlearn.metrics import MetricFrame, demographic_parity_difference
from sklearn.metrics import recall_score, false_positive_rate
import pandas as pd

# Demographic Parity: do approval rates differ across groups?
dp_difference = demographic_parity_difference(
    y_true=df_test['actual_outcome'],
    y_pred=df_test['model_decision'],
    sensitive_features=df_test['demographic_group']
)
print(f'Demographic parity difference: {dp_difference:.3f}')
# A value near 0 indicates similar approval rates across groups;
# a large value indicates one group is approved at a much higher
# or lower rate than another, regardless of whether this
# difference is 'justified' by genuine qualification differences

# Equalized Odds: are true positive rate and false positive rate
# equal across groups? (a different question than demographic parity)
metric_frame = MetricFrame(
    metrics={'true_positive_rate': recall_score,
             'false_positive_rate': false_positive_rate},
    y_true=df_test['actual_outcome'],
    y_pred=df_test['model_decision'],
    sensitive_features=df_test['demographic_group']
)
print(metric_frame.by_group)
# Shows TPR/FPR broken down by group -- equalized odds is
# satisfied when these rates are similar across groups, even if
# overall approval rates (demographic parity) differ because the
# groups have genuinely different underlying qualification rates

Key tension to navigate in any real bias audit:
  If group A has a genuinely higher rate of the qualifying
  condition (e.g. higher historical default rate in a lending
  context, for reasons that may themselves reflect historical
  inequity, an important and separate consideration), demographic
  parity (equal approval rates) and equalized odds (equal
  error rates) cannot both be satisfied simultaneously
  Choosing which fairness definition to prioritize requires
  explicit legal and ethical judgment (often requiring input from
  legal/compliance, similar to the AIA stakeholder consultation
  principle), not a purely technical/mathematical decision
  Document the chosen fairness definition and the reasoning
  explicitly (similar to the Architecture Decision Record
  practice), since this choice has real legal and ethical
  significance that should be deliberate, not implicit
```
16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.use_when: Conduct bias audits measuring multiple relevant fairness definitions (not just one) for any consequential AI decision system, explicitly discussing with legal/compliance and, where appropriate, affected stakeholder representatives (connecting to the AIA material) which specific fairness definition(s) are most relevant and legally appropriate for the specific use case and jurisdiction, since this choice is not purely technical.
16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.avoid_when: Don't apply demographic parity as a default fairness requirement without considering whether it's actually the legally and ethically appropriate standard for the specific use case -- in some contexts (e.g. certain insurance underwriting, where actuarial fairness based on genuine risk differences is the legally recognized standard), equalized odds or calibration may be more appropriate than demographic parity, and applying the wrong standard can itself create problems.
16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.what_goes_wrong:
- Optimizing for one fairness metric without disclosing the trade-off against others: a team adjusts a model specifically to satisfy demographic parity, without recognizing or disclosing to stakeholders that this adjustment necessarily degrades equalized odds (different error rates across groups) as a mathematical consequence, presenting an incomplete picture of the actual fairness trade-offs being made. Fix: always report and discuss multiple fairness metrics together, explicitly surfacing trade-offs rather than presenting improvement on one metric as if it represents unambiguous, complete fairness improvement.
- Bias audit conducted once at deployment and never repeated as the model or population evolves: a model's fairness characteristics, measured and approved at initial deployment, can drift over time as the underlying population or model behavior changes (model drift, similar to the data drift concerns covered in observability material), and without periodic re-auditing, a fairness issue that develops post-deployment can go undetected. Fix: establish a periodic bias audit cadence (similar to the model risk management ongoing-monitoring principle) rather than treating fairness validation as a one-time pre-deployment gate.
16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.real_example: A bank's mortgage underwriting AI bias audit found that the model satisfied equalized odds reasonably well (similar true/false positive rates across racial groups) but showed a meaningful demographic parity gap (lower overall approval rates for one group) -- the bank's fair lending compliance team, after consulting with legal counsel on the relevant regulatory standards (which in mortgage lending generally focus more on disparate impact in outcomes and the justifiability of any disparities by legitimate, non-discriminatory factors, closer to a demographic-parity-adjacent concern than equalized odds), determined that the demographic parity gap required further investigation into whether specific input features were acting as unjustified proxies for the protected characteristic (directly connecting to the proxy discrimination concern covered in the earlier bias and fairness testing material), leading to a feature review and model adjustment specifically targeting the demographic parity gap rather than treating the already-acceptable equalized odds result as sufficient evidence of overall fairness.

16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.what_it_is: Model cards, datasheets, and system cards are three related, increasingly standardized documentation formats for transparently describing AI models and the data used to build them. A model card (a format popularized by Google researchers) documents a specific trained model's intended use cases, performance characteristics across different conditions/subgroups, known limitations, and ethical considerations -- the connecting documentation between the technical model risk management material (model development documentation) and the EU AI Act's technical documentation requirements covered elsewhere. A datasheet (extending the 'datasheets for datasets' concept) documents the training data itself -- provenance, collection methodology, known biases or gaps, and intended/inappropriate uses for that specific dataset. A system card is a broader documentation format (increasingly used by major AI labs for their flagship model releases) describing not just the model itself but the entire system context -- safety testing conducted, deployment safeguards, and broader risk assessment -- essentially a more comprehensive, often externally-published version combining and extending model card concepts for major model releases.
16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.why_it_exists: AI models and the datasets that train them are often opaque to anyone other than their original developers -- a downstream user or integrator of a model has no easy way to know what it was actually trained on, what its known failure modes and limitations are, or what populations/use cases it was and wasn't validated for, leading to inappropriate use (deploying a model in a context it wasn't designed or tested for) or unrealistic trust. Model cards, datasheets, and system cards exist to make this critical context explicit and standardized, similar in spirit to a product's technical specification sheet or nutrition label -- giving downstream users (including an FDE evaluating whether a given model fits their specific use case) the information needed to make an informed decision about appropriate use.
16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.how_it_works:
```
Model card structure (typical sections):

Model details: architecture, training data summary, version,
  license, intended use cases

Intended use: the specific use cases the model was designed and
  validated for (directly relevant to the AIA's necessity/
  proportionality assessment covered elsewhere -- is this model
  actually appropriate for our intended use case, per its own
  documentation?)

Factors affecting performance: known subgroups or conditions
  where performance may differ (connecting directly to the bias
  audit material -- a well-documented model card should disclose
  known fairness/performance gaps across demographic groups,
  saving downstream users from having to discover these
  independently)

Metrics: quantitative performance results, ideally broken down
  by relevant subgroups, not just an aggregate score

Ethical considerations and limitations: explicit disclosure of
  known risks, inappropriate use cases, and limitations

Datasheet for the training dataset (separate, complementary
document):
  Motivation and collection process: who collected this data, why,
  and how?
  Composition: what does the dataset actually contain, and what
  are its known gaps or biases (e.g. demographic representation
  imbalances)?
  Uses: what has this dataset been used for, and what uses would
  be inappropriate given its known characteristics?

System card (broader, often for major foundation model releases):
  Extends model card concepts to cover deployment-level safety
  testing, red-teaming results (connecting to the red-teaming
  material covered elsewhere), and deployment safeguards --
  essentially documenting the full system, not just the model
  artifact in isolation

Practical FDE use:
  Before selecting a third-party model for a specific use case,
  review its model card/system card explicitly for documented
  limitations relevant to your specific deployment context (e.g.
  does it disclose known performance gaps for a demographic or
  use case relevant to your application?) rather than assuming
  uniform, undocumented suitability
```
16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.use_when: Produce model cards (and datasheets for any custom training datasets) for any internally-developed AI model moving toward production, as part of the technical documentation required for model risk management and EU AI Act compliance covered elsewhere. Review third-party model providers' published model/system cards explicitly during model selection, treating documented limitations as genuine, actionable information about appropriate use boundaries rather than boilerplate to skim past.
16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.avoid_when: Don't produce an elaborate, comprehensive model card for a quick internal experiment or prototype that will never reach production -- reserve the full documentation rigor for models genuinely moving toward production deployment or external release, similar to the proportionality principle covered throughout this governance material.
16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.what_goes_wrong:
- Model card produced but not actually informed by genuine subgroup performance testing: a model card claims to disclose performance characteristics across different conditions/subgroups, but the underlying evaluation that the card's content is based on wasn't actually rigorous or comprehensive enough to support the claims being made, creating a misleadingly reassuring document. Fix: ensure model card content is genuinely grounded in the actual bias audit and evaluation work conducted (covered elsewhere), not aspirational or templated language that doesn't reflect real, rigorous testing.
- Model card limitations disclosed but ignored by a downstream team selecting the model: a model's published card clearly discloses a specific known limitation (e.g. reduced accuracy for a particular demographic group or use case), but a team evaluating the model for a new use case doesn't actually read or act on this disclosed limitation, deploying the model inappropriately despite the documentation existing. Fix: make model card review an explicit, required step in model selection processes (connecting to the build-vs-buy decision matrix material covered elsewhere), not just published documentation that downstream teams may or may not actually consult.
16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.real_example: An FDE team evaluating a third-party open-weight model for a customer service application specifically reviewed the model's published model card before committing to it, finding explicit disclosure that the model's training data had limited representation of certain non-English language patterns, with correspondingly lower documented performance on those specific languages -- since the customer's user base included a meaningful proportion of speakers of one of the specifically flagged underrepresented languages, this disclosed limitation directly informed the team's decision to conduct additional, targeted evaluation specifically for that language before deployment, rather than assuming the model's generally strong overall benchmark scores meant uniform performance across all the customer's actual user population.

16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.what_it_is: MIG (Multi-Instance GPU), time-slicing, and MPS (Multi-Process Service) are three distinct NVIDIA GPU sharing technologies that allow multiple workloads to share a single physical GPU more efficiently, directly addressing GPU cost optimization (extending the broader cloud cost optimization material covered elsewhere specifically to the GPU utilization dimension, which is often the largest cost driver for AI infrastructure). MIG (available on newer NVIDIA GPU architectures like A100/H100) partitions a single physical GPU into multiple genuinely isolated GPU instances, each with dedicated memory and compute resources -- true hardware-level isolation, suitable for running multiple independent, performance-isolated workloads. Time-slicing allows multiple processes to share a GPU by taking turns using the full GPU for short time windows, without MIG's hardware partitioning -- simpler to configure but without the same performance isolation guarantees (one workload's burst of activity can affect others' latency). MPS allows multiple processes to share a GPU concurrently (rather than time-slicing between them) with better resource utilization than time-slicing for many small/light workloads, but again without MIG's strict hardware isolation.
16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.why_it_exists: GPUs, especially high-end ones used for AI inference and training, are expensive, and many real AI inference workloads (especially smaller models, or inference requests with bursty, often-idle traffic patterns) don't actually need an entire high-end GPU's full capacity continuously -- running each such workload on its own dedicated, often underutilized GPU wastes significant compute capacity and cost. These GPU sharing technologies exist specifically to allow multiple workloads to share GPU hardware more efficiently, directly reducing the GPU infrastructure cost (the largest cost category in many AI TCO calculations covered elsewhere) for workloads that don't need a full GPU's dedicated capacity.
16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.how_it_works:
```
GPU sharing technology comparison and selection:

MIG (Multi-Instance GPU):
  Hardware-level partitioning into genuinely isolated instances
  (e.g. splitting an A100 80GB GPU into 7 smaller MIG instances,
  each with dedicated memory and compute slice)
  Use case: multiple genuinely independent workloads needing
  guaranteed, predictable performance isolation from each other
  -- e.g. serving several different small models in production
  where one model's traffic spike shouldn't affect another
  model's latency
  Trade-off: each MIG instance has a fixed, smaller capacity --
  not suitable for workloads needing to occasionally burst beyond
  their partition's fixed allocation

Time-slicing:
  Multiple processes take turns using the full GPU, configured at
  the Kubernetes/scheduler level (e.g. via the NVIDIA Kubernetes
  device plugin's time-slicing configuration)
  Use case: workloads that are individually bursty but rarely
  need the full GPU simultaneously -- e.g. several development/
  testing workloads sharing a GPU where occasional latency
  variability is acceptable
  Trade-off: no performance isolation -- one workload's heavy
  usage can cause latency spikes for others sharing the same GPU

MPS (Multi-Process Service):
  Allows concurrent (not just time-sliced) execution of multiple
  processes' GPU kernels, generally providing better aggregate
  throughput than time-slicing for many small, light workloads
  that don't individually saturate the GPU
  Use case: many small inference requests (e.g. from many
  different lightweight model serving instances) that benefit
  from concurrent execution rather than strict time-division

Selection guidance for AI inference cost optimization:
  Production workloads requiring guaranteed performance isolation
  across multiple models/tenants: MIG
  Development/testing environments, or many small, latency-
  tolerant workloads: time-slicing or MPS, depending on whether
  concurrent execution (MPS) or strict turn-taking (time-slicing)
  better fits the specific workload pattern
```
16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.use_when: Apply MIG specifically for production multi-tenant or multi-model GPU sharing scenarios requiring genuine performance isolation guarantees (the same isolation rigor that the resource limits material in deployment infrastructure covers more generally, here specifically at the GPU level). Use time-slicing or MPS for development/testing environments or production scenarios with many small, latency-tolerant workloads where the cost savings from higher GPU utilization outweigh the lack of strict isolation.
16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.avoid_when: Don't apply GPU sharing technologies to workloads genuinely requiring dedicated, maximum GPU performance (large model training runs, latency-critical production inference at scale) where sharing overhead or resource contention risk would meaningfully degrade the workload's actual performance requirements -- dedicated, unshared GPU allocation remains appropriate for these cases despite the higher cost.
16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.what_goes_wrong:
- Time-slicing applied to a latency-sensitive production workload, causing unacceptable latency variability: a team applies time-slicing to share a GPU across multiple production inference services to save cost, discovering that the lack of performance isolation causes unpredictable latency spikes whenever one service experiences a traffic burst, violating the latency SLA of the other co-located services. Fix: use MIG (genuine hardware isolation) rather than time-slicing for any production workload with a hard latency SLA that must not be affected by co-located workloads' activity, even though MIG's fixed partition sizing is less flexible than time-slicing's full-GPU access.
- MIG partition sizing mismatched to actual workload requirements: a team partitions a GPU into MIG instances sized based on initial assumptions, discovering later that a specific model actually needs more memory/compute than its assigned MIG partition provides, requiring either repartitioning (disruptive) or moving that workload to a larger, dedicated allocation. Fix: profile actual workload resource requirements (memory and compute utilization under realistic load) before finalizing MIG partition sizing, rather than guessing at appropriate partition sizes without empirical validation.
16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.real_example: A company serving multiple distinct, smaller fine-tuned models for different customer segments initially ran each model on its own dedicated GPU, resulting in significant underutilization since individual customer segments' traffic volume didn't require a full GPU's capacity each. The team migrated to MIG-based GPU partitioning, running several models as separate MIG instances on shared physical GPUs -- each model retained guaranteed, isolated compute and memory allocation (so one customer segment's traffic spike couldn't degrade another's latency), while the overall GPU fleet's utilization and corresponding infrastructure cost improved significantly compared to the previous one-model-per-dedicated-GPU approach, directly reducing the GPU cost line item in the system's overall TCO.

16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.what_it_is: This note extends the spot/preemptible instance cost optimization strategy (introduced at a general level in the cloud cost optimization material covered in Multi-Cloud & Hybrid Deployment) with specific application to batch AI inference workloads -- running large-scale, non-real-time model inference jobs (e.g. nightly scoring of an entire customer database, bulk document processing, batch embedding generation for a large document corpus) on deeply-discounted spot/preemptible compute instances, since batch inference workloads are generally well-suited to tolerating occasional preemption (unlike real-time, user-facing inference) given their inherent flexibility around exact completion timing and their ability to checkpoint and resume processing.
16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.why_it_exists: Batch inference workloads share key characteristics that make them ideal candidates for spot instance cost savings (the same 60-90% discount potential covered in the general cloud cost optimization material): they're fault-tolerant by nature (a preempted batch job can simply resume processing the remaining unprocessed items), they're not latency-sensitive in the way real-time, user-facing inference is, and they often represent a significant, ongoing cost category (large-scale periodic batch inference can consume substantial compute resources) where the spot instance discount translates into meaningful absolute cost savings.
16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.how_it_works:
```python
# Batch inference job designed for spot instance resilience
# (conceptual pattern, using a job queue for resumability)

import boto3
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class BatchJob:
    item_id: str
    status: str  # pending, processing, completed, failed

def process_batch_inference_queue(queue_table, model_endpoint):
    '''Process items from a queue, resilient to spot preemption'''
    while True:
        # Claim the next pending item (atomic operation, so a
        # preempted worker's claimed-but-incomplete items can be
        # reclaimed by another worker after a timeout)
        item = claim_next_pending_item(queue_table, claim_timeout_minutes=10)
        if item is None:
            break  # queue empty, job complete

        try:
            result = model_endpoint.predict(item.data)
            mark_completed(queue_table, item.item_id, result)
        except Exception as e:
            mark_failed_for_retry(queue_table, item.item_id, str(e))

# Spot instance preemption handling:
# Cloud providers typically give a short warning (e.g. AWS gives
# a 2-minute warning via the instance metadata service) before
# reclaiming a spot instance -- a well-designed batch worker
# listens for this signal and gracefully stops claiming new work,
# allowing in-progress items to either complete or be cleanly
# released back to the queue for another worker to pick up

import requests
def check_spot_termination_warning() -> bool:
    try:
        response = requests.get(
            'http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/spot/termination-time',
            timeout=1
        )
        return response.status_code == 200  # termination notice present
    except requests.exceptions.RequestException:
        return False  # no warning, or not running on spot

# Main loop checks for termination warning between items,
# stopping gracefully rather than being abruptly killed mid-item
while not check_spot_termination_warning():
    process_next_item()
```
16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.use_when: Use spot/preemptible instances as the default compute choice for batch inference workloads -- nightly scoring jobs, bulk document processing, periodic embedding generation -- whenever the job is designed (or can be redesigned) with queue-based, resumable processing that gracefully handles preemption, capturing the substantial cost savings these workloads are generally well-suited for.
16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.avoid_when: Don't use spot instances for batch jobs with a hard, inflexible completion deadline where the unpredictability of spot capacity availability (a spot instance request can occasionally be unfulfillable entirely, not just preempted after starting) creates unacceptable schedule risk -- for time-critical batch jobs, on-demand or reserved capacity (covered in the broader cost optimization material) may be more appropriate despite the higher cost, trading cost savings for schedule reliability.
16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.what_goes_wrong:
- Batch job lacks proper resumability design, causing significant rework on preemption: a batch inference job processes items sequentially without a queue-based, item-level resumability design, meaning a preemption partway through requires restarting the entire job from the beginning rather than just resuming the remaining unprocessed items. Fix: design batch inference jobs around a resumable queue or checkpoint pattern from the start (as shown in the example above), treating spot-instance resilience as a core design requirement, not an afterthought.
- Spot capacity unavailability causes unexpected batch job delays: during periods of high regional demand for a specific instance type, spot capacity can become entirely unavailable (not just preempted, but simply unfulfillable for new requests), and a batch job relying entirely on spot instances without any fallback can experience unexpected delays beyond what preemption-resilience alone addresses. Fix: implement a fallback to on-demand instances if spot capacity remains unavailable beyond an acceptable threshold, ensuring the batch job still completes within an acceptable timeframe even during spot capacity shortages, accepting the higher on-demand cost only as a fallback rather than the default.
16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.real_example: An e-commerce company's nightly batch job re-scoring product recommendation embeddings for their entire 5-million-item catalog was redesigned from a sequential, all-or-nothing processing script to a queue-based architecture (using a database table tracking per-item processing status) specifically to run reliably on spot GPU instances -- when spot instances were occasionally preempted during the multi-hour nightly run, the job simply resumed processing the remaining unclaimed queue items on newly-provisioned spot capacity, completing the full catalog re-scoring well within the required overnight window at roughly 70% lower compute cost than the previous on-demand instance approach had cost for the same workload.

16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.what_it_is: FinOps (Financial Operations) for AI applies the broader FinOps discipline (a cross-functional practice combining finance, engineering, and business teams to manage and optimize cloud/infrastructure spend) specifically to AI workload costs, with showback and chargeback as the two primary cost-allocation models: Showback provides visibility into which team/project/cost-center is responsible for which portion of AI infrastructure spend (e.g. LLM API costs, GPU compute) without actually billing that cost back to their budget -- purely informational, building cost awareness. Chargeback goes further, actually allocating and billing the AI infrastructure costs to the specific consuming team's budget, creating direct financial accountability and incentive for that team to optimize their own AI usage costs, similar to how internal IT chargeback models have long operated for traditional infrastructure.
16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.why_it_exists: AI costs (particularly LLM API spend, which scales directly and sometimes unpredictably with usage, unlike more fixed traditional infrastructure costs) can grow rapidly and become difficult to control without clear visibility into which specific teams or use cases are driving the spend -- without showback or chargeback, AI costs often land in a shared, centrally-managed budget with no direct connection to the teams actually generating the usage, removing any natural incentive for individual teams to optimize their own AI usage efficiency (the model tiering, caching, and other cost optimization techniques covered earlier in this phase). FinOps practices exist specifically to create this cost visibility and, with chargeback, genuine financial accountability, driving more responsible, cost-conscious AI usage behavior across the organization.

```
   Actual budget transfer/billing of AI costs to the consuming

   Creates direct financial incentive for teams to apply the cost

4. Governance integration:
```

16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.use_when: Implement showback as a foundational first step for any organization with growing, multi-team AI usage where cost visibility doesn't currently exist -- this is generally lower-friction to introduce than full chargeback and builds the cultural and technical foundation (cost attribution infrastructure) that chargeback later depends on. Move to full chargeback once the organization has mature cost attribution and wants to create genuine financial accountability and optimization incentive at the team level.
16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.avoid_when: Don't implement chargeback prematurely, before cost attribution infrastructure is mature and accurate enough to fairly and reliably allocate costs -- inaccurate or unfair chargeback (e.g. misattributing shared infrastructure costs, or billing a team for usage they didn't actually generate) creates organizational friction and distrust that can undermine the broader FinOps initiative's credibility.
16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.what_goes_wrong:
- Cost attribution tagging incomplete or inconsistently applied, producing unreliable showback/chargeback data: if not every AI service call or infrastructure resource is consistently tagged with the correct consuming team, showback/chargeback reports show significant 'unattributed' cost or, worse, incorrectly attribute costs to the wrong team, undermining trust in the entire cost allocation system. Fix: build tagging/attribution enforcement into the platform layer itself (e.g. requiring team identification as a mandatory parameter for any AI Gateway call, similar to the API design discipline covered elsewhere) rather than relying on voluntary, inconsistent tagging discipline from individual engineers.
- Chargeback creates perverse incentives to avoid using AI capabilities that would genuinely benefit the business: if chargeback is implemented without adequate context (a team's budget bears the full AI cost without a corresponding accounting of the value/savings that AI usage generates for the business), teams may become overly conservative about adopting beneficial AI capabilities purely to protect their own budget, even when the broader business case (covered in the ROI/TCO material) clearly favors the investment. Fix: pair chargeback with visibility into the value side of the equation as well (connecting to the ROI modeling material), helping teams and finance leadership see the full cost-benefit picture, not just the cost side in isolation.

16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.what_it_is: CodeCarbon is an open-source Python library for estimating and tracking the carbon emissions associated with running computational workloads -- including AI model training and inference -- by monitoring actual hardware power consumption (CPU, GPU, RAM usage) during a code execution and combining this with the carbon intensity of the electricity grid powering that specific compute (which varies significantly by region/data center location based on the local energy mix), producing an estimated CO2 emissions figure for a given training run or inference workload. This represents the emerging practice of explicitly measuring and reporting AI's environmental footprint, as growing AI compute demand (particularly large model training and high-volume inference) has drawn increasing attention to AI's energy consumption and associated carbon emissions.
16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.why_it_exists: AI model training, particularly for large models, can consume substantial energy, and as organizations increasingly face both voluntary sustainability commitments and, in some jurisdictions, emerging regulatory reporting requirements around environmental impact, there's growing need to actually measure (rather than just estimate informally or ignore) the carbon footprint of AI workloads specifically -- CodeCarbon and similar tools exist to make this measurement practical and integrated directly into the development workflow, rather than requiring a separate, disconnected sustainability reporting exercise.

```python
# Track cumulative emissions across an organization's AI
```

16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.use_when: Integrate carbon footprint tracking into AI development workflows for organizations with explicit sustainability commitments or emerging environmental reporting requirements, particularly for large-scale model training workloads where the cumulative emissions impact is most significant -- this is increasingly relevant as part of a comprehensive AI governance program covering not just risk/fairness/compliance (the other governance dimensions covered in this phase) but also environmental impact.
16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.avoid_when: Don't treat carbon footprint measurement as the primary lens for every AI infrastructure decision when more directly consequential factors (cost, latency, accuracy, the broader TCO and risk considerations covered throughout this material) should generally take priority -- carbon tracking is a valuable, increasingly important consideration, but typically a complementary factor alongside, not a replacement for, the broader cost/performance/governance decision framework covered elsewhere.
16|🟡 T2 AI Governance & TCO|AI Governanc.what_goes_wrong:
- Carbon estimation accuracy limitations not understood or disclosed: CodeCarbon and similar tools necessarily rely on estimation models (especially for hardware without direct power monitoring interfaces, or for regional grid carbon intensity data that may be based on averages rather than real-time actual generation mix), and presenting these estimates with false precision (as if they were exact measurements) can create a misleading sense of accuracy. Fix: present carbon footprint estimates with appropriate caveats about the underlying estimation methodology's limitations, similar to how cost projections should be presented with sensitivity analysis (covered in the Project Scoping material) rather than false single-point precision.
- Carbon tracking implemented but never actually used to inform any decisions: a team integrates CodeCarbon tracking into their training pipelines, generating emissions data that's logged but never actually reviewed or used to inform infrastructure location choices, model architecture decisions, or sustainability reporting -- collecting the data without acting on it provides limited actual value. Fix: explicitly connect carbon footprint data to actual decision points (e.g. comparing emissions across candidate training configurations before choosing one, or feeding aggregate data into actual sustainability reporting processes) rather than treating tracking as an end in itself.
